seemlyhed.c: Seemlyhed Seem"ly*hed (sēm"ly̆*hĕd), n. [See -hood.] Comely or decent appearance. [Obs.] Rom. of R. Spenser.

sipe.c: Sipe Seep { Seep (?), or Sipe (?), } v. i. [AS. sīpan to distill.] To run or soak through fine pores and interstices; to ooze. [Scot. & U. S.]
Sipe Sipe (sīp), v. i. See Seep. [Scot. & U.S.]

sipage.c: Sipage Seepage { Seep"age (?), or Sip"age }, n. Water that seeped or oozed through a porous soil. [Scot. & U. S.]

seepage.c: Seepage Seep"age, n. 1. The act or process of seeping; percolation.

sipy.c: Sipy Seepy { Seep"y (?), or Sip"y }, a. Oozy; -- applied to land under cultivation that is not well drained.

seer.c: Seer Seer (sēr), a. Sore; painful. [Prov. Eng.] Ray.
Seer Se"er (sē"ẽr), n. One who sees. Addison.
Seer Seer (sēr), n. [From See.] A person who foresees events; a prophet. Milton.

seeress.c: Seeress Seer"ess, n. A female seer; a prophetess.

seerfish.c: Seerfish Seer"fish` (sēr"fĭsh), n. (Zool.) A scombroid food fish of Madeira (Cybium Commersonii).

seerhand.c: Seerhand Seer"hand (?), n. [Etymol. uncertain.] A kind of muslin of a texture between nainsook and mull.

seership.c: Seership Seer"ship, n. The office or quality of a seer.

seersucker.c: Seersucker Seer"suck`er (?), n. A light fabric, originally made in the East Indies, of silk and linen, usually having alternating stripes, and a slightly craped or puckered surface; also, a cotton fabric of similar appearance.

seerwood.c: Seerwood Seer"wood` (?), n. [See Sear.] Dry wood. [Written also searwood.] [Obs.] Dryden.

seesaw.c: Seesaw See"saw` (?), n. [Probably a reduplication of saw, to express the alternate motion to and fro, as in the act of sawing.] 1. A play among children in which they are seated upon the opposite ends of a plank which is balanced in the middle, and move alternately up and down.
Seesaw See"saw`, v. i. [imp. & p. p. Seesawad (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Seesawing.] To move with a reciprocating motion; to move backward and forward, or upward and downward.
Seesaw See"saw`, v. t. To cause to move backward and forward in seesaw fashion.
Seesaw See"saw`, a. Moving up and down, or to and fro; having a reciprocating motion.

seet.c: Seet Seet (?), obs. imp. of Sit. Sate; sat. Chaucer.

seeth.c: Seeth Seeth (?), obs. imp. of Seethe. Chaucer.

seethe.c: Seethe Seethe (?), v. t. [imp. Seethed (?) (Sod (?), obs.); p. p. Seethed, Sodden (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Seething.] [OE. sethen, AS. seó?an; akin to D. sieden, OHG. siodan, G. sieden, Icel. sj??a, Sw. sjuda, Dan. syde, Goth. saubs a burnt offering. Cf. Sod, n., Sodden, Suds.] To decoct or prepare for food in hot liquid; to boil; as, to seethe flesh. [Written also seeth.]
Seethe Seethe, v. i. To be a state of ebullition or violent commotion; to be hot; to boil. 1 Sam. ii. 13.

seether.c: Seether Seeth"er (?), n. A pot for boiling things; a boiler.

seg.c: Seg Seg, n. [Probably from the root of L. secare to cut.] A castrated bull. [Prov. Eng. & Scot.] Halliwell.

seggar.c: Seggar Seg"gar (?), n. [Prov. E. saggard a seggar, seggard a sort of riding surtout, contr. fr. safeguard.] A case or holder made of fire clay, in which fine pottery is inclosed while baking in the kin. [Written also saggar, sagger, and segger.] Ure.

segge.c: Segge Segge (?), n. (Zool.) The hedge sparrow. [Prov. Eng.] Halliwell.

segment.c: Segment Seg"ment (?), n. [L. segmentum, fr. secare to cut, cut off: cf. F. segment. See Saw a cutting instrument.] 1. One of the parts into which any body naturally separates or is divided; a part divided or cut off; a section; a portion; as, a segment of an orange; a segment of a compound or divided leaf.
Segment Seg"ment (?), v. i. (Biol.) To divide or separate into parts in growth; to undergo segmentation, or cleavage, as in the segmentation of the ovum.

segmental.c: Segmental Seg*men"tal (?), a. 1. Relating to, or being, a segment.

segmentation.c: Segmentation Seg`men*ta"tion (?), n. The act or process of dividing into segments; specifically (Biol.), a self-division into segments as a result of growth; cell cleavage; cell multiplication; endogenous cell formation.

segmented.c: Segmented Seg"ment*ed (?), a. Divided into segments or joints; articulated.

segnity.c: Segnity Segnitude { Seg"ni*tude (?), Seg"ni*ty (?), } n. [L. segnitas, fr. segnis slow, sluggish.] Sluggishness; dullness; inactivity. [Obs.]

segno.c: Segno ‖Se"gno (?), n. [It. See Sign.] (Mus.) A sign. See Al segno, and Dal segno.

sego.c: Sego Se"go (?), n. (Bot.) A liliaceous plant (Calochortus Nuttallii) of Western North America, and its edible bulb; -- so called by the Ute Indians and the Mormons.

segregate.c: Segregate Seg"re*gate (?), a. [L. segregatus, p. p. of segregare to separate; pref. se- aside + grex, gregis, a flock or herd. See Gregarious.] 1. Separate; select.
Segregate Seg"re*gate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Segregated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Segregating.] To separate from others; to set apart.
Segregate Seg"re*gate, v. i. (Geol.) To separate from a mass, and collect together about centers or along lines of fracture, as in the process of crystallization or solidification.

segregation.c: Segregation Seg`re*ga"tion (?), n. [L. segregatio: cf. F. ségrégation.] 1. The act of segregating, or the state of being segregated; separation from others; a parting.

seiches.c: Seiches ‖Seiches (?), n. pl. [F.] (Geol.) Local oscillations in level observed in the case of some lakes, as Lake Geneva.

seid.c: Seid Seid (?), n. [Ar seyid prince.] A descendant of Mohammed through his daughter Fatima and nephew Ali.

seidlitz.c: Seidlitz Seid"litz (?), a. Of or pertaining to Seidlitz, a village in Bohemia. [Written also Sedlitz.]

seigh.c: Seigh Seigh (sā), obs. imp. sing. of See. Saw. Chaucer.

seigneurial.c: Seigneurial Seign*eu"ri*al (sēn*ū"rĭ*ail), a. [F., fr. seigneur. See Seignior.] 1. Of or pertaining to the lord of a manor; manorial. Sir W. Temple.

seignior.c: Seignior Seign"ior (?), n. [OF. seignor, F. seigneur, cf. It. signore, Sp. señor from an objective case of L. senier elder. See Senior.] 1. A lord; the lord of a manor.

seigniorage.c: Seigniorage Seign"ior*age (?), n. [F. seigneuriage, OF. seignorage.] 1. Something claimed or taken by virtue of sovereign prerogative; specifically, a charge or toll deducted from bullion brought to a mint to be coined; the difference between the cost of a mass of bullion and the value as money of the pieces coined from it.

seignioral.c: Seignioral Seign"ior*al (?), a. Of or pertaining to a seignior; seigneurial. “Kingly or seignioral patronage.” Burke.

seignioralty.c: Seignioralty Seign"ior*al*ty (?), n. The territory or authority of a seignior, or lord. Milman.

seigniorize.c: Seigniorize Seign"ior*ize (?), v. t. To lord it over. [Obs.]

seigniory.c: Seigniory Seign"ior*y (?), n.; pl. -ies (#). [OE. seignorie, OF. seigneurie, F. seigneurie; cf. It. signoria.] 1. The power or authority of a lord; dominion.

seine.c: Seine Seine (?), n. [F. seine, or AS. segene, b?th fr. L. sagena, Gr.????.] (Fishing.) A large net, one edge of which is provided with sinkers, and the other with floats. It hangs vertically in the water, and when its ends are brought together or drawn ashore incloses the fish.

seiner.c: Seiner Sein"er (?), n. One who fishes with a seine.

seining.c: Seining Sein"ing, n. Fishing with a seine.

seint.c: Seint Seint (?), n. [See Cincture.] A girdle. [Obs.] “Girt with a seint of silk.” Chaucer.

seirospore.c: Seirospore Sei"ro*spore (?), n. [Gr.??? a cord + E. spore.] (Bot.) One of several spores arranged in a chain as in certain algae of the genus Callithamnion.

seise.c: Seise Seise (?), v. t. See Seize. Spenser.

seismal.c: Seismal Seismic { Seis"mic (?), Seis"mal (?), } a. [Gr. seismo`s an earthquake, from sei`ein to shake.] Of or pertaining to an earthquake; caused by an earthquake.

seismogram.c: Seismogram Seis"mo*gram (?), n. [Gr.? earthquake + -gram.] (Physics) The trace or record of an earth tremor, made by means of a seismograph.

seismograph.c: Seismograph Seis"mo*graph (?), n. [Gr.??? an earthquake + -graph.] (Physics) An apparatus for registering the shocks and undulatory motions of earthquakes.

seismographic.c: Seismographic Seis`mo*graph"ic (?), a. Of or pertaining to a seismograph; indicated by a seismograph.

seismography.c: Seismography Seis*mog"ra*phy (?), n. 1. A writing about, or a description of, earthquakes.

seismological.c: Seismological Seis`mo*log"ic*al (?), a. Of or pertaining to seismology. -- Seis`mo*log"ic*al*ly, adv.

seismology.c: Seismology Seis*mol"o*gy (?), n. [Gr.??? an earthquake + -logy.] The science of earthquakes.

seismometer.c: Seismometer Seis*mom"e*ter (?), n. [Gr.??? an earthquake + -meter.] (Physics) An instrument for measuring the direction, duration, and force of earthquakes and like concussions.

seismometric.c: Seismometric Seis`mo*met"ric (?), a. Of or pertaining to seismometry, or seismometer; as, seismometric instruments; seismometric measurements.

seismometry.c: Seismometry Seis*mom"e*try (?), n. The mensuration of such phenomena of earthquakes as can be expressed in numbers, or by their relation to the coordinates of space.

seismoscope.c: Seismoscope Seis"mo*scope (?), n. [Gr.??? an earthquake + -scope.] (Physics) A seismometer.

seity.c: Seity Se"i*ty (?), n. [L. se one's self.] Something peculiar to one's self. [R.] Tatler.

seizable.c: Seizable Seiz"a*ble (?), a. That may be seized.

seize.c: Seize Seize (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Seized (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Seizing.] [OE. seisen, saisen, OF. seisir, saisir, F. saisir, of Teutonic origin, and akin to E. set. The meaning is properly, to set, put, place, hence, to put in possession of. See Set, v. t.] 1. To fall or rush upon suddenly and lay hold of; to gripe or grasp suddenly; to reach and grasp.

seizer.c: Seizer Seiz"er (?), n. One who, or that which, seizes.

seizin.c: Seizin Sei"zin (?), n. [F. saisine. See Seize.] 1. (Law) Possession; possession of an estate of froehold. It may be either in deed or in law; the former when there is actual possession, the latter when there is a right to such possession by construction of law. In some of the United States seizin means merely ownership. Burrill.

seizing.c: Seizing Seiz"ing (?), n. 1. The act of taking or grasping suddenly.

seizor.c: Seizor Sei"zor (?), n. (Law) One who seizes, or takes possession.

seizure.c: Seizure Sei"zure (?), n. 1. The act of seizing, or the state of being seized; sudden and violent grasp or gripe; a taking into possession; as, the seizure of a thief, a property, a throne, etc.

sejeant.c: Sejeant Sejant { Se"jant, Se"jeant } (?), a. [F. séant, p. pr. of seoir to sit, L. sedere.] (Her.) Sitting, as a lion or other beast.

sejein.c: Sejein Se*jein" (?), v. t. [L. sejungere; pref. se- aside + jungere to join. See Join.] To separate. [Obs.]

sejunction.c: Sejunction Se*junc"tion (?), n. [L. sejunctio. See Sejoin.] The act of disjoining, or the state of being disjoined. [Obs.] Bp. Pearson.

sejungible.c: Sejungible Se*jun"gi*ble (?), a. [See Sejoin.] Capable of being disjoined. [Obs.] Bp. Pearson.

seke.c: Seke Seke (?), v. t. & i. To seek. [Obs.] Chaucer.

sekes.c: Sekes ‖Se"kes (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr.??? a pen, a sacred inclosure, a shrine.] (Arch.) A place in a pagan temple in which the images of the deities were inclosed.

selachian.c: Selachian Se*la"chi*an (?), n. (Zool.) One of the Selachii. See Illustration in Appendix.

selachii.c: Selachii ‖Se*la"chi*i (?), n. pl. [NL., fr. Gr.??? a fish having cartilages instead of bones.] (Zool.) An order of elasmobranchs including the sharks and rays; the Plagiostomi. Called also Selacha, Selache, and Selachoidei.

selachoidei.c: Selachoidei ‖Sel`a*choi"de*i (?), n. pl. [NL. See Selachii, and -oid.] (Zool.) Same as Selachii.

selachostomi.c: Selachostomi ‖Sel`a*chos"to*mi (?), n. pl. [NL. See Selachii, and Stoma.] (Zool.) A division of ganoid fishes which includes the paddlefish, in which the mouth is armed with small teeth.

selaginella.c: Selaginella ‖Sel`a*gi*nel"la (?), n. [NL., fr. L. selago, -inis, a kind of plant.] (Bot.) A genus of cryptogamous plants resembling Lycopodia, but producing two kinds of spores; also, any plant of this genus. Many species are cultivated in conservatories.

selah.c: Selah Se"lah (?), n. [Heb. selāh.] (Script.) A word of doubtful meaning, occuring frequently in the Psalms; by some, supposed to signify silence or a pause in the musical performance of the song.

selcouth.c: Selcouth Sel"couth (sĕl"kōoth), a. [AS. selcūð, seldcūð; seld rare + cūð known. See Uncouth.] Rarely known; unusual; strange. [Obs.]

seld.c: Seld Seld (sĕld), a. [See Seldom.] Rare; uncommon; unusual. [Obs.] Chaucer. Spenser.

seldom.c: Seldom Sel"dom (sĕl"dŭm), adv. [Usually, Compar. More seldom (mōr" sĕl"dŭm); superl. Most seldom (mōst" sĕl"dŭm); but sometimes also, Seldomer (sĕl"dŭm*ẽr), Seldomest.] [AS. seldan, seldon, seldum, fr. seld rare; akin to OFries. sielden, D. zelden, G. selten, OHG. seltan, Icel. sjaldan, Dan. sielden, Sw. sällan, Goth. sildaleiks marvelous.] Rarely; not often; not frequently.
Seldom Sel"dom (?), a. Rare; infrequent. [Archaic.] “A suppressed and seldom anger.” Jer. Taylor.

seldseen.c: Seldseen Seld"seen` (?), a. [AS. seldsiene.] Seldom seen. [Obs.] Drayton.

seldshewn.c: Seldshewn Seld"shewn` (?), a. [Seld + shown.] Rarely shown or exhibited. [Obs.] Shak.

select.c: Select Se*lect" (?), a. [L. selectus, p. p. of seligere to select; pref. se- aside + levere to gather. See Legend.] Taken from a number by preferance; picked out as more valuable or exellent than others; of special value or exellence; nicely chosen; selected; choice.

Select Se*lect", v. t. [imp. & p. p. Selected; p. pr. & vb. n. Selecting.] To choose and take from a number; to take by preference from among others; to pick out; to cull; as, to select the best authors for perusal. “One peculiar nation to select.” Milton.

selectedly.c: Selectedly Se*lect"ed*ly, adv. With care and selection. [R.]

selection.c: Selection Se*lec"tion (?), n. [L. selectio: cf. F. sélection.]. The act of selecting, or the state of being selected; choice, by preference.

selective.c: Selective Se*lect"ive (?), a. Selecting; tending to select.

selectman.c: Selectman Se*lect"man (?), n.; pl. Selectmen (?). One of a board of town officers chosen annually in the New England States to transact the general public business of the town, and have a kind of executive authority. The number is usually from three to seven in each town.

selectness.c: Selectness Se*lect"ness, n. The quality or state of being select.

selenate.c: Selenate Sel"e*nate (?), n. (Chem.) A salt of selenic acid; -- formerly called also seleniate.

selenhydric.c: Selenhydric Sel`en*hy"dric (?), a. (Chem.) Of, pertaining to, or designating, hydrogen selenide, H2Se, regarded as an acid analogous to sulphydric acid.

selenic.c: Selenic Se*len"ic (?), a. [Cf. F. sélénique.] (Chem.) Of or pertaining to selenium; derived from, or containing, selenium; specifically, designating those compounds in which the element has a higher valence as contrasted with selenious compounds.

selenide.c: Selenide Sel"e*nide (?), n. (Chem.) A binary compound of selenium, or a compound regarded as binary; as, ethyl selenide.

seleniferous.c: Seleniferous Sel`e*nif"er*ous (?), a. [Selenium + -ferous. ] Containing, or impregnated with, selenium; as, seleniferous pyrites.

selenio.c: Selenio- Se*le"ni*o- (?). (Chem.) A combining form (also used adjectively) denoting the presence of selenium or its compounds; as, selenio-phosphate, a phosphate having selenium in place of all, or a part, of the oxygen.

selenious.c: Selenious Se*le"ni*ous (?), a. [Cf. F. sélénieux.] (Chem.) Of, pertaining to, or containing, selenium; specifically, designating those compounds in which the element has a lower valence as contrasted with selenic compounds.

selenite.c: Selenite Sel"e*nite (?), n. (Chem.) A salt of selenious acid.

Selenite Sel"e*nite, n. [L. selenites, Gr.???? (sc.???), from selh`nh the moon. So called from a fancied resemblance in luster or appearance to the moon.] (Min.) A variety of gypsum, occuring in transparent crystals or crystalline masses.

selenitical.c: Selenitical Selenitic { Sel`e*nit"ic (?), Sel`e*nit"ic*al (?), } a. (Min.) Of or pertaining to selenite; resembling or containing selenite.

selenium.c: Selenium Se*le"ni*um (?), n. [NL., from Gr. selh`nh the moon. So called because of its chemical analogy to tellurium (from L. tellus the earth), being, as it were, a companion to it.] (Chem.) A nonmetallic element of the sulphur group of atomic number 34, analogous to sulphur in its compounds. It is found in small quantities with sulphur and some sulphur ores, and obtained in the free state as a dark reddish powder or crystalline mass, or as a dark metallic-looking substance. It exhibits under the action of light a remarkable variation in electric conductivity, and is used in certain electric apparatus. Symbol Se. Atomic weight 78.96.

seleniureted.c: Seleniureted Sel`e*ni"u*ret`ed (?), a. (Chem.) Combined with selenium as in a selenide; as, seleniureted hydrogen. [Written also seleniuretted.] [Obsoles.]

selenocentric.c: Selenocentric Se*le`no*cen"tric (?), a. [Gr. selh`nh the moon + E. centric.] (Astron.) As seen or estimated from the center of the moon; with the moon central.

selenograph.c: Selenograph Se*le"no*graph (?), n. A picture or delineation of the moon's surface, or of any part of it.

selenographer.c: Selenographer Sel`e*nog"ra*pher (?), n. One skilled in selenography. Wright.

selenographical.c: Selenographical Selenographic { Sel`e*no*graph"ic (?), Sel`e*no*graph"i*cal (?), } a. [Cf. F. sélénographique.] Of or pertaining to selenography.

selenography.c: Selenography Sel`e*nog"ra*phy (?), n. [Gr. selh`nh the moon + -graphy.] The science that treats of the physical features of the moon; -- corresponding to physical geography in respect to the earth. “Accurate selenography, or description of the moon.” Sir T. Browne.

selenology.c: Selenology Sel`e*nol"o*gy, n. [Gr. selh`nh the moonn + -logy.] That branch of astronomy which treats of the moon. -- Sel`e*no*log"i*cal (#), a.

selenonium.c: Selenonium Sel`e*no"ni*um (?), n. [Selenium + sulphonium.] (Chem.) A hypothetical radical of selenium, analogous to sulphonium. [R.]

self.c: Self Self (sĕlf), a. [AS. self, seolf, sylf; akin to OS. self, OFries. self, D. zelf, G. selb, selber, selbst, Dan. selv. Sw. sjelf, Icel. sjālfr, Goth. silba. Cf. Selvage.] 1. Same; particular; very; identical. [Obs., except in the compound selfsame.] “On these self hills.” Sir. W. Raleigh.

Self Self, n.; pl. Selves (?). 1. The individual as the object of his own reflective consciousness; the man viewed by his own cognition as the subject of all his mental phenomena, the agent in his own activities, the subject of his own feelings, and the possessor of capacities and character; a person as a distinct individual; a being regarded as having personality. “Those who liked their real selves.” Addison.

selfabased.c: Self-abased Self`-a*based" (?), a. Humbled by consciousness of inferiority, unworthiness, guilt, or shame.

selfabasement.c: Self-abasement Self`-a*base"ment (?), n. 1. Degradation of one's self by one's own act.

Self-seeking Self"-seek`ing, n. The act or habit of seeking one's own interest or happiness; selfishness.

selfstarter.c: Self-starter Self`-start"er, n. A mechanism (usually one operated by electricity, compressed air, a spring, or an explosive gas), attached to an internal-combustion engine, as on an automobile, and used as a means of starting the engine without cranking it by hand; -- called also a starter.

selfsufficiency.c: Self-sufficiency Self`-suf*fi"cien*cy (?), n. The quality or state of being self-sufficient.

selfsufficient.c: Self-sufficient Self`-suf*fi"cient (?), a. 1. Sufficient for one's self without external aid or cooperation.

selfsufficing.c: Self-sufficing Self`-suf*fi"cing (?), a. Sufficing for one's self or for itself, without needing external aid; self-sufficient. -- Self`-suf*fi"cing*ness, n. J. C. Shairp.

selfsuspended.c: Self-suspended Self`-sus*pend"ed (?), a. Suspended by one's self or by itself; balanced. Southey.

selfsuspicious.c: Self-suspicious Self`-sus*pi"cious (?), a. Suspicious or distrustful of one's self. Baxter.

selftaught.c: Self-taught Self"-taught` (?), a. Taught by one's own efforts.

selftormentor.c: Self-tormentor Self`-tor*ment"or (?), n. One who torments himself.

selftorture.c: Self-torture Self`-tor"ture (?), n. The act of inflicting pain on one's self; pain inflicted on one's self.

selftrust.c: Self-trust Self"-trust`, n. Faith in one's self; self-reliance.

selfuned.c: Self-uned Self`-uned" (?), a. [E. self + L. unus one.] One with itself; separate from others. [Obs.] Sylvester.

selfview.c: Self-view Self"-view` (?), n. A view of one's self; specifically, carefulness or regard for one's own interests.

selfwill.c: Self-will Self`-will" (?), n. [AS. selfwill.] One's own will, esp. when opposed to that of others; obstinacy.

selfwilled.c: Self-willed Self`-willed" (?), a. Governed by one's own will; not yielding to the wishes of others; obstinate.

selfwilledness.c: Self-willedness Self`-willed"ness, n. Obstinacy. Sir W. Scott.

selfworship.c: Self-worship Self"-wor`ship (?), n. The idolizing of one's self; immoderate self-conceit.

selfwrong.c: Self-wrong Self"-wrong` (?), n. Wrong done by a person to himself. Shak.

selion.c: Selion Sel"ion (?), n. [OF. seillon a measure of land, F. sillon a ridge, furrow, LL. selio a measure of land.] A short piece of land in arable ridges and furrows, of uncertain quantity; also, a ridge of land lying between two furrows. [Obs. or Prov. Eng.]

seljukian.c: Seljukian Sel*juk"i*an (?), a. Of or pertaining to Seljuk, a Tartar chief who embraced Mohammedanism, and began the subjection of Western Asia to that faith and rule; of or pertaining to the dynasty founded by him, or the empire maintained by his descendants from the 10th to the 13th century. J. H. Newman.

seljuckian.c: Seljuckian Sel*juck"i*an, n. A member of the family of Seljuk; an adherent of that family, or subject of its government; (pl.) the dynasty of Turkish sultans sprung from Seljuk.

sell.c: Sell Sell (sĕl), n. Self. [Obs. or Scot.] B. Jonson.
Sell Sell (sĕl), n. A cell; a house. [Obs.] Chaucer.
Sell Sell (sĕl), n. [F. selle, L. sella, akin to sedere to sit. See Sit.] 1. A saddle for a horse. [Obs.]

Sell Sell (sĕl), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Sold (sōld); p. pr. & vb. n. Selling.] [OE. sellen, sillen, AS. sellan, syllan, to give, to deliver; akin to OS. sellian, OFries. sella, OHG. sellen, Icel. selja to hand over, to sell, Sw. sälja to sell, Dan. sælge, Goth. saljan to offer a sacrifice; all from a noun akin to E. sale. Cf. Sale.] 1. To transfer to another for an equivalent; to give up for a valuable consideration; to dispose of in return for something, especially for money. It is the correlative of buy.
Sell Sell (sĕl), v. i. 1. To practice selling commodities.
Sell Sell, n. An imposition; a cheat; a hoax. [Colloq.]

sellenders.c: Sellenders Sellanders { Sel"lan*ders (?), Sel"len*ders (?), } n. pl. (Far.) See Sallenders.

seller.c: Seller Sell"er (?), n. One who sells. Chaucer.

selters.c: Selters water Sel"ters wa"ter (?). A mineral water from Sellers, in the district of Nassan, Germany, containing much free carbonic acid.

seltzer.c: Seltzer water Selt"zer wa"ter (?). See Selters water.

seltzogene.c: Seltzo-gene Selt"zo-gene (?), n. [Seltzer water + the root of Gr.??? to be born.] A gazogene.

selvedge.c: Selvedge Selvage { Sel"vage, Sel"vedge } (?), n. [Self + edge, i. e., its own proper edge; cf. OD. selfegge.] 1. The edge of cloth which is woven in such a manner as to prevent raveling.

selvedged.c: Selvedged Selvaged { Sel"vaged, Sel"vedged } (?), a. Having a selvage.

selvagee.c: Selvagee Sel`va*gee" (?), n. (Naut.) A skein or hank of rope yarns wound round with yarns or marline, -- used for stoppers, straps, etc.

semaeostomata.c: Semaeostomata ‖Se*mae`o*stom"a*ta (?), n. pl. [NL., fr. Gr.???? a military standard +???,???, mouth.] (Zool.) A division of Discophora having large free mouth lobes. It includes Aurelia, and Pelagia. Called also Semeostoma. See Illustr. under Discophora, and Medusa.

semaphore.c: Semaphore Sem"a*phore (?), n. [Gr. sh^ma a sign + fe`rein to bear: cf. F. sémaphore.] A signal telegraph; an apparatus for giving signals by the disposition of lanterns, flags, oscillating arms, etc.

semaphorical.c: Semaphorical Semaphoric { Sem`a*phor"ic (?), Sem`a*phor"ic*al (?) } a. [Cf. F. sémaphorique.] Of or pertaining to a semaphore, or semaphores; telegraphic.

semaphorically.c: Semaphorically Sem`a*phor"ic*al*ly, adv. By means of a semaphore.

semaphorist.c: Semaphorist Se*maph"o*rist (?), n. One who manages or operates a semaphore.

semasiology.c: Semasiology Se*ma`si*ol"o*gy (?), n. [Gr. shmasi`a signification + -logy.] (Philol.) The science of meanings or sense development (of words); the explanation of the development and changes of the meanings of words; -- more commonly referred to as semantics. -- Se*ma`si*o*log"ic*al (#), a.

sematic.c: Sematic Se*mat"ic (se*măt"ĭk), a. [Gr. sh^ma, sh`matos, sign, token.] Significant; ominous; serving as a warning of danger; -- applied esp. to the warning colors or forms of certain animals.

sematology.c: Sematology Sem`a*tol"o*gy (?), n. [Gr. sh^ma, sh`matos, sign + -logy.] The doctrine of signs as the expression of thought or reasoning; the science of indicating thought by signs. Smart.

sematrope.c: Sematrope Sem"a*trope (?), n. [Gr. sh^ma sign + tre`pein to turn. ] An instrument for signaling by reflecting the rays of the sun in different directions. Knight.

semblable.c: Semblable Sem"bla*ble (?), a. [F., from sembler to seem, resemble, L. similare, simulare. See Simulate.] Like; similar; resembling. [Obs.] Chaucer.

semblably.c: Semblably Sem"bla*bly, adv. In like manner. [Obs.] Shak.

semblance.c: Semblance Sem"blance (?), n. [F. See Semblable, a.] 1. Seeming; appearance; show; figure; form.

semblant.c: Semblant Sem"blant (?), a. [F. semblant, p. pr.] 1. Like; resembling. [Obs.] Prior.
Semblant Sem"blant, n. [F.] 1. Show; appearance; figure; semblance. [Obs.] Spenser.

semble.c: Semble Sem"ble (?), v. i. [F. sembler. See Semblable, a.] 1. To imitate; to make a representation or likeness. [Obs.]
Semble Sem"ble, a. Like; resembling. [Obs.] T. Hudson.

sembling.c: Sembling Sem"bling (?), n. [Cf. Assemble.] (Zool.) The practice of attracting the males of Lepidoptera or other insects by exposing the female confined in a cage.

seme.c: Seme ‖Se*mé" (?), a. [F. semé, fr. semer to sow.] (Her.) Sprinkled or sown; -- said of field, or a charge, when strewed or covered with small charges.

semiography.c: Semiography Semeiography { Se`mei*og"ra*phy (sē`mi*ŏg"rȧ*fy̆), or Se`mi*og"ra*phy (sē`mĭ*ŏg"rȧ*fy̆), } n. [Gr. shmei^on sign + -graphy.] (Med.) A description of the signs of disease.

semiologioal.c: Semiologioal Semeiological { Se`mei*o*log"ic*al (?), or Se`mi*o*log"io*al }, a. Of or pertaining to the science of signs, or the systematic use of signs; as, a semeiological classification of the signs or symptoms of disease; a semeiological arrangement of signs used as signals.

semiology.c: Semiology Semeiology { Se`mei*ol"o*gy (sē`me*ŏl"o*jy̆ or sē`mi*ŏl"o*jy̆), or Se`mi*ol"o*gy (sĕm`e*ŏl"o*jy̆) }, n. [Gr. shmei^on a mark, a sign + -logy.] The study of signs as an element of communication; the analysis of systems of communication; -- also called semiotics. Specifically: (a) (Med.) The science of the signs or symptoms of disease; symptomatology. (b) The art of using signs in signaling.

semiotic.c: Semiotic Semeiotic { Se`mei*ot"ic (sē`me*ŏt"ĭk or sĕ`me*ŏt"ĭk), or Se`mi*ot"ic }, a. [Gr. shmeiwtiko`s, fr. shmei^on a mark, a sign.] 1. Relating to signs or indications; pertaining to the language of signs, or to language generally as indicating thought.

semele.c: Semele Sem"e*le (?), n. [L., fr. Gr.???.] (Gr. Myth.) A daughter of Cadmus, and by Zeus mother of Bacchus.

semen.c: Semen ‖Se"men (sē"mĕn), n.; pl. Semina (sĕm"ĭ*nȧ). [L., from the root of serere, satum, to sow. See Sow to scatter seed.] 1. (Bot.) The seed of plants.

semester.c: Semester Se*mes"ter (se*mĕs"tẽr), n. [G., from L. semestris half-yearly; sex six + mensis a month.] A period of six months; especially, a term in a college or university which divides the year into two terms.

semi.c: Semi- Sem"i- (?). [L. semi; akin to Gr.???, Skr. sāmi-, AS. sām-, and prob. to E. same, from the division into two parts of the same size. Cf. Hemi-, Sandelend.] A prefix signifying half, and sometimes partly or imperfectly; as, semiannual, half yearly; semitransparent, imperfectly transparent.
Semi circumference Sem`i cir*cum"fer*ence (?), n. Half of a circumference.
Semi crustaceous Sem`i crus*ta"ceous (?), a. Half crustaceous; partially crustaceous.
Semi pupa Sem`i pu"pa (sĕm`ĭ*pū"pȧ), n. (Zool.) The young of an insect in a stage between the larva and pupa.

semiamplexicaul.c: Semiamplexicaul Sem`i*am*plex"i*caul (?), a. (Bot.) Partially amplexicaul; embracing the stem half round, as a leaf.

semiangle.c: Semiangle Sem"i*an`gle (?), n. (Geom.) The half of a given, or measuring, angle.

semiannular.c: Semiannular Sem`i*an"nu*lar (?), a. Having the figure of a half circle; forming a semicircle. Grew.

semiarian.c: Semi-Arian Sem`i-A"ri*an (?), n. [See Arian.] (Eccl. Hist.) A member of a branch of the Arians which did not acknowledge the Son to be consubstantial with the Father, that is, of the same substance, but admitted him to be of a like substance with the Father, not by nature, but by a peculiar privilege.
Semi-Arian Sem"i-A"ri*an, a. Of or pertaining to Semi-Arianism.

semiarianism.c: Semi-Arianism Sem`i-A"ri*an*ism (?), n. The doctrines or tenets of the Semi-Arians.

semiaxis.c: Semiaxis Sem`i*ax"is (?), n. (Geom.) One half of the axis of an?llipse or other figure.

semibarbarian.c: Semibarbarian Sem`i*bar*ba"ri*an (?), a. Half barbarous; partially civilized. -- n. One partly civilized.

semibarbaric.c: Semibarbaric Sem`i*bar*bar"ic (?), a. Half barbarous or uncivilized; as, semibarbaric display.

semibarbarism.c: Semibarbarism Sem`i*bar"ba*rism (?), n. The quality or state of being half barbarous or uncivilized.

semibreve.c: Semibreve Sem"i*breve` (?), n. [Pref. semi- + breve: cf. F. semi-breve, It. semibreve.] [Formerly written semibref.] (Mus.) A note of half the time or duration of the breve; -- now usually called a whole note. It is the longest note in general use.

semibull.c: Semibull Sem"i*bull` (?), n. (R.C.Ch.) A bull issued by a pope in the period between his election and coronation.

semicalcareous.c: Semicalcareous Sem`i*cal*ca"re*ous (?), a. Half or partially calcareous; as, a semicalcareous plant.

semicalcined.c: Semicalcined Sem`i*cal*cined" (?), a. Half calcined; as, semicalcined iron.

semicastrate.c: Semicastrate Sem`i*cas"trate (?), v. t. To deprive of one testicle. -- Sem`i*cas*tra"tion (#),n.

semicentennial.c: Semicentennial Sem`i*cen*ten"ni*al (?), a. Of or pertaining to half of a century, or a period of fifty years; as, a semicentennial commemoration.

semichorus.c: Semichorus Sem"i*cho`rus, n. (Mus.) A half chorus; a passage to be sung by a selected portion of the voices, as the female voices only, in contrast with the full choir.

semicircle.c: Semicircle Sem"i*cir`cle (?), n. 1. (a) The half of a circle; the part of a circle bounded by its diameter and half of its circumference. (b) A semicircumference.

semicircular.c: Semicircular Sem`i*cir"cu*lar (?), a. Having the form of half of a circle. Addison.

semicirque.c: Semicirque Sem"i*cirque (?), n. A semicircular hollow or opening among trees or hills. Wordsworth.

semicolon.c: Semicolon Sem"i*co`lon (?), n. The punctuation mark [;] indicating a separation between parts or members of a sentence more distinct than that marked by a comma.

semicolumn.c: Semicolumn Sem"i*col`umn (?), n. A half column; a column bisected longitudinally, or along its axis.

semicolumnar.c: Semicolumnar Sem`i*co*lum"nar (?), a. Like a semicolumn; flat on one side and round on the other; imperfectly columnar.

semicompact.c: Semicompact Sem`i*com*pact" (?), a. Half compact; imperfectly indurated.

semiconscious.c: Semiconscious Sem`i*con"scious (?), a. Half conscious; imperfectly conscious. De Quincey.

semicope.c: Semicope Sem"i*cope` (?), n. A short cope, or an inferier kind of cope. [Obs.] Chaucer.

semicrystalline.c: Semicrystalline Sem`i*crys"tal*line (?), a. (Min.) Half crystalline; -- said of certain cruptive rocks composed partly of crystalline, partly of amorphous matter.

semicubical.c: Semicubical Sem`i*cu"bic*al (?), a. (Math.) Of or pertaining to the square root of the cube of a quantity.

semicupium.c: Semicupium Semicubium { Sem`i*cu"bi*um (?), Sem`i*cu"pi*um (?), } n. [LL., fr. L. semi half + cupa tub, cask.] A half bath, or one that covers only the lewer extremities and the hips; a sitz-bath; a half bath, or hip bath.

semicylyndrical.c: Semicylyndrical Semicylindric { Sem`i*cy*lin"dric (?), Sem`i*cy*lyn"dric*al (?) } a. Half cylindrical.

semideistical.c: Semideistical Sem`i*de*is"tic*al (?), a. Half deisticsl; bordering on deism. S. Miller.

semidemiquaver.c: Semidemiquaver Sem`i*dem"i*qua`ver (?), n. (Mus.) A demisemiquaver; a thirty-second note.

semidetached.c: Semidetached Sem`i*de*tached" (?), a. Half detached; partly distinct or separate.

semidiameter.c: Semidiameter Sem`i*di*am"e*ter (?), n. (Math.) Half of a diameter; a right line, or the length of a right line, drawn from the center of a circle, a sphere, or other curved figure, to its circumference or periphery; a radius.

semidiapente.c: Semidiapente Sem`i*di`a*pen"te (?), n. (Mus.) An imperfect or diminished fifth. Busby.

semidiaphaneity.c: Semidiaphaneity Sem`i*di`a*pha*ne"i*ty (?), n. Half or imperfect transparency; translucency. [R.] Boyle.

semidiaphanous.c: Semidiaphanous Sem`i*di*aph"a*nous (?), a. Half or imperfectly transparent; translucent. Woodward.

semidiatessaron.c: Semidiatessaron Sem`i*di`a*tes"sa*ron (?), n. (Mus.) An imperfect or diminished fourth. [R.]

semidiesel.c: Semi-Diesel Sem`i-Die"sel (?), a. Designating an internal-combustion engine of a type resembling the Diesel engine in using as fuel heavy oil which is injected in a spray just before the end of the compression stroke and is fired without electrical ignition. The fuel is sprayed into an iron box (called a hot bulb or hot pot) opening into the combustion chamber, and heated for ignition by a blast-lamp until the engine is running, when it is, ordinarily, kept red hot by the heat of combustion.

semiditone.c: Semiditone Sem`i*di"tone` (?), n. [Pref. semi- + ditone: cf. It. semiditono. Cf. Hemiditone.] (Gr. Mus.) A lesser third, having its terms as 6 to 5; a hemiditone. [R.]

semidiurnal.c: Semidiurnal Sem`i*di*ur"nal (?), a. 1. Pertaining to, or accomplished in, half a day, or twelve hours; occurring twice every day.

semidome.c: Semidome Sem"i*dome` (?), n. (Arch.) A roof or ceiling covering a semicircular room or recess, or one of nearly that shape, as the apse of a church, a niche, or the like. It is approximately the quarter of a hollow sphere.

semidouble.c: Semidouble Sem"i*dou`ble (?), n. (Eccl.) An office or feast celebrated with less solemnity than the double ones. See Double, n., 8.
Semidouble Sem`i*dou"ble, a. (Bot.) Having the outermost stamens converted into petals, while the inner ones remain perfect; -- said of a flower.

semifable.c: Semifable Sem"i*fa`ble (?), n. That which is part fable and part truth; a mixture of truth and fable. De Quincey.

semifloscule.c: Semifloscule Sem"i*flos`cule (?), n. (Bot.) A floscule, or florest, with its corolla prolonged into a strap-shaped petal; -- called also semifloret.

semiflosculous.c: Semiflosculous Sem`i*flos"cu*lous (?), a. (Bot.) Having all the florets ligulate, as in the dandelion.

semifluid.c: Semifluid Sem`i*flu"id (?), a. Imperfectly fluid. -- n. A semifluid substance.

semiform.c: Semiform Sem"i*form` (?), n. A half form; an imperfect form.

semiformed.c: Semiformed Sem"i*formed` (?), a. Half formed; imperfectly formed; as, semiformed crystals.

semiglutin.c: Semiglutin Sem`i*glu"tin (?), n. (Physiol. Chem.) A peptonelike body, insoluble in alcohol, formed by boiling collagen or gelatin for a long time in water. Hemicollin, a like body, is also formed at the same time, and differs from semiglutin by being partly soluble in alcohol.

semihistorical.c: Semihistorical Sem`i*his*tor"i*cal (?), a. Half or party historical. Sir G. C. Lewis.

semiindurated.c: Semiindurated Sem`i*in"du*ra`ted (?), a. Imperfectly indurated or hardened.

semilapidified.c: Semilapidified Sem`i*la*pid"i*fied (?), a. Imperfectly changed into stone. Kirwan.

semilens.c: Semilens Sem"i*lens` (?), n. (Opt.) The half of a lens divided along a plane passing through its axis.

semilenticular.c: Semilenticular Sem`i*len*tic"u*lar (?), a. Half lenticular or convex; imperfectly resembling a lens. Kirwan.

semiligneous.c: Semiligneous Sem`i*lig"ne*ous (?), a. Half or partially ligneous, as a stem partly woody and partly herbaceous.

semiliquidity.c: Semiliquidity Sem`i*li*quid"i*ty (?), n. The quality or state of being semiliquid; partial liquidity.

semilogical.c: Semilogical Sem`i*log"ic*al (?), a. Half logical; partly logical; said of fallacies. Whately.

semilor.c: Semilor Sem"i*lor (?), n. [Cf. G. similor, semilor.] A yellowish alloy of copper and zinc. See Simplor.

semilunar.c: Semilunar Sem`i*lu"nar (?), a. Shaped like a half moon.

semilune.c: Semilune Sem"i*lune` (?), n. (Geom.) The half of a lune.

semimetal.c: Semimetal Sem"i*met`al (?), n. (Chem.) An element possessing metallic properties in an inferior degree and not malleable, as arsenic, antimony, bismuth, molybdenum, uranium, etc. [Obs.]

semimetallic.c: Semimetallic Sem`i*me*tal"lic (?), a. (Chem.) Of or pertaining to a semimetal; possessing metallic properties in an inferior degree; resembling metal.

semimonthly.c: Semimonthly Sem`i*month"ly (?) a. Coming or made twice in a month; as, semimonthly magazine; a semimonthly payment. -- n. Something done or made every half month; esp., a semimonthly periodical. -- adv. In a semimonthly manner; at intervals of half a month.

semimute.c: Semimute Sem`i*mute" (?), a. Having the faculty of speech but imperfectly developed or partially lost.

seminal.c: Seminal Sem"i*nal (?), a. [L. seminalis, fr. semen, seminis, seed, akin to serere to sow: cf. F. seminal. See Sow to scatter seed.] 1. Pertaining to, containing, or consisting of, seed or semen; as, the seminal fluid.
Seminal Sem"i*nal (?), n. A seed. [Obs.] Sir T. Browne.

seminality.c: Seminality Sem`i*nal"i*ty (?), n. The quality or state of being seminal. Sir T. Browne.

seminar.c: Seminar Sem`i*nar" (?), n. [G. See Seminary, n.] A group of students engaged, under the guidance of an instructor, in original research in a particular line of study, and in the exposition of the results by theses, lectures, etc.; -- formerly called also seminary, now seldom used in this sense.

seminarist.c: Seminarist Seminarian { Sem`i*na"ri*an (?), Sem"i*na*rist (?), } n. [Cf. F. séminariste.] A member of, or one educated in, a seminary; specifically, an ecclesiastic educated for the priesthood in a seminary.

seminary.c: Seminary Sem"i*na*ry (?), n.; pl. Seminaries (#). [L. seminarium, fr. seminarius belonging to seed, fr. semon, seminis, seed. See Seminal.] 1. A piece of ground where seed is sown for producing plants for transplantation; a nursery; a seed plat. [Obs.] Mortimer.
Seminary Sem"i*na*ry, a. [L. seminarius.] Belonging to seed; seminal. [R.]

seminate.c: Seminate Sem"i*nate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Seminated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Seminating.] [L. seminatus, p. p. of seminare to sow, fr. semen, seminis, seed.] To sow; to spread; to propagate. [R.] Waterhouse.

semination.c: Semination Sem`i*na"tion (?), n. [L. seminatio: cf. F. sémination.] 1. The act of sowing or spreading. [R.]

semined.c: Semined Sem"ined (?), a. [See Semen.] Thickly covered or sown, as with seeds. [Obs.] B. Jonson.

seminiferous.c: Seminiferous Sem`i*nif"er*ous (?), a. [L. semen, semenis, seed -ferous.] (Biol.) Seed-bearing; producing seed; pertaining to, or connected with, the formation of semen; as, seminiferous cells or vesicles.

seminifical.c: Seminifical Seminific { Sem`i*nif"ic (?), Sem`i*nif"ic*al (?), } a. [L. semen, seminis, seed + facere to make.] (Biol.) Forming or producing seed, or the male generative product of animals or of plants.

seminification.c: Seminification Sem`i*ni*fi*ca"tion (?), n. Propagation from seed. [R.] Sir M. Hale.

seminist.c: Seminist Sem"i*nist (?), n. (Biol.) A believer in the old theory that the newly created being is formed by the admixture of the seed of the male with the supposed seed of the female.

seminoles.c: Seminoles Sem"i*noles (?), n. pl.; sing. Seminole (?). (Ethnol.) A tribe of Indians who formerly occupied Florida, where some of them still remain. They belonged to the Creek Confideration.

seminose.c: Seminose Sem"i*nose` (?), n. [L. semen seed + glucose.] (Chem.) A carbohydrate of the glucose group found in the thickened endosperm of certain seeds, and extracted as yellow sirup having a sweetish-bitter taste.

seminude.c: Seminude Sem`i*nude" (?), a. Partially nude; half naked.

seminymph.c: Seminymph Sem"i*nymph` (?), n. (Zool.) The pupa of insects which undergo only a slight change in passing to the imago state.

semioccasionally.c: Semioccasionally Sem`i*oc*ca"sion*al*ly (?), adv. Once in a while; on rare occasions. [Colloq. U. S.]

semiofficial.c: Semiofficial Sem`i*of*fi"cial (?), a. Half official; having some official authority or importance; as, a semiofficial statement. -- Sem`i*of*fi"cial*ly, adv.

semiological.c: Semiological Semiology Semiography { Se`mi*og"ra*phy (?), Se`mi*ol"o*gy (?), Se`mi*o*log"ic*al (?) }. Same as Semeiography, Semeiology, Semeiological.

semiopal.c: Semiopal Sem"i*o`pal (?), n. (Min.) A variety of opal not possessing opalescence.

semiopaque.c: Semiopaque Sem`i*o*paque" (?), a. Half opaque; only half transparent.

semiorbicular.c: Semiorbicular Sem`i*or*bic"u*lar (?), a. Having the shape of a half orb or sphere.

semioxygenated.c: Semioxygenated Sem`i*ox"y*gen*a`ted (?), a. Combined with oxygen only in part. Kirwan.

semipalmated.c: Semipalmated Semipalmate { Sem`i*pal"mate (?), Sem`i*pal"ma*ted (?), } a. (Zool.) Having the anterior toes joined only part way down with a web; half-webbed; as, a semipalmate bird or foot. See Illust. k under Aves.

semiparabola.c: Semiparabola Sem`i*pa*rab"o*la (?), n. (Geom.) One branch of a parabola, being terminated at the principal vertex of the curve.

semiped.c: Semiped Sem"i*ped (?), n. [L. semipes, semipedis; pref. semi- half + pes, pedis, a foot.] (Pros.) A half foot in poetry.

semipedal.c: Semipedal Se*mip"e*dal (?), a. (Pres.) Containing a half foot.

semipelagian.c: Semi-Pelagian Sem`i-Pe*la"gi*an (?), n. (Eccl. Hist.) A follower of John Cassianus, a French monk (died about 448), who modified the doctrines of Pelagius, by denying human merit, and maintaining the necessity of the Spirit's influence, while, on the other hand, he rejected the Augustinian doctrines of election, the inability of man to do good, and the certain perseverance of the saints.
Semi-Pelagian Sem`i-Pe*la"gi*an, a. Of or pertaining to the Semi-Pelagians, or their tenets.

semipelagianism.c: Semi-Pelagianism Sem`i-Pe*la"gi*an*ism (sĕm`ĭ*pe*lā"jĭ*ain*ĭz'm), n. The doctrines or tenets of the Semi-Pelagians.

semipellucid.c: Semipellucid Sem`i*pel*lu"cid (sĕm`ĭ*pĕl*lū"sĭd), a. Half clear, or imperfectly transparent; as, a semipellucid gem.

semipellucidity.c: Semipellucidity Sem`i*pel`lu*cid"i*ty (sĕm`ĭ*pĕl`lu*sĭd"ĭ*ty̆), n. The quality or state of being imperfectly transparent.

semipenniform.c: Semipenniform Sem`i*pen"ni*form (sĕm`ĭ*pĕn"nĭ*fôrm), a. (Anat.) Half or partially penniform; as, a semipenniform muscle.

semipermanent.c: Semipermanent Sem`i*per"ma*nent, n. Half or partly permanent.

semiperspicuous.c: Semiperspicuous Sem`i*per*spic"u*ous (sĕm`ĭ*pẽr*spĭk"u*ŭs), a. Half transparent; imperfectly clear; semipellucid.

semiphlogisticated.c: Semiphlogisticated Sem`i*phlo*gis"ti*ca`ted (sĕm`ĭ*flo*jĭs"tĭ*kā`tĕd), a. (Old Chem.) Partially impregnated with phlogiston. [Obs.]

semiplume.c: Semiplume Sem"i*plume` (sĕm`ĭ*plūm), n. (Zool.) A feather which has a plumelike web, with the shaft of an ordinary feather.

semiprecious.c: Semiprecious Sem`i*pre"cious (sĕm`ĭ*prĕsh"ŭs), a. Somewhat precious; as, semiprecious stones or metals. Used mostly of gemstones used in jewelry, such as amethyst, garnet, or iolite, which are sufficiently rare to have commercial value, but are not considered as precious, as are the diamond, emerald, and ruby.

semiproof.c: Semiproof Sem"i*proof` (sĕm"ĭ*prōof`), n. Half proof; evidence from the testimony of a single witness. [Obs.] Bailey.

semiquartile.c: Semiquartile Semiquadrate { Sem"i*quad`rate (sĕm"ĭ*kwŏd`rat), Sem"i*quar`tile (sĕm"ĭ*kwär`tĭl), } n. (Astrol.) An aspect of the planets when distant from each other the half of a quadrant, or forty-five degrees, or one sign and a half. Hutton.

semiquaver.c: Semiquaver Sem"i*qua`ver (sĕm"ĭ*kwā`vẽr), n. (Mus.) A note of half the duration of the quaver; -- now usually called a sixteenth note.

semiquintile.c: Semiquintile Sem"i*quin`tile (sĕm"ĭ*kwĭn`tĭl), n. (Astrol.) An aspect of the planets when distant from each other half of the quintile, or thirty-six degrees.

semiradial.c: Semiradial engine Semiradial engine. (Mach.) See Radial engine, above.

semirecondite.c: Semirecondite Sem`i*rec"on*dite (sĕm`ĭ*rĕk"ŏn*dīt or sĕm`ĭ*re*kŏn"dĭt), a. (Zool.) Half hidden or half covered; said of the head of an insect when half covered by the shield of the thorax.

semiring.c: Semiring Sem"i*ring` (sĕm"ĭ*rĭng`), n. (Anat.) One of the incomplete rings of the upper part of the bronchial tubes of most birds. The semirings form an essential part of the syrinx, or musical organ, of singing birds.

semisavage.c: Semisavage Sem"i*sav`age, n. One who is half savage.

semisaxon.c: Semi-Saxon Sem`i-Sax"on (?), a. Half Saxon; -- specifically applied to the language intermediate between Saxon and English, belonging to the period 1150-1250.

semisextile.c: Semisextile Sem"i*sex"tile (?), n. (Astrol.) An aspect of the planets when they are distant from each other the twelfth part of a circle, or thirty degrees. Hutton.

semisoun.c: Semisoun Sem"i*soun (-sōon), n. A half sound; a low tone. [Obs.] “Soft he cougheth with a semisoun.” Chaucer.

semispherical.c: Semispherical Semispheric { Sem`i*spher"ic (?), Sem`i*spher"ic*al (?), } a. Having the figure of a half sphere. Kirwan.

semispheroidal.c: Semispheroidal Sem`i*sphe*roid"al (?), a. Formed like a half spheroid.

semita.c: Semita ‖Sem"i*ta (?), n.; pl. Semitae. [L., a path.] (Zool.) A fasciole of a spatangoid sea urchin.

semitangent.c: Semitangent Sem"i*tan`gent (?), n. (Geom.) The tangent of half an arc.

semite.c: Semite Sem"ite (?), n. One belonging to the Semitic race. Also used adjectively. [Written also Shemite.]

semitertian.c: Semitertian Sem`i*ter"tian (?), a. (Med.) Having the characteristics of both a tertian and a quotidian intermittent. -- n. An intermittent combining the characteristics of a tertian and a quotidian.

semitic.c: Semitic Sem*it"ic (?), a. Of or pertaining to Shem or his descendants; belonging to that division of the Caucasian race which includes the Arabs, Jews, and related races. [Written also Shemitic.]

semitism.c: Semitism Sem"i*tism (?), n. A Semitic idiom; a word of Semitic origin. [Written also Shemitism.]

semitone.c: Semitone Sem"i*tone (?), n. [Pref. semi- + tone. CF. Hemitone.] (Mus.) Half a tone; -- the name commonly applied to the smaller intervals of the diatonic scale.

semitonic.c: Semitonic Sem`i*ton"ic (?), a. Of or pertaining to a semitone; consisting of a semitone, or of semitones.

semitontine.c: Semitontine Sem`i*ton*tine" (?), a. (LIfe Insurance) Lit., half-tontine; -- used to designate a form of tontine life insurance. See Tontine insurance. -- Sem`i*ton*tine", n.

semitransept.c: Semitransept Sem"i*tran`sept (?), n. (Arch.) The half of a transept; as, the north semitransept of a church.

semitranslucent.c: Semitranslucent Sem`i*trans*lu"cent (?), a. Slightly clear; transmitting light in a slight degree.

semitransparency.c: Semitransparency Sem`i*trans*par"en*cy (?), n. Imperfect or partial transparency.

semitransparent.c: Semitransparent Sem`i*trans*par"ent (?), a. Half or imperfectly transparent.

semivif.c: Semivif Sem"i*vif (?), a. [L. semivivus.] Only half alive. [Obs.] Piers Plowman.

semivitrification.c: Semivitrification Sem`i*vit"ri*fi*ca"tion (?), n. 1. The quality or state of being semivitrified.

semivitrified.c: Semivitrified Sem`i*vit"ri*fied (?), a. Half or imperfectly vitrified; partially converted into glass.

semivocal.c: Semivocal Sem`i*vo"cal (?), a. (Phon.) Of or pertaining to a semivowel; half cocal; imperfectly sounding.

semivowel.c: Semivowel Sem"i*vow`el (?), n. (Phon.) (a) A sound intermediate between a vowel and a consonant, or partaking of the nature of both, as in the English w and y. (b) The sign or letter representing such a sound.

semiweekly.c: Semiweekly Sem`i*week"ly (?), a. Coming, or made, or done, once every half week; as, a semiweekly newspaper; a semiweekly trip. -- n. That which comes or happens once every half week, esp. a semiweekly periodical. -- adv. At intervals of half a week each.

semolina.c: Semolina Sem`o*li"na (?), n. [It. semolino, from semola bran, L. simila the finest wheat flour. Cf. Semoule, Simnel.] The purified fine, hard parts of durum wheat, derived mostly from the endosperm, rounded by the attrition of the millstones, -- used in cookery, such as in the preparation of Italian pasta.

sempervirent.c: Sempervirent Sem`per*vi"rent (?), a. [L. semper always + virens, p. pr. of virere to be green.] Always fresh; evergreen. [R.] Smart.

sempervive.c: Sempervive Sem"per*vive (?), n. [L. semperviva, sempervivum, fr. sempervivus ever-living; semper always + vivus living.] (Bot.) The houseleek.

sempervivum.c: Sempervivum ‖Sem`per*vi"vum (?), n. (Bot.) A genus of fleshy-leaved plants, of which the houseleek (Sempervivum tectorum) is the commonest species.

sempiternal.c: Sempiternal Sem`pi*ter"nal (?), a. [L. sempiternus, fr. semper always: cf. F. sempiternel.] 1. Of neverending duration; everlasting; endless; having beginning, but no end. Sir M. Hale.

sempiternity.c: Sempiternity Sem`pi*ter"ni*ty (?), n. [L. sempiternitas.] Future duration without end; the relation or state of being sempiternal. Sir M. Hale.

sempre.c: Sempre Sem"pre (?), adv. [It., fr. L. semper.] (Mus.) Always; throughout; as, sempre piano, always soft.

semuncia.c: Semuncia ‖Se*mun"ci*a (?), n. [L., fr. semi half + uncia ounce.] (Rom. Antiq.) A Roman coin equivalent to one twenty-fourth part of a Roman pound.

sen.c: Sen Sen (?), n. A Japanese coin, worth about one half of a cent.
Sen Sen, adv., prep., & conj. [See Since.] Since. [Obs.]

senary.c: Senary Sen"a*ry (?), a. [L. senarius, fr. seni six each, fr. sex six. See Six.] Of six; belonging to six; containing six. Dr. H. More.

senate.c: Senate Sen"ate (?), n. [OE. senat, F. sénat, fr. L. senatus, fr. senex, gen. senis, old, an old man. See Senior, Sir.] 1. An assembly or council having the highest deliberative and legislative functions. Specifically: (a) (Anc. Rom.) A body of elders appointed or elected from among the nobles of the nation, and having supreme legislative authority.

senator.c: Senator Sen"a*tor (?), n. [OE. senatour, OF. senatour, F. sénateur, fr. L. senator.] 1. A member of a senate.

senatorial.c: Senatorial Sen`a*to"ri*al (?), a. [F. sénatorial, or L. senatorius.] 1. Of or pertaining to a senator, or a senate; becoming to a senator, or a senate; as, senatorial duties; senatorial dignity.

senatorially.c: Senatorially Sen`a*to"ri*al*ly, adv. In a senatorial manner.

senatorship.c: Senatorship Sen"a*tor*ship (?), n. The office or dignity of a senator. Carew.

senatusconsult.c: Senatusconsult Se*na`tus*con*sult" (?), n. [L. senatus consultum.] A decree of the Roman senate.

send.c: Send Send (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Sent (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Sending.] [AS. sendan; akin to OS. sendian, D. zenden, G. senden, OHG. senten, Icel. senda, Sw. sända, Dan. sende, Goth. sandjan, and to Goth. sinp a time (properly, a going), gasinpa companion, OHG. sind journey, AS. sī?, Icel. sinni a walk, journey, a time. W. hynt a way, journey, OIr. s?t. Cf. Sense.] 1. To cause to go in any manner; to dispatch; to commission or direct to go; as, to send a messenger.
Send Send (?), v. i. 1. To dispatch an agent or messenger to convey a message, or to do an errand.
Send Send, n. (Naut.) The impulse of a wave by which a vessel is carried bodily. [Written also scend.] W. C. Russell. “The send of the sea”. Longfellow.

sendal.c: Sendal Sen"dal (?), n. [OF. cendal (cf. Pr. & Sp. cendal, It. zendale), LL. cendallum, Gr.??? a fine Indian cloth.] A light thin stuff of silk. [Written also cendal, and sendal.] Chaucer.

sender.c: Sender Send"er (?), n. One who sends. Shak.

senecas.c: Senecas Sen"e*cas (?), n. pl.; sing. Seneca (?). (Ethnol.) A tribe of Indians who formerly inhabited a part of Western New York. This tribe was the most numerous and most warlike of the Five Nations.

senecio.c: Senecio ‖Se*ne"ci*o (?), n. [L., groundsel, lit., an old man. So called in allusion to the hoary appearance of the pappus.] (Bot.) A very large genus of composite plants including the groundsel and the golden ragwort.

senectitude.c: Senectitude Se*nec"ti*tude (?), n. [L. senectus aged, old age, senex old.] Old age. [R.] “Senectitude, weary of its toils.” H. Miller.

senegal.c: Senegal Sen"e*gal (?), n. Gum senegal. See under Gum.

senegin.c: Senegin Sen"e*gin (?), n. (Med. Chem.) A substance extracted from the rootstock of the Polygala Senega (Seneca root), and probably identical with polygalic acid.

senescence.c: Senescence Se*nes"cence (?), n. [See Senescent.] The state of growing old; decay by time.

senescent.c: Senescent Se*nes"cent (?), a. [L. senescent, p. pr. of senescere to grow old, incho. fr. senere to be old.] Growing old; decaying with the lapse of time. “The night was senescent.” Poe. “With too senescent air.” Lowell.

seneschal.c: Seneschal Sen"es*chal (?), n. [OF. seneschal, LL. seniscalcus, of Teutonic origin; cf. Goth. sineigs old, skalks, OHG. scalch, AS. scealc. Cf. Senior, Marshal.] An officer in the houses of princes and dignitaries, in the Middle Ages, who had the superintendence of feasts and domestic ceremonies; a steward. Sometimes the seneschal had the dispensing of justice, and was given high military commands.

seneschalship.c: Seneschalship Sen"es*chal*ship, n. The office, dignity, or jurisdiction of a seneschal.

senge.c: Senge Senge (?), v. t. To singe. [Obs.] Chaucer.

sengreen.c: Sengreen Sen"green (?), n.[AS. singr?ne, properly, evergreen, fr. sin (in composition) always + grëne green; akin to OHG. sin- ever, L. semper.] (Bot.) The houseleek.

senhor.c: Senhor ‖Se*nhor" (?), n. [Pg. Cf. Señor, Senior.] A Portuguese title of courtesy corresponding to the Spanish señor or the English Mr. or sir; also, a gentleman.

senhora.c: Senhora ‖Se*nho"ra (?), n. [Pg. Cf. Señora.] A Portuguese title of courtesy given to a lady; Mrs.; Madam; also, a lady.

senile.c: Senile Se"nile (?), a. [L. senilis, from senex, gen. senis, old, an old man: cf. F. sénile. See Senior.] Of or pertaining to old age; proceeding from, or characteristic of, old age; affected with the infirmities of old age; as, senile weakness. “Senile maturity of judgment.” Boyle.

senility.c: Senility Se*nil"i*ty (?), n. [Cf. F. sénilité.] The quality or state of being senile; old age.

senior.c: Senior Sen"ior (?), a. [L. senior, compar. of senex, gen. senis, old. See Sir.] 1. More advanced than another in age; prior in age; elder; hence, more advanced in dignity, rank, or office; superior; as, senior member; senior counsel.
Senior Sen"ior, n. 1. A person who is older than another; one more advanced in life.

seniority.c: Seniority Sen*ior"i*ty (?), n. The quality or state of being senior.

seniorize.c: Seniorize Sen"ior*ize (?), v. i. To exercise authority; to rule; to lord it. [R.] Fairfax.

senna.c: Senna Sen"na (?), n. [Cf. It. & Sp. sena, Pg. sene, F. séné; all fr. Ar. sanā.] 1. (Med.) The leaves of several leguminous plants of the genus Cassia. (Cassia acutifolia, Cassia angustifolia, etc.). They constitute a valuable but nauseous cathartic medicine.

sennet.c: Sennet Sen"net (?), n. [Properly, a sign given for the entrance or exit of actors, from OF. sinet, signet, dim. of signe. See Signet.] A signal call on a trumpet or cornet for entrance or exit on the stage. [Obs.]

sennight.c: Sennight Sen"night (?), n. [Contr. fr. sevennight.] The space of seven nights and days; a week. [Written also se'nnight.] [Archaic.] Shak. Tennyson.

sennit.c: Sennit Sen"nit (?), n. [Seven + knit.] 1. (Naut.) A braided cord or fabric formed by plaiting together rope yarns or other small stuff.

senocular.c: Senocular Se*noc"u*lar (?), a. [L. seni six each (fr. sex six) + oculus eye.] Having six eyes. [R.] Derham.

senonian.c: Senonian Se*no"ni*an (?), a. [F. sénonien, from the district of Sénonais, in France.] (Geol.) In european geology, a name given to the middle division of the Upper Cretaceous formation.

senor.c: Senor Senyor ‖Se*ñor" (?), n. [Sp. Cf. Senior.] A Spanish title of courtesy corresponding to the English Mr. or Sir; also, a gentleman.

senora.c: Senora Senyora ‖Se*ño"ra (?), n. [Sp.] A Spanish title of courtesy given to a lady; Mrs.; Madam; also, a lady.

senorita.c: Senorita Senyorita ‖Se`ño*ri"ta (?), n. [Sp.] A Spanish title of courtesy given to a young lady; Miss; also, a young lady.

sensate.c: Sensate Sen"sate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Sensated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Sensating.] [See Sensated.] To feel or apprehend more or less distinctly through a sense, or the senses; as, to sensate light, or an odor.

sensated.c: Sensated Sensate { Sen"sate (?), Sen"sa*ted (?), } a. [L. sensatus gifted with sense, intelligent, fr. sensus sense. See Sense.] Felt or apprehended through a sense, or the senses. [R.] Baxter.

sensation.c: Sensation Sen*sa"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. sensation. See Sensate.] 1. (Physiol.) An impression, or the consciousness of an impression, made upon the central nervous organ, through the medium of a sensory or afferent nerve or one of the organs of sense; a feeling, or state of consciousness, whether agreeable or disagreeable, produced either by an external object (stimulus), or by some change in the internal state of the body.

sensational.c: Sensational Sen*sa"tion*al (?), a. 1. Of or pertaining to sensation; as, sensational nerves.

sensationalism.c: Sensationalism Sen*sa"tion*al*ism (?), n. 1. (Metaph.) The doctrine held by Condillac, and by some ascribed to Locke, that our ideas originate solely in sensation, and consist of sensations transformed; sensualism; -- opposed to intuitionalism, and rationalism.

sensationalist.c: Sensationalist Sen*sa"tion*al*ist, n. 1. (Metaph.) An advocate of, or believer in, philosophical sensationalism.

sense.c: Sense Sense (?), n. [L. sensus, from sentire, sensum, to perceive, to feel, from the same root as E. send; cf. OHG. sin sense, mind, sinnan to go, to journey, G. sinnen to meditate, to think: cf. F. sens. For the change of meaning cf. See, v. t. See Send, and cf. Assent, Consent, Scent, v. t., Sentence, Sentient.] 1. (Physiol.) A faculty, possessed by animals, of perceiving external objects by means of impressions made upon certain organs (sensory or sense organs) of the body, or of perceiving changes in the condition of the body; as, the senses of sight, smell, hearing, taste, and touch. See Muscular sense, under Muscular, and Temperature sense, under Temperature.
Sense Sense (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Sensed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Sensing.] To perceive by the senses; to recognize. [Obs. or Colloq.]

senseful.c: Senseful Sense"ful (?), a. Full of sense, meaning, or reason; reasonable; judicious. [R.] “Senseful speech.” Spenser. “Men, otherwise senseful and ingenious.” Norris.

senseless.c: Senseless Sense"less, a. Destitute of, deficient in, or contrary to, sense; without sensibility or feeling; unconscious; stupid; foolish; unwise; unreasonable.

sensibility.c: Sensibility Sen`si*bil"i*ty (?), n.; pl. Sensibilities (#). [Cf. F. sensibilité, LL. sensibilitas.] 1. (Physiol.) The quality or state of being sensible, or capable of sensation; capacity to feel or perceive.

sensible.c: Sensible Sen"si*ble (?), a. [F., fr. L. sensibilis, fr. sensus sense.] 1. Capable of being perceived by the senses; apprehensible through the bodily organs; hence, also, perceptible to the mind; making an impression upon the sense, reason, or understanding; as, sensible heat; sensible resistance.
Sensible Sen"si*ble (?), n. 1. Sensation; sensibility. [R.] “Our temper changed... which must needs remove the sensible of pain.” Milton.

sensibleness.c: Sensibleness Sen"si*ble*ness, n. 1. The quality or state of being sensible; sensibility; appreciation; capacity of perception; susceptibility. “The sensibleness of the eye.” Sharp. “Sensibleness and sorrow for sin.” Hammond.

sensibly.c: Sensibly Sen"si*bly, adv. 1. In a sensible manner; so as to be perceptible to the senses or to the mind; appreciably; with perception; susceptibly; sensitively.

sensifacient.c: Sensifacient Sen`si*fa"cient (?), a. [L. sensus sense + facere to make.] Converting into sensation. Huxley.

sensiferous.c: Sensiferous Sen*sif"er*ous (?), a. [L. sensifer; sensus sense + ferre to bear.] Exciting sensation; conveying sensation. Huxley.

sensific.c: Sensific Sen*sif"ic (?), a. [L. sensificus; sensus sense + facere to make.] Exciting sensation.

sensificatory.c: Sensificatory Sen*sif"i*ca*to*ry (?), a. Susceptible of, or converting into, sensation; as, the sensificatory part of a nervous system. Huxley.

sensigenous.c: Sensigenous Sen*sig"e*nous (?), a. [L. sensus sense + -genous.] Causing or exciting sensation. Huxley.

sensist.c: Sensist Sens"ist, n. One who, in philosophy, holds to sensism.

sensitive.c: Sensitive Sen"si*tive (?), a. [F. sensitif. See Sense.] 1. Having sense of feeling; possessing or exhibiting the capacity of receiving impressions from external objects; as, a sensitive soul.

sensitivity.c: Sensitivity Sen`si*tiv"i*ty (?), n. The quality or state of being sensitive; -- used chiefly in science and the arts; as, the sensitivity of iodized silver.

sensitize.c: Sensitize Sen"si*tize (?), v. t. (Photog.) To render sensitive, or susceptible of being easily acted on by the actinic rays of the sun; as, sensitized paper or plate.

sensitizer.c: Sensitizer Sen"si*ti`zer (?), n. (Photog.) An agent that sensitizes.

sensitometer.c: Sensitometer Sen`si*tom"e*ter (?), n. [See Sensitive; -meter.] (Photog.) An instrument or apparatus for comparing and grading the sensitiveness of plates, films, etc., as a screen divided into squares of different shades or colors, from which a picture is made on the plate to be tested.

sensive.c: Sensive Sens"ive (?), a. Having sense or sensibility; sensitive. [Obs.] Sir P. Sidney.

sensor.c: Sensor Sen"sor (?), a. Sensory; as, the sensor nerves.

sensorial.c: Sensorial Sen*so"ri*al (?), a. [Cf. F. sensorial. See Sensorium.] Of or pertaining to the sensorium; as, sensorial faculties, motions, powers. A. Tucker.

sensorium.c: Sensorium Sen*so"ri*um (?), n.; pl. E. Sensoriums (#), L. Sensoria (#). [L., fr. sentire, sensum, to discern or perceive by the senses.] (Physiol.) The seat of sensation; the nervous center or centers to which impressions from the external world must be conveyed before they can be perceived; the place where external impressions are localized, and transformed into sensations, prior to being reflected to other parts of the organism; hence, the whole nervous system, when animated, so far as it is susceptible of common or special sensations.

sensorivolitional.c: Sensori-volitional Sen*so`ri-vo*li"tion*al (?), a. (Physiol.) Concerned both in sensation and volition; -- applied to those nerve fibers which pass to and from the cerebro-spinal axis, and are respectively concerned in sensation and volition. Dunglison.

sensory.c: Sensory Sen"so*ry (?), n.; pl. Sensories (?). (Physiol.) Same as Sensorium.

Sensory Sen"so*ry, a. (Physiol.) Of or pertaining to the sensorium or sensation; as, sensory impulses; -- especially applied to those nerves and nerve fibers which convey to a nerve center impulses resulting in sensation; also sometimes loosely employed in the sense of afferent, to indicate nerve fibers which convey impressions of any kind to a nerve center.

sensual.c: Sensual Sen"su*al (?), a. [L. sensualis, from sensus sense: cf. F. sensuel.] 1. Pertaining to, consisting in, or affecting, the sense, or bodily organs of perception; relating to, or concerning, the body, in distinction from the spirit.

sensualism.c: Sensualism Sen"su*al*ism (?), n. [Cf. F. sensualisme.] 1. The condition or character of one who is sensual; subjection to sensual feelings and appetite; sensuality.

sensualist.c: Sensualist Sen"su*al*ist, n. [CF. F. sensualiste.] 1. One who is sensual; one given to the indulgence of the appetites or senses as the means of happiness.

sensuality.c: Sensuality Sen`su*al"i*ty (?), n. [CF. F. sensualité, L. sensualitas sensibility, capacity for sensation.] The quality or state of being sensual; devotedness to the gratification of the bodily appetites; free indulgence in carnal or sensual pleasures; luxuriousness; voluptuousness; lewdness.

sensualization.c: Sensualization Sen`su*al*i*za"tion (?), n. The act of sensualizing, or the state of being sensualized.

sensualize.c: Sensualize Sen"su*al*ize (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Sensualized (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Sensualizing (?).] To make sensual; to subject to the love of sensual pleasure; to debase by carnal gratifications; to carnalize; as, sensualized by pleasure. Pope.

sensually.c: Sensually Sen"su*al*ly, adv. In a sensual manner.

sensuosity.c: Sensuosity Sen`su*os"i*ty (?), n. The quality or state of being sensuous; sensuousness. [R.]

sensuous.c: Sensuous Sen"su*ous (?), a. 1. Of or pertaining to the senses, or sensible objects; addressing the senses; suggesting pictures or images of sense.

sent.c: Sent Sent (?), v. & n. See Scent, v. & n. [Obs.] Spenser.
Sent Sent, obs. 3d pers. sing. pres. of Send, for sendeth.
Sent Sent, imp. & p. p. of Send.

sentence.c: Sentence Sen"tence (?), n. [F., from L. sententia, for sentientia, from sentire to discern by the senses and the mind, to feel, to think. See Sense, n., and cf. Sentiensi.] 1. Sense; meaning; significance. [Obs.]
Sentence Sen"tence, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Sentenced (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Sentencing (?).] 1. To pass or pronounce judgment upon; to doom; to condemn to punishment; to prescribe the punishment of.

Sentence method Sen"tence meth`od. (Education) A method of teaching reading by giving first attention to phrases and sentences and later analyzing these into their verbal and alphabetic components; -- contrasted with alphabet method and word method. See also phonics.

sentencer.c: Sentencer Sen"ten*cer (?), n. One who pronounced a sentence or condemnation.

sentential.c: sentential sen*ten"tial (?), a. 1. Comprising sentences; as, a sentential translation. Abp. Newcome.

sententially.c: Sententially Sen*ten"tial*ly, adv. In a sentential manner.

sententiarist.c: Sententiarist Sen*ten"ti*a*rist (?), n. A sententiary. Barnas Sears (Life of Luther).

sententiary.c: Sententiary Sen*ten"ti*ary (?), n. [LL. sententiarius.] One who read lectures, or commented, on the Sentences of Peter Lombard, Bishop of Paris (1159-1160), a school divine. R. Henry.

sententiosity.c: Sententiosity Sen*ten`ti*os"i*ty (?), n. The quality or state of being sententious. [Obs.] Sir T. Browne.

sententious.c: Sententious Sen*ten"tious (?), a.[L. sentenciosus: cf. F. sentencieux.] 1. Abounding with sentences, axioms, and maxims; full of meaning; terse and energetic in expression; pithy; as, a sententious style or discourse; sententious truth.

sentiency.c: Sentiency Sentience { Sen"ti*ence (?), Sen"ti*en*cy (?), } n. [See Sentient, Sentence.] The quality or state of being sentient; esp., the quality or state of having sensation. G. H. Lewes.

sentient.c: Sentient Sen"ti*ent (?), a. [L. sentiens, -entis, p. pr. of sentire to discern or perceive by the senses. See Sense.] Having a faculty, or faculties, of sensation and perception. Specif. (Physiol.), especially sensitive; as, the sentient extremities of nerves, which terminate in the various organs or tissues.
Sentient Sen"ti*ent, n. One who has the faculty of perception; a sentient being.

sentiently.c: Sentiently Sen"ti*ent*ly, adv. In a sentient or perceptive way.

sentiment.c: Sentiment Sen"ti*ment (?), n. [OE. sentement, OF. sentement, F. sentiment, fr. L. sentire to perceive by the senses and mind, to feel, to think. See Sentient, a.] 1. A thought prompted by passion or feeling; a state of mind in view of some subject; feeling toward or respecting some person or thing; disposition prompting to action or expression.

sentimental.c: Sentimental Sen`ti*men"tal (?), a. [Cf. F. sentimental.] 1. Having, expressing, or containing a sentiment or sentiments; abounding with moral reflections; containing a moral reflection; didactic. [Obsoles.]

sentimentalism.c: Sentimentalism Sen`ti*men"tal*ism (?), n. [Cf. F. sentimentalisme.] The quality of being sentimental; the character or behavior of a sentimentalist; sentimentality.

sentimentalist.c: Sentimentalist Sen`ti*men"tal*ist, n. [Cf. F. sentimentaliste.] One who has, or affects, sentiment or fine feeling.

sentimentality.c: Sentimentality Sen`ti*men*tal"i*ty (?), n. [CF. F. sentimentalité.] The quality or state of being sentimental.

sentimentalize.c: Sentimentalize Sen`ti*men"tal*ize (?), v. t. To regard in a sentimental manner; as, to sentimentalize a subject.
Sentimentalize Sen`ti*men"tal*ize, v. i. To think or act in a sentimental manner, or like a sentimentalist; to affect exquisite sensibility. C. Kingsley.

sentimentally.c: Sentimentally Sen`ti*men"tal*ly, adv. In a sentimental manner.

sentine.c: Sentine Sen"tine (?), n. [L. sentina bilge water, hold of a ship, dregs: cf. F. sentine.] A place for dregs and dirt; a sink; a sewer. [Obs.] Latimer.

sentinel.c: Sentinel Sen"ti*nel, n. [F. sentinelle (cf. It. sentinella); probably originally, a litle path, the sentinel's beat,, and a dim. of a word meaning, path; cf. F. sente path. L. semita; and OF. sentine, sentele, senteret, diminutive words. Cf. Sentry.] 1. One who watches or guards; specifically (Mil.), a soldier set to guard an army, camp, or other place, from surprise, to observe the approach of danger, and give notice of it; a sentry.

Sentinel Sen"ti*nel, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Sentineled (?) or Sentinelled; p. pr. & vb. n. Sentineling or Sentinelling.] 1. To watch over like a sentinel. “To sentinel enchanted land.” [R.] Sir W. Scott.

sentisection.c: Sentisection Sen`ti*sec"tion (?), n. [L. sentire to feel + E. section.] Painful vivisection; -- opposed to callisection. B. G. Wilder.

sentry.c: Sentry Sen"try (?), n.; pl. Sentires (#). [Probably from OF. senteret a little patch; cf. F. sentier path, and OF. sente. See Sentinel.] 1. (Mil.) A soldier placed on guard; a sentinel.

senza.c: Senza ‖Sen"za (?), prep. [It.] (Mus.) Without; as, senza stromenti, without instruments.

sepal.c: Sepal Se"pal (?), n. [NL. sepalum, formed in imitation of NL. petalum, petal, to denote one of the divisions of the calyx: cf. F. sépale.] (Bot.) A leaf or division of the calyx.

sepaled.c: Sepaled Se"paled (?), a. (Bot.) Having one or more sepals.

sepaline.c: Sepaline Sep"al*ine (?), a. (Bot.) Relating to, or having the nature of, sepals.

sepalody.c: Sepalody Se*pal"o*dy (?), n. [Sepal + Gr. e'i^dos form.] (Bot.) The metamorphosis of other floral organs into sepals or sepaloid bodies.

sepaloid.c: Sepaloid Sep"al*oid (?), a. [Sepal + -oid.] (Bot.) Like a sepal, or a division of a calyx.

sepalous.c: Sepalous Sep"al*ous (?), a. (Bot.) Having, or relating to, sepals; -- used mostly in composition. See under Sepal.

separability.c: Separability Sep`a*ra*bil"i*ty (?), n. Quality of being separable or divisible; divisibility; separableness.

separable.c: Separable Sep"a*ra*ble (?), a. [L. separabilis: cf. F. séparable.] Capable of being separated, disjoined, disunited, or divided; as, the separable parts of plants; qualities not separable from the substance in which they exist. -- Sep"a*ra*ble*ness, n. -- Sep"a*ra*bly, adv.

separate.c: Separate Sep"a*rate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Separated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Separating.] [L. separatus, p. p. of separare to separate; pfref. se- aside + parare to make ready, prepare. See Parade, and cf. Sever.] 1. To disunite; to divide; to disconnect; to sever; to part in any manner.
Separate Sep"a*rate, v. i. To part; to become disunited; to be disconnected; to withdraw from one another; as, the family separated.
Separate Sep"a*rate (?), p. a. [L. separatus, p. p. ] 1. Divided from another or others; disjoined; disconnected; separated; -- said of things once connected.

separatical.c: Separatical Sep`a*rat"ic*al (?), a. Of or pertaining to separatism in religion; schismatical. [R.] Dr. T. Dwight.

separating.c: Separating Sep"a*ra`ting (?), a. Designed or employed to separate.

separation.c: Separation Sep`a*ra"tion (?), n. [L. separatio: cf. F. séparation.] The act of separating, or the state of being separated, or separate. Specifically: (a) Chemical analysis. (b) Divorce. (c) (Steam Boilers) The operation of removing water from steam.

separatism.c: Separatism Sep"a*ra*tism (?), n. [CF. F. séparatisme.] The character or act of a separatist; disposition to withdraw from a church; the practice of so withdrawing.

separatist.c: Separatist Sep`a*ra*tist (?), n. [Cf. F. séparatiste.] One who withdraws or separates himself; especially, one who withdraws from a church to which he has belonged; a seceder from an established church; a dissenter; a nonconformist; a schismatic; a sectary.

separatistic.c: Separatistic Sep`a*ra*tis"tic (?), a. Of or pertaining to separatists; characterizing separatists; schismatical.

separative.c: Separative Sep"a*ra*tive (?), a. [L. separativus.] Causing, or being to cause, separation. “Separative virtue of extreme cold.” Boyle.

separator.c: Separator Sep"a*ra`tor (?), n. [L.] One who, or that which, separates. Specifically: (a) (Steam Boilers) A device for depriving steam of particles of water mixed with it. (b) (Mining) An apparatus for sorting pulverized ores into grades, or separating them from gangue. (c) (Weaving) An instrument used for spreading apart the threads of the warp in the loom, etc.

separatory.c: Separatory Sep"a*ra*to*ry, n. [Cf. F. séparatoire.] 1. (Chem.) An apparatus used in separating, as a separating funnel.

separatrix.c: Separatrix Sep`a*ra"trix (?), n.; pl. L. -trices (#), E. -trixes (#). [L., she that separates.] (Arith.) The decimal point; the dot placed at the left of a decimal fraction, to separate it from the whole number which it follows. The term is sometimes also applied to other marks of separation.

sepelible.c: Sepelible Sep"e*li*ble (?), a. [L. sepelibilis, fr. sepelire to bury.] Admitting of burial. [Obs.] Bailey.

sephardic.c: Sephardic Se*phar"dic (?), a. [From Sephardim, a name applied to the Spanish Jews, fr. Sephard, name of a place where Jews were held in captivity (Ob. 20).] Of, pertaining to, or designating, the Jews (the Sephardim, also called Spanish or Portuguese Jews) descended from Jewish families driven from Spain by the Inquisition.

sephardim.c: Sephardim Se*phar"dim (?), n. pl. [NHeb.; orig. uncert.] Jews who are descendants of the former Jews of Spain and Portugal. They are as a rule darker than the northern Jews, and have more delicate features.

sephen.c: Sephen Se"phen (?), n. (Zool.) A large sting ray of the genus Trygon, especially Trygon sephen of the Indian Ocean and the Red Sea. The skin is an article of commerce.

sepia.c: Sepia Se"pi*a (?), n.; pl. E. Sepias (#), L. Sepiae (#). [L., fr. Gr.??? the cuttlefish, or squid.] 1. (Zool.) (a) The common European cuttlefish. (b) A genus comprising the common cuttlefish and numerous similar species. See Illustr. under Cuttlefish.
Sepia Se"pi*a, a. Of a dark brown color, with a little red in its composition; also, made of, or done in, sepia.

sepic.c: Sepic Se"pic (?), a. Of or pertaining to sepia; done in sepia; as, a sepic drawing.

sepidaceous.c: Sepidaceous Sep`i*da"ceous (?), a. (Zool.) Like or pertaining to the cuttlefishes of the genus Sepia.

sepiment.c: Sepiment Sep"i*ment (?), n. [L. sepimentum, saepimentum, from sepire, saepire, to hedge in.] Something that separates; a hedge; a fence. [R.] Bailey.

sepiostare.c: Sepiostare Se"pi*o*stare` (?), n. [Sepia + Gr.??? a bone.] (Zool.) The bone or shell of cuttlefish. See Illust. under Cuttlefish.

sepose.c: Sepose Se*pose" (?), v. t. [L. pref se- aside + E. pose.] To set apart. [Obs.] Donne.

seposit.c: Seposit Se*pos"it (?), v. t. [L. sepositus, p. p. of seponere to set aside.] To set aside; to give up. [Obs.]

seposition.c: Seposition Sep`o*si"tion (?), n. [L. sepositio.] The act of setting aside, or of giving up. [Obs.] Jer. Taylor.

sepoy.c: Sepoy Se"poy (?), n. [Per. sipāhī, fr. sipāh an army. Cf. Spahi.] A native of India employed as a soldier in the service of a European power, esp. of Great Britain; an Oriental soldier disciplined in the European manner.

sepsin.c: Sepsin Sep"sin (?), n. [Gr.??? putrefaction.] (Physiol. Chem.) A soluble poison (ptomaine) present in putrid blood. It is also formed in the putrefaction of proteid matter in general.

sepsis.c: Sepsis ‖Sep"sis (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr.??? putrefaction.] (Med.) The poisoning of the system by the introduction of putrescent material into the blood.

sept.c: Sept Sept (?), n. [A corruption of sect, n.] A clan, tribe, or family, proceeding from a common progenitor; -- used especially of the ancient clans in Ireland.

septaemia.c: Septaemia ‖Sep*tae"mi*a (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr.??? putrid +??? blood.] (Med.) Septicaemia.

septal.c: Septal Sep"tal (?), a. Of or pertaining to a septum or septa, as of a coral or a shell.

septane.c: Septane Sep"tane (?), n. [L. septem seven.] (Chem.) See Heptane. [R.]

septangle.c: Septangle Sep"tan`gle (?), n. [Septi- + angle.] (Geom.) A figure which has seven angles; a heptagon. [R.]

septarium.c: Septarium ‖Sep*ta"ri*um (?), n.;pl. Septaria (#). [NL., fr. L. septum, saeptum, an inclosure, a partition, fr. sepire, saepire, to inclose.] (Geol.) A flattened concretionary nodule, usually of limestone, intersected within by cracks which are often filled with calcite, barite, or other minerals.

septate.c: Septate Sep"tate (?), a. [L. septum, saeptum, partition.] Divided by partition or partitions; having septa; as, a septate pod or shell.

september.c: September Sep*tem"ber (?), n. [L., fr. septem seven, as being the seventh month of the Roman year, which began with March: cf. F. septembre. See Seven.] The ninth month of the year, containing thurty days.

septembrist.c: Septembrist Sep*tem"brist (?), n. [F. septembriste.] An agent in the massacres in Paris, committed in patriotic frenzy, on the 22d of September, 1792.

septemfluous.c: Septemfluous Sep*tem"flu*ous (?), a.[L. septemfluus; septem seven + fluere to flow.] Flowing sevenfold; divided into seven streams or currents. [R.] Fuller.

septempartite.c: Septempartite Sep*tem"par*tite (?), a. [L. septem seven + E. partite.] Divided nearly to the base into seven parts; as, a septempartite leaf.
