smatterer.c: Smatterer Smat"ter*er (?), n. One who has only a slight, superficial knowledge; a sciolist.

smattering.c: Smattering Smat"ter*ing, n. A slight, superficial knowledge of something; sciolism.

smear.c: Smear Smear (smēr), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Smeared (smērd); p. pr. & vb. n. Smearing.] [OE. smeren, smerien, AS. smierwan, smyrwan, fr. smeoru fat, grease; akin to D. smeren, OHG. smirwen, G. schmieren, Icel. smyrja to anoint. See Smear, n.] 1. To overspread with anything unctuous, viscous, or adhesive; to daub; as, to smear anything with oil. “Smear the sleepy grooms with blood.” Shak.

Smear Smear, n. [OE. smere,. smeoru fat, grease; akin to D. smeer, G. schmeer, OHG. smero, Icel. smjör, Sw. & Dan. smör butter, Goth. smaírþr fatness, smarna dung; cf. Lith. smarsas fat. Cf. Smirch.] 1. A fat, oily substance; oinment. Johnson.
Smear dab Smear" dab" (?). (Zool.) The sand fluke (b). [Prov. Eng.]

smearcase.c: Smearcase Smear"case` (?), n. [G. schmierkäse; schmier grease (or schmieren to smear) + käse cheese.] Cottage cheese. [Local, U. S.]

smeared.c: Smeared Smeared (?), a. (Zool.) Having the color mark ings ill defined, as if rubbed; as, the smeared dagger moth (Apatela oblinita).

smeary.c: Smeary Smear"y (?), a. Tending to smear or soil; adhesive; viscous. Rowe.

smectite.c: Smectite Smec"tite (?), n. [G. smectit, fr. Gr.????? a kind of fuller's earth, fr.????? to wipe off.] (Min.) A hydrous silicate of alumina, of a greenish color, which, in certain states of humidity, appears transparent and almost gelatinous.

smee.c: Smee Smee (?), n. [Cf. Smew.] (Zool.) (a) The pintail duck. (b) The widgeon. (c) The poachard. (d) The smew. [Prov. Eng.]

smeeth.c: Smeeth Smeeth (?), v. t. [Etymol. uncertain.] To smoke; to blacken with smoke; to rub with soot. [Obs.]
Smeeth Smeeth (?), v. t. [OE. sme?en, AS. sm??ian. See Smooth.] To smooth. [Prov. Eng.] Halliwell.

smegma.c: Smegma Smeg"ma (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr.???? soap, fr.????? to wash off.] (Physiol.) The matter secreted by any of the sebaceous glands. Specifically: (a) The soapy substance covering the skin of newborn infants. (b) The cheesy, sebaceous matter which collects between the glans penis and the foreskin.

smegmatic.c: Smegmatic Smeg*mat"ic (?), a. Being of the nature of soap; soapy; cleansing; detersive.

smeir.c: Smeir Smeir (?), n. A salt glaze on pottery, made by adding common salt to an earthenware glaze.

smell.c: Smell Smell (smĕl), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Smelled (?), Smelt (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Smelling.] [OE. smellen, smillen, smullen; cf. LG. smellen, smelen, smölen, schmelen, to smoke, to reek, D. smeulen to smolder, and E. smolder. Cf. Smell, n.] 1. To perceive by the olfactory nerves, or organs of smell; to have a sensation of, excited through the nasal organs when affected by the appropriate materials or qualities; to obtain the scent of; as, to smell a rose; to smell perfumes.
Smell Smell, v. i. 1. To affect the olfactory nerves; to have an odor or scent; -- often followed by of; as, to smell of smoke, or of musk.

Smell Smell, n. [OE. smel, smil, smul, smeol. See Smell, v. t.] (Physiol.) 1. The sense or faculty by which certain qualities of bodies are perceived through the instrumentally of the olfactory nerves. See Sense.

smeller.c: Smeller Smell"er (?), n. 1. One who smells, or perceives by the sense of smell; one who gives out smell.

smellfeast.c: Smell-feast Smell"-feast` (?), n. 1. One who is apt to find and frequent good tables; a parasite; a sponger.

smelling.c: Smelling Smell"ing, n. 1. The act of one who smells.
Smelling salts Smell"ing salts. An aromatic preparation of carbonate of ammonia and, often, some scent, to avoid or relieve faintness, headache, or the like.

smellless.c: Smell-less Smell"-less, a. Destitute of smell; having no odor.

smelt.c: Smelt Smelt (?), imp. & p. p. of Smell.

Smelt Smelt, n. [AS. smelt, smylt; akin to Dan. smelt.] 1. (Zool.) Any one of numerous species of small silvery salmonoid fishes of the genus Osmerus and allied genera, which ascend rivers to spawn, and sometimes become landlocked in lakes. They are esteemed as food, and have a peculiar odor and taste.

Smelt Smelt, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Smelted; p. pr. & vb. n. Smelting.] [Of foreign origin; cf. Sw. smälta, D. smelten, Dan. smelte, Icel. smelta, G. schmelzen OHG. smelzan, smelzen; probably akin to Gr.?????. Cf. Enamel, Melt, Mute, v. i., Smalt.] (Metal.) To melt or fuse, as, ore, for the purpose of separating and refining the metal; hence, to reduce; to refine; to flux or scorify; as, to smelt tin.

smelter.c: Smelter Smelt"er (?), n. One who, or that which, smelts.

smeltery.c: Smeltery Smelt"er*y (?), n. A house or place for smelting.

smeltie.c: Smeltie Smelt"ie (?), n. A fish, the bib. [Prov. Eng.]

smerky.c: Smerky Smerk { Smerk (?), Smerk"y (?), } a. Smart; jaunty; spruce. See Smirk, a. [Obs.]

smew.c: Smew Smew (?), n. [Perhaps for ice-mew.] (Zool.) (a) small European merganser (Mergus albellus) which has a white crest; -- called also smee, smee duck, white merganser, and white nun. (b) The hooded merganser. [Local, U.S.]

smicker.c: Smicker Smick"er (?), v. i. [Akin to Sw. smickra to flatter, Dan. smigre, and perhaps to G. schmeicheln, and E. smile. Cf. Smicker, a.] To look amorously or wantonly; to smirk.
Smicker Smick"er, a. [AS. smicere tasteful, trim. See Smicker, v.] Amorous; wanton; gay; spruce. [Obs.]

smickering.c: Smickering Smick"er*ing, n. Amorous glance or inclination. [Obs.] “A smickering to our young lady.” Dryden.

smicket.c: Smicket Smick"et (?), n. [Dim. of smock.] A woman's under-garment; a smock. [Obs. or Prov. Eng.] Johnson.

smiddy.c: Smiddy Smid"dy (?), n. [See Smithy.] A smithy. [Prov. Eng. & Scot.]

smift.c: Smift Smift (?), n. A match for firing a charge of powder, as in blasting; a fuse.

smight.c: Smight Smight (?), v. t. To smite. [Obs.] Spenser.

smilacin.c: Smilacin Smil"a*cin (?), n. [Cf. F. similacine. See Smilax.] (Chem.) See Parrilin.

smilax.c: Smilax Smi"lax (?), n. [L., bindweed, Gr.???.] (Bot.) (a) A genus of perennial climbing plants, usually with a prickly woody stem; green brier, or cat brier. The rootstocks of certain species are the source of the medicine called sarsaparilla. (b) A delicate trailing plant (Myrsiphyllum asparagoides) much used for decoration. It is a native of the Cape of Good Hope.

smile.c: Smile Smile (smīl), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Smiled (smīld); p. pr. & vb. n. Smiling.] [OE. smilen; akin to Dan. smile, Sw. smila, MHG. smielen, smieren, L. mirari to wonder at, Skr. smi to smile; and probably to E. smicker. √173. Cf. Admire, Marvel, Smirk.] 1. To express amusement, pleasure, moderate joy, or love and kindness, by the features of the face; to laugh silently.
Smile Smile, v. t. 1. To express by a smile; as, to smile consent; to smile a welcome to visitors.

Smile Smile, n. [CF. Dan. smiil, Sw. smil. See Smile, v. i.] 1. The act of smiling; a peculiar change or brightening of the face, which expresses pleasure, moderate joy, mirth, approbation, or kindness; -- opposed to frown.

smileless.c: Smileless Smile"less (?), a. Not having a smile.

smiler.c: Smiler Smil"er (?), n. One who smiles. Tennyson.

smilingly.c: Smilingly Smil"ing*ly, adv. In a smiling manner. Shak.

smilingness.c: Smilingness Smil"ing*ness, n. Quality or state of being smiling.

smilodon.c: Smilodon Smi"lo*don (?), n. [Gr.??? a carving knife +???,???, tooth.] (Paleon.) An extinct genus of saber-toothed tigers. See Mach?rodus.

smilt.c: Smilt Smilt (?), v. i. To melt. [Obs.] Mortimer.

sminthurid.c: Sminthurid Smin*thu"rid (?), n. [Gr.??? a mouse +??? tail.] (Zool.) Any one of numerous small species of springtails, of the family Sminthuridae, -- usually found on flowers. See Illust. under Collembola.

smirch.c: Smirch Smirch (?), v. t. [From the root of smear.] To smear with something which stains, or makes dirty; to smutch; to begrime; to soil; to sully.
Smirch Smirch (?), n. A smutch; a dirty stain.

smirk.c: Smirk Smirk (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Smirked (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Smirking.] [OE. smirken, ASS. smercian, smearcian; cf. MHG. smieren, smielen, to smile. See Smile, v. i.] To smile in an affected or conceited manner; to smile with affected complaisance; to simper.
Smirk Smirk, n. A forced or affected smile; a simper.
Smirk Smirk, a. Nice,; smart; spruce; affected; simpering. “So smirk, so smooth.” Spenser.

smirkingly.c: Smirkingly Smirk"ing*ly, adv. With smirking; with a smirk.

smit.c: Smit Smit (?), rare imp. & p. p. of Smite. Spenser.
Smit Smit, obs. 3d. pers. sing. pres. of Smite. Chaucer.

smite.c: Smite Smite (smīt), v. t. [imp. Smote (smōt), rarely Smit (smĭt); p. p. Smitten (smĭt"t'n), rarely Smit, or Smote; p. pr. & vb. n. Smiting (smīt"ĭng).] [AS. smītan to smite, to soil, pollute; akin to OFries. smīta to smite, LG. smiten, D. smijten, G. schmeissen, OHG. smīzan to smear, stroke, OSw. & dial. Sw. smita to smite, Dan. smide to throw, Goth. bismeitan, to anoint, besmear; cf. Skr. mēd to be fat. The original sense seems to have been, to daub on, to smear. Cf. Smut.] 1. To strike; to inflict a blow upon with the hand, or with any instrument held in the hand, or with a missile thrown by the hand; as, to smite with the fist, with a rod, sword, spear, or stone.
Smite Smite, v. i. To strike; to collide; to beat. [Archaic]
Smite Smite, n. The act of smiting; a blow.

smith.c: Smith Smith (smĭth), n. [AS. smið; akin to D. smid, G. schmied, OHG. smid, Icel. smiðr, Dan. & Sw. smed, Goth. smiþa (in comp.); cf. Gr. smi`lh a sort of knife, sminy`h a hoe, mattock.] 1. One who forges with the hammer; one who works in metals; as, a blacksmith, goldsmith, silversmith, and the like. Piers Plowman.
Smith Smith, v. t. [AS. smiðian. See Smith, n.] To beat into shape; to forge. [Obs.] Chaucer.

smithcraft.c: Smithcraft Smith"craft` (-krȧft`), n. The art or occupation of a smith; smithing. [R.] Sir W. Raleigh.

smither.c: Smither Smith"er (smĭth"ẽr), n. 1. Light, fine rain. [Prov. Eng.]

smithereens.c: Smithereens Smith`er*eens" (smĭth`ẽr*ēnz"), n. pl. Fragments; atoms; smithers. [Colloq.] W. Black.

smithery.c: Smithery Smith"er*y (smĭth"ẽr*y̆), n.; pl. -ies (-ĭz). 1. The workshop of a smith; a smithy or stithy.

smithing.c: Smithing Smith"ing, n. The act or art of working or forging metals, as iron, into any desired shape. Moxon.

smithsonian.c: Smithsonian Smith*so"ni*an (-sō"nĭ*ain), a. Of or pertaining to the Englishman J. L. M. Smithson, or to the national institution of learning which he endowed at Washington, D. C.; as, the Smithsonian Institution; Smithsonian Reports. -- n. The Smithsonian Institution.

smithsonite.c: Smithsonite Smith"son*ite (?), n. [See Smithsonian.] (Min.) Native zinc carbonate. It generally occurs in stalactitic, reniform, or botryoidal shapes, of a white to gray, green, or brown color. See Note under Calamine.

smithy.c: Smithy Smith"y (-y̆), n. [AS. smiððe, fr. smið; akin to D. smidse, smids, OHG. smitta, G. schmiede, Icel. smiðja. See Smith, n.] The workshop of a smith, esp. a blacksmith; a smithery; a stithy. [Written also smiddy.]

smitt.c: Smitt Smitt (smĭt), n. [CF. G. schmitz a stain, schmitzen besmear. See Smite, v. t.] Fine clay or ocher made up into balls, used for marking sheep. [Eng.] Woodward.

smittle.c: Smittle Smit"tle (-t'l), v. t. [Freq. fr. OE. smitten to befoul. See Smite, v. t.] To infect. [Prov. Eng.]

smittlish.c: Smittlish Smittle { Smit"tle (smĭt"t'l), Smit"tlish (-tlĭsh), } a. Infectious; catching. [Scot. & Prov. Eng.] H. Kingsley.

smock.c: Smock Smock (smŏk), n. [AS. smocc; akin to OHG. smocho, Icel. smokkr, and from the root of AS. smūgan to creep, akin to G. schmiegen to cling to, press close, MHG. smiegen, Icel. smjūga to creep through, to put on a garment which has a hole to put the head through; cf. Lith. smukti to glide. Cf. Smug, Smuggle.] 1. A woman's under-garment; a shift; a chemise.
Smock Smock (?), a. Of or pertaining to a smock; resembling a smock; hence, of or pertaining to a woman.
Smock Smock, v. t. To provide with, or clothe in, a smock or a smock frock. Tennyson.
Smock frock Smock" frock` (?). A coarse frock, or shirt, worn over the other dress, as by farm laborers. Macaulay.

smockfaced.c: Smock-faced Smock"-faced` (?), a. Having a feminine countenance or complexion; smooth-faced; girlish. Fenton.

smockless.c: Smockless Smock"less, a. Lacking a smock. Chaucer.

smokable.c: Smokable Smok"a*ble (?), a. Capable of being smoked; suitable or ready to be smoked; as, smokable tobacco.

smoke.c: Smoke Smoke (smōk), n. [AS. smoca, fr. smeócan to smoke; akin to LG. & D. smook smoke, Dan. smög, G. schmauch, and perh. to Gr.??? to burn in a smoldering fire; cf. Lith. smaugti to choke.] 1. The visible exhalation, vapor, or substance that escapes, or expelled, from a burning body, especially from burning vegetable matter, as wood, coal, peat, or the like.

Smoke Smoke, v. i. [imp. & p. p. Smoked (?); p. pr. & vb n. Smoking.] [AS. smocian; akin to D. smoken, G. schmauchen, Dan. smöge. See Smoke, n.] 1. To emit smoke; to throw off volatile matter in the form of vapor or exhalation; to reek.
Smoke Smoke, v. t. 1. To apply smoke to; to hang in smoke; to disinfect, to cure, etc., by smoke; as, to smoke or fumigate infected clothing; to smoke beef or hams for preservation.
Smoke ball Smoke ball. Same as Puffball.

smokedry.c: Smoke-dry Smoke"-dry` (?), v. t. To dry by or in smoke.

smokehouse.c: Smokehouse Smoke"house` (?), n. A building where meat or fish is cured by subjecting it to a dense smoke.

smokejack.c: Smokejack Smoke"jack` (?), n. A contrivance for turning a spit by means of a fly or wheel moved by the current of ascending air in a chimney.

smokeless.c: Smokeless Smoke"less, a. Making or having no smoke. “Smokeless towers.” Pope.
Smokeless powder Smoke"less pow"der. A high-explosive gunpowder whose explosion produces little, if any, smoke. It is usually based on guncotton (nitrocellulose).

smoker.c: Smoker Smok"er (?), n. 1. One who dries or preserves by smoke.

smokestack.c: Smokestack Smoke"stack` (?), n. A chimney; esp., a pipe serving as a chimney, as the pipe which carries off the smoke of a locomotive, the funnel of a steam vessel, etc.

smokily.c: Smokily Smok"i*ly (?), adv. In a smoky manner.

smokiness.c: Smokiness Smok"i*ness, n. The quality or state of being smoky.

smoky.c: Smoky Smok"y (?), a. [Compar. Smokier (?); superl. Smokiest.] 1. Emitting smoke, esp. in large quantities or in an offensive manner; fumid; as, smoky fires.

smoulder.c: Smoulder Smolder { Smol"der, Smoul"der } (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Smoldered (?) or Smouldered; p. pr. & vb. n. Smoldering or Smouldering.] [OE. smolderen; cf. Prov. G. smölen, smelen, D. smeulen. Cf. Smell.] 1. To burn and smoke without flame; to waste away by a slow and supressed combustion.
Smoulder Smolder { Smol"der, Smoul"der, } v. t. To smother; to suffocate; to choke. [Obs.] Holinshed. Palsgrave.
Smoulder Smolder { Smol"der, Smoul"der, } n. Smoke; smother. [Obs.]

smouldering.c: Smouldering Smoldering { Smol"der*ing, Smoul"der*ing, } a. Being in a state of suppressed activity; quiet but not dead.

smoulderingness.c: Smoulderingness Smolderingness { Smol"der*ing*ness, Smoul"der*ing*ness } (?), n. The state of smoldering.

smouldry.c: Smouldry Smoldry { Smol"dry, Smoul"dry } (?), a. Smoldering; suffocating; smothery. [Obs.]

smolt.c: Smolt Smolt (?), n. (Zool.) A young salmon two or three years old, when it has acquired its silvery color.

smoor.c: Smoor Smoor (?), v. t. [AS. smorian; akin to D. & LG. smoren, G. schmoren to stew. Cf. Smother.] To suffocate or smother. [Written also smore.] [Obs. or Prov. Eng. & Scot.] Sir T. More. Burns.

smooth.c: Smooth Smooth (smōoth), a. [Compar. Smoother (smōoth"ẽr); superl. Smoothest.] [OE. smothe, smethe, AS. smēðe, smœðe, where ē, œ, come from an older ō; cf. LG. smöde, smöe, smödig; of uncertain origin.] 1. Having an even surface, or a surface so even that no roughness or points can be perceived by the touch; not rough; as, smooth glass; smooth porcelain. Chaucer.
Smooth Smooth, n. 1. The act of making smooth; a stroke which smooths. Thackeray.

Smooth Smooth, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Smoothed (smōothd); p. pr. & vb. n. Smoothing.] [OE. smothen, smethen, AS. smēðian; cf. LG. smöden. See Smooth, a.] To make smooth; to make even on the surface by any means; as, to smooth a board with a plane; to smooth cloth with an iron. Specifically: --
Smooth Smooth, v. i. To flatter; to use blandishment.

smoothbore.c: Smoothbore Smooth"bore` (?), a. (Gun.) Having a bore of perfectly smooth surface; -- distinguished from rifled. -- n. A smoothbore firearm.

smoothchinned.c: Smooth-chinned Smooth"-chinned` (?), a. Having a smooth chin; beardless. Drayton.

smoothen.c: Smoothen Smooth"en (?), v. t. To make smooth. [Obs.]

smoother.c: Smoother Smooth"er (?), n. One who, or that which, smooths.

smoothing.c: Smoothing Smooth"ing, a. & n. fr. Smooth, v.

smoothly.c: Smoothly Smooth"ly, adv. In a smooth manner.

smoothness.c: Smoothness Smooth"ness, n. Quality or state of being smooth.

smoothspoken.c: Smooth-spoken Smooth"-spo`ken (?), a. Speaking smoothly; plausible; flattering; smooth-tongued.

smoothtongued.c: Smooth-tongued Smooth"-tongued` (?), a. Having a smooth tongue; plausible; flattering.

smore.c: Smore Smore (?), v. t. To smother. See Smoor. [Obs.]

smorsato.c: Smorsato Smorzando { ‖Smor*zan"do (?), ‖Smor*sa"to (?), } a. [It.] (Mus.) Growing gradually fainter and softer; dying away; morendo.

smote.c: Smote Smote (?), imp. (and rare p. p.) of Smite.

smoterlich.c: Smoterlich Smo"ter*lich (?), a. [CF. Smut.] Dirty; foul. [Obs.] Chaucer.

smother.c: Smother Smoth"er (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Smothered (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Smothering.] [OE. smotheren; akin to E. smoor. See Smoor.] 1. To destroy the life of by suffocation; to deprive of the air necessary for life; to cover up closely so as to prevent breathing; to suffocate; as, to smother a child.
Smother Smoth"er, v. i. 1. To be suffocated or stifled.
Smother Smoth"er, n. [OE. smorther. See Smother, v. t.] 1. Stifling smoke; thick dust. Shak.

smothered.c: Smothered mate Smoth"ered mate. (Chess) Checkmate given when movement of the king is completely obstructed by his own men. This can only occur when an opponent moves a knight into a position to give a check to the king.

smotheriness.c: Smotheriness Smoth"er*i*ness (?), n. The quality or state of being smothery.

smotheringly.c: Smotheringly Smoth"er*ing*ly, adv. In a smothering manner.

smothery.c: Smothery Smoth"er*y (?), a. Tending to smother; stifling.

smouch.c: Smouch Smouch (?), v. t. [Akin to smack.] To kiss closely. [Obs.] P. Stubbes.
Smouch Smouch, v. t. [See Smutch.] To smutch; to soil; as, to smouch the face.
Smouch Smouch, n. A dark soil or stain; a smutch.

smudge.c: Smudge Smudge (?), n. [Cf. Dan. smuds smut, E. smutch, or smoke.] 1. A suffocating smoke. Grose.
Smudge Smudge, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Smudged (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Smudging.] 1. To stifle or smother with smoke; to smoke by means of a smudge.

smudginess.c: Smudginess Smudg"i*ness (?), n. The quality or state of being smudged, soiled, or blurred. C. A. Young.

smug.c: Smug Smug (?), a. [Of. Scand. or Low German origin; cf. LG. smuck, G. schmuck, Dan. smuk, OSw. smuck, smöck, and E. smock, smuggle; cf. G. schmuck ornament. See Smock.] Studiously neat or nice, especially in dress; spruce; affectedly precise; smooth and prim.
Smug Smug, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Smugged (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Smugging.] To make smug, or spruce. [Obs.]

smuggle.c: Smuggle Smug"gle (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Smuggled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Smuggling (?).] [Of Low German or Scand. origin; cf. LG. smuggeln, D. smokkelen, G. schmuggeln, Dan. smugle, Sw. smyga to introduce or convey secretly, Dan. i smug secretly, D. smuigen to eat in secret, AS. sm?gan to creep. See Smock.] 1. To import or export secretly, contrary to the law; to import or export without paying the duties imposed by law; as, to smuggle lace.
Smuggle Smug"gle, v. i. To import or export in violation of the customs laws.

smugly.c: Smugly Smug"ly, adv. In a smug manner. [R.] Gay.

smugness.c: Smugness Smug"ness, n. The quality or state of being smug.

smut.c: Smut Smut (?), n. [Akin to Sw. smuts, Dan. smuds, MHG. smuz, G. schmutz, D. smet a spot or stain, smoddig, smodsig, smodderig, dirty, smodderen to smut; and probably to E. smite. See Smite, v. t., and cf. Smitt, Smutch.] 1. Foul matter, like soot or coal dust; also, a spot or soil made by such matter.
Smut Smut (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Smutted; p. pr. & vb. n. Smutting.] 1. To stain or mark with smut; to blacken with coal, soot, or other dirty substance.
Smut Smut, v. i. 1. To gather smut; to be converted into smut; to become smutted. Mortimer.

smutch.c: Smutch Smutch (?), n. [Prob. for smuts. See Smut, n.] A stain; a dirty spot. B. Jonson.
Smutch Smutch, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Smutched (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Smutching.] To blacken with smoke, soot, or coal. [Written also smooch.] B. Jonson.

smutty.c: Smutty Smut"ty (?), a. [Compar. Smuttier (?); superl. Smuttiest.] 1. Soiled with smut; smutted.

smyrniot.c: Smyrniot Smyr"ni*ot (?), a. Of or pertaining to Smyrna. -- n. A native or inhabitant of Smyrna.

snack.c: Snack Snack (?), n. [See Snatch, v. t.] 1. A share; a part or portion; -- obsolete, except in the colloquial phrase, to go snacks, i. e., to share.

snacot.c: Snacot Snac"ot (?), n. [Said to be corrupted fr. NL. syngnathus, fr. Gr. sy`n together + gna`qos jaw, because the jaws can be only slightly separated.] (Zool.) A pipefish of the genus Syngnathus. See Pipefish.

snaffle.c: Snaffle Snaf"fle (?), n. [D. snavel a beak, bill, snout; akin to G. schnabel, OHG. snabul,. sneb, snebbe, OFries. snavel mouth, Dan. & Sw. snabel beak, bill, Lith. snapas, and to E. snap, v. See Snap, and cf. Neb.] A kind of bridle bit, having a joint in the part to be placed in the mouth, and rings and cheek pieces at the ends, but having no curb; -- called also snaffle bit.
Snaffle Snaf"fle, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Snaffled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Snaffling (?).] To put a snaffle in the mouth of; to subject to the snaffle; to bridle.

snag.c: Snag Snag (?), n. [Prov. E., n., a lump on a tree where a branch has been cut off; v., to cut off the twigs and small branches from a tree, of Celtic origin; cf. Gael. snaigh, snaidh, to cut down, to prune, to sharpen, p. p. snaighte, snaidhte, cut off, lopped, Ir. snaigh a hewing, cutting.] 1. A stump or base of a branch that has been lopped off; a short branch, or a sharp or rough branch; a knot; a protuberance.
Snag Snag, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Snagged (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Snagging (?).] 1. To cut the snags or branches from, as the stem of a tree; to hew roughly. [Prov. Eng.] Halliwell.

snagged.c: Snagged Snag"ged (?), a. Full of snags; snaggy.

snaggy.c: Snaggy Snag"gy (?), a. 1. Full of snags; full of short, rough branches or sharp points; abounding with knots. “Upon a snaggy oak.” Spenser.

snail.c: Snail Snail (snāl), n. [OE. snaile, AS. snægel, snegel, snægl; akin to G. schnecke, OHG. snecko, Dan. snegl, Icel. snigill.] 1. (Zool.) (a) Any one of numerous species of terrestrial air-breathing gastropods belonging to the genus Helix and many allied genera of the family Helicidae. They are abundant in nearly all parts of the world except the arctic regions, and feed almost entirely on vegetation; a land snail. (b) Any gastropod having a general resemblance to the true snails, including fresh-water and marine species. See Pond snail, under Pond, and Sea snail.

snaillike.c: Snail-like Snail"-like` (?), a. Like or suiting a snail; as, snail-like progress.
Snail-like Snail"-like`, adv. In the manner of a snail; slowly.

snailpaced.c: Snail-paced Snail"-paced` (?), a. Slow-moving, like a snail.

snails.c: Snails 'Snails (?), interj. God's nails, or His nails, that is, the nails with which the Savior was fastened to the cross; -- an ancient form of oath, corresponding to 'Od's bodikins (dim. of body, i.e., God's dear body). Beau. & Fl.

snake.c: Snake Snake (?), n. [AS. snaca; akin to LG. snake, schnake, Icel. snākr, sn?kr, Dan. snog, Sw. snok; of uncertain origin.] (Zool.) Any species of the order Ophidia; an ophidian; a serpent, whether harmless or venomous. See Ophidia, and Serpent.
Snake Snake, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Snaked (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Snaking.] 1. To drag or draw, as a snake from a hole; -- often with out. [Colloq. U.S.] Bartlett.
Snake Snake, v. i. To crawl like a snake.

snakebird.c: Snakebird Snake"bird` (?), n. [So named from its snakelike neck.] (Zool.) 1. Any one of four species of aquatic birds of the genus Anhinga or Plotus. They are allied to the gannets and cormorants, but have very long, slender, flexible necks, and sharp bills.

snakefish.c: Snakefish Snake"fish` (?), n. (Zool.) (a) The band fish. (b) The lizard fish.

snakehead.c: Snakehead Snake"head` (?), n. 1. A loose, bent-up end of one of the strap rails, or flat rails, formerly used on American railroads. It was sometimes so bent by the passage of a train as to slip over a wheel and pierce the bottom of a car.

snakeroot.c: Snakeroot Snake"root` (?), n. (Bot.) Any one of several plants of different genera and species, most of which are (or were formerly) reputed to be efficacious as remedies for the bites of serpents; also, the roots of any of these.

snakeshead.c: Snake's-head Snake's"-head` (?), n. (Bot.) The Guinea-hen flower; -- so called in England because its spotted petals resemble the scales of a snake's head. Dr. Prior.

snakestone.c: Snakestone Snake"stone` (?), n. 1. A kind of hone slate or whetstone obtained in Scotland.

snakeweed.c: Snakeweed Snake"weed` (?), n. (Bot.) (a) A kind of knotweed (Polygonum Bistorta). (b) The Virginia snakeroot. See Snakeroot.

snakewood.c: Snakewood Snake"wood` (?), n. (Bot.) (a) An East Indian climbing plant (Strychnos colubrina) having a bitter taste, and supposed to be a remedy for the bite of the hooded serpent. (b) An East Indian climbing shrub (Ophioxylon serpentinum) which has the roots and stems twisted so as to resemble serpents. (c) Same as Trumpetwood. (d) A tropical American shrub (Plumieria rubra) which has very fragrant red blossoms. (e) Same as Letterwood.

snakish.c: Snakish Snak"ish (?), a. Having the qualities or characteristics of a snake; snaky.

snaky.c: Snaky Snak"y (?), a. 1. Of or pertaining to a snake or snakes; resembling a snake; serpentine; winding.

snap.c: Snap Snap (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Snapped (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Snapping.] [LG. or D. snappen to snap up, to snatch; akin to G. schnappen, MHG. snaben, Dan. snappe, and to D. snavel beak, bill. Cf. Neb, Snaffle, n.] 1. To break at once; to break short, as substances that are brittle.
Snap Snap, v. i. 1. To break short, or at once; to part asunder suddenly; as, a mast snaps; a needle snaps.
Snap Snap, n. [Cf. D. snap a snatching. See Snap, v. t.] 1. A sudden breaking or rupture of any substance.
Snap Snap, a. Done, performed, made, executed, carried through, or the like, quickly and without deliberation; as, a snap judgment or decision; a snap political convention. [Colloq.]
Snap shot Snapshot Snap"shot` (?), n. 1. Commonly Snap shot. (a) A quick offhand shot, made without deliberately taking aim over the sights. (b) (Photog.) Act of taking a snapshot (in sense 2).

snapdragon.c: Snapdragon Snap"drag`on (?), n. 1. (Bot.) (a) Any plant of the scrrophulariaceous genus Antirrhinum, especially the cultivated Antirrhinum majus, whose showy flowers are fancifully likened to the face of a dragon. (b) A West Indian herb (Ruellia tuberosa) with curiously shaped blue flowers.

snape.c: Snape Snape (?), v. t. (Shipbuilding) To bevel the end of a timber to fit against an inclined surface.

snaphance.c: Snaphance Snap"hance` (?), n. [D. snaphaan a gun, originally, the snapping cock of a gun. See Snap, and Hen.] 1. A spring lock for discharging a firearm; also, the firearm to which it is attached. [Obs.]

snaphead.c: Snaphead Snap"head` (?), n. A hemispherical or rounded head to a rivet or bolt; also, a swaging tool with a cavity in its face for forming such a rounded head.

snapper.c: Snapper Snap"per (?), n. 1. One who, or that which, snaps; as, a snapper up of trifles; the snapper of a whip.

snapping.c: Snapping Snap"ping (?), a. & n. from Snap, v.

snappish.c: Snappish Snap"pish (?), a. 1. Apt to snap at persons or things; eager to bite; as, a snapping cur.

snapsack.c: Snapsack Snap"sack` (?), n. [Cf. Sw. snappsäck, G. schnappsack.] A knapsack. [Obs.] South.

snar.c: Snar Snar (?), v. i. [Akin to LG. & OD. snarren, G. schnarren, E. snore. See Snore, and cf. Snarl to growl.] To snarl. [Obs.] Spenser.

snare.c: Snare Snare (?), n. [AS. sneara cord, a string; akin to D. snoer, G. schnur, OHG. snour a cord, snarahha a noose, Dan. snare, Sw. & Icel. snara, Goth. sn?rj? a basket; and probably also to E. needle. See Needle, and cf. Snarl to entangle.] 1. A contrivance, often consisting of a noose of cord, or the like, by which a bird or other animal may be entangled and caught; a trap; a gin.
Snare Snare, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Snared (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Snaring.] To catch with a snare; to insnare; to entangle; hence, to bring into unexpected evil, perplexity, or danger.

snarer.c: Snarer Snar"er (?), n. One who lays snares, or entraps.

snarl.c: Snarl Snarl (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Snarled (?); p. pr. & vvb. n. Snarling.] [Etymol. uncertain.] To form raised work upon the outer surface of (thin metal ware) by the repercussion of a snarling iron upon the inner surface.
Snarl Snarl, v. t. [From Snare, v. t.] 1. To entangle; to complicate; to involve in knots; as, to snarl a skein of thread. “Her snarled hair.” Spenser.
Snarl Snarl, n. A knot or complication of hair, thread, or the like, difficult to disentangle; entanglement; hence, intricate complication; embarrassing difficulty.
Snarl Snarl, v. i. [From Snar.] 1. To growl, as an angry or surly dog; to gnarl; to utter grumbling sounds. “An angry cur snarls while he feeds.” Dryden & Lee.
Snarl Snarl, n. The act of snarling; a growl; a surly or peevish expression; an angry contention.

snarler.c: Snarler Snarl"er (?), n. One who snarls; a surly, growling animal; a grumbling, quarrelsome fellow.
Snarler Snarl"er, n. One who makes use of a snarling iron.

snarling.c: Snarling Snarl"ing, a. & n. from Snarl, v.

snary.c: Snary Snar"y (?), a. [From Snare.] Resembling, or consisting of, snares; entangling; insidious.

snast.c: Snast Snast (?), n. [Cf. Snite, v. t.] The snuff, or burnt wick, of a candle. [Obs.] Bacon.

snatch.c: Snatch Snatch (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Snatched (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Snatching.] [OE. snachen, snechen; akin to D. snakken to gasp, to long (for), to desire. Cf. Snack, n., Sneck.] 1. To take or seize hastily, abruptly, or without permission or ceremony; as, to snatch a loaf or a kiss.
Snatch Snatch, v. i. To attempt to seize something suddenly; to catch; -- often with at; as, to snatch at a rope.
Snatch Snatch (?), n. 1. A hasty catching or seizing; a grab; a catching at, or attempt to seize, suddenly.
Snatch block Snatch block (Naut.), a kind of block with an opening in one side to receive the bight of a rope.

snatcher.c: Snatcher Snatch"er (?), n. One who snatches, or takes abruptly.

snath.c: Snath Snath (snăth), n. [Cf. AS. snīðan to cut, to mow, snǣd a bite, bit, snip.] The handle of a scythe; a snead. [Variously written in England snead, sneed, sneath, sneeth, snathe, etc.; in Scotland written sned.]

snathe.c: Snathe Snathe (snāth), v. t. [Cf. Icel. sneiða to cut into alices, snīða to cut; akin to AS. besnǣdan, snīðan, G. schneiden, OHG. snīdan, Goth. sneiþan to cut, to reap, and E. snath, snithe.] To lop; to prune. [Prov. Eng.]

snattock.c: Snattock Snat"tock (snăt"tŭk), n. [See Snathe.] A chip; a slice. [Prov. Eng.] Gayton.

snaw.c: Snaw Snaw (snä), n. Snow. [Obs. or Scot.] Burns.

sneak.c: Sneak Sneak (snēk), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Sneaked (snēkt); p. pr. & vb. n. Sneaking.] [OE. sniken, AS. snīcan to creep; akin to Dan. snige sig; cf. Icel. snīkja to hanker after.] 1. To creep or steal (away or about) privately; to come or go meanly, as a person afraid or ashamed to be seen; as, to sneak away from company. imp. & p. p. "snuck" is more common now, but not even mentioned here. In MW10, simply "sneaked or snuck" -->
Sneak Sneak, v. t. To hide, esp. in a mean or cowardly manner. [Obs.] “[Slander] sneaks its head.” Wake.
Sneak Sneak, n. 1. A mean, sneaking fellow.
Sneak current Sneak current. (Elec.) A current which, though too feeble to blow the usual fuse or to injure at once telegraph or telephone instruments, will in time burn them out.

sneakcup.c: Sneak-cup Sneak"-cup` (?), n. One who sneaks from his cups; one who balks his glass. [Obs.] Shak.

sneaker.c: Sneaker Sneak"er (snēk"ẽr), n. 1. One who sneaks. Lamb.

sneakiness.c: Sneakiness Sneak"i*ness (?), n. The quality of being sneaky.

sneaking.c: Sneaking Sneak"ing, a. Marked by cowardly concealment; deficient in openness and courage; underhand; mean; crouching. -- Sneak"ing*ly, adv. -- Sneak"ing*ness, n.

sneaksby.c: Sneaksby Sneaks"by (?), n. A paltry fellow; a sneak. [Obs.] “Such a bashful sneaksby.” Barrow.

sneaky.c: Sneaky Sneak"y (?), n. Like a sneak; sneaking.

sneap.c: Sneap Sneap (?), v. t. [Cf. Icel. sneypa to dishonor, disgrace, chide, but also E. snip, and snub.] 1. To check; to reprimand; to rebuke; to chide. [Obs.] Bp. Hall.
Sneap Sneap, n. A reprimand; a rebuke. [Obs.]

sneathe.c: Sneathe Sneath { Sneath (?), Sneathe (?), } n. See Snath.

sneb.c: Sneb Sneb (?), v. t. [See Snib.] To reprimand; to sneap. [Obs.] “Scold and sneb the good oak.” Spenser.

sneck.c: Sneck Sneck (?), v. t. [See Snatch.] To fasten by a hatch; to latch, as a door. [Scot. & Prov. Eng.]
Sneck Sneck, n. A door latch. [Scot. & Prov. Eng.]

snecket.c: Snecket Sneck"et (?), n. A door latch, or sneck. [Prov. Eng.]

sned.c: Sned Sned (?), v. t. To lop; to snathe. [Prov. Eng.]

sneed.c: Sneed Sned { Sned (?), Sneed (?), } n. See Snath.

sneer.c: Sneer Sneer (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Sneered (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Sneering.] [OE. sneren, Dan. sn?rre to snarl or grin (like a dog); cf. Prov. E. sneer to grin, sner to snort, snert to sneer at. See Snore, v. i.] 1. To show contempt by turning up the nose, or by a particular facial expression.
Sneer Sneer, v. t. 1. To utter with a grimace or contemptuous expression; to utter with a sneer; to say sneeringly; as, to sneer fulsome lies at a person. Congreve.
Sneer Sneer, n. 1. The act of sneering.

sneeringly.c: Sneeringly Sneer"ing*ly, adv. In a sneering manner.

sneeze.c: Sneeze Sneeze (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Sneezed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Sneezing.] [OE. snesen; of uncertain origin; cf. D. snuse to sniff, E. neese, and AS. fneósan.] To emit air, chiefly through the nose, audibly and violently, by a kind of involuntary convulsive force, occasioned by irritation of the inner membrane of the nose.
Sneeze Sneeze, n. A sudden and violent ejection of air with an audible sound, chiefly through the nose.

sneezeweed.c: Sneezeweed Sneeze"weed` (?), n. (Bot.) A yellow-flowered composite plant (Helenium autumnale) the odor of which is said to cause sneezing.

sneezewood.c: Sneezewood Sneeze"wood` (?), n. (Bot.) The wood of a South African tree. See Neishout.

sneezewort.c: Sneezewort Sneeze"wort` (?), n. (Bot.) A European herbaceous plant (Achillea Ptarmica) allied to the yarrow, having a strong, pungent smell.

sneezing.c: Sneezing Sneez"ing, n. (Physiol.) The act of violently forcing air out through the nasal passages while the cavity of the mouth is shut off from the pharynx by the approximation of the soft palate and the base of the tongue.

snell.c: Snell Snell (?), a. [AS. snell; akin to D. snel, G. schnell, OHG. snel, Icel. snjallr valiant.] Active; brisk; nimble; quick; sharp. [Archaic or Prov. Eng. & Scot.]
Snell Snell, n. A short line of horsehair, gut, etc., by which a fishhook is attached to a longer line.

snet.c: Snet Snet (?), n. [Cf. G. schnitt that which is cut, fr. schneiden to cut, E. snath.] The fat of a deer. [Obs. or Prov. Eng.]
Snet Snet, v. t. [See Snot.] The clear of mucus; to blow. [Obs.] “Snetting his nose.” Holland.

snew.c: Snew Snew (?), v. i. To snow; to abound. [Obs.]

snib.c: Snib Snib (?), v. t. [OE. snibben; cf. Dan. snibbe, and E. snub, v. t.] To check; to sneap; to sneb. [Obs.]
Snib Snib, n. A reprimand; a snub. [Obs.] Marston.

snick.c: Snick Snick (?), n. [Prov. E. snick a notch; cf. Icel. snikka nick, cut.] 1. A small cut or mark.
Snick Snick, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Snicked (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Snicking.] 1. To cut slightly; to strike, or strike off, as by cutting. H. Kingsley.
Snick Snick, n. & v. t. See Sneck. [Prov. Eng. & Scot.]

snicker.c: Snicker Snick"er (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Snickered (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Snickering.] [Cf. D. snikken to sob, to sigh.] [Written also snigger.] 1. To laugh slyly; to laugh in one's sleeve.
Snicker Snick"er, n. A half suppressed, broken laugh. [Written also snigger.]

snide.c: Snide Snide (?), a. 1. Tricky; deceptive; contemptible; as, a snide lawyer; snide goods. [Slang, archaic]

snider.c: Snider Snider rifle { Sni"der ri"fle, or Sni"der, } n. (Mil.) A breech-loading rifle formerly used in the British service; -- so called from the inventor.

sniff.c: Sniff Sniff (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Sniffed (?) or Snift; p. pr. & vb. n. Sniffing.] [OE. sneven; akin to snivel, snuff; cf. Dan. snive to sniff. See Snuff, v. t.] To draw air audibly up the nose; to snuff; -- sometimes done as a gesture of suspicion, offense, or contempt.
Sniff Sniff, v. t. 1. To draw in with the breath through the nose; as, to sniff the air of the country.
Sniff Sniff, n. The act of sniffing; perception by sniffing; that which is taken by sniffing; as, a sniff of air.

sniffing.c: Sniffing Sniff"ing, n. (Physiol.) A rapid inspiratory act, in which the mouth is kept shut and the air drawn in through the nose.

sniffle.c: Sniffle Snif"fle (?), v. i. [Freq. of sniff. See Snivel.] To snuffle, as one does with a catarrh. [Prov. Eng.]

snift.c: Snift Snift (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Snifted; p. pr. & vb. n. Snifting.] [From Sniff.] 1. To snort. [Obs.] “Resentment expressed by snifting.” Johnson.
Snift Snift, n. 1. A moment. [Prov. Eng.] Halliwell.

snig.c: Snig Snig (?), v. t. [See Snick a small cut.] To chop off; to cut. [Prov. Eng.]
Snig Snig, v. i. [See Sneak.] To sneak. [Prov. Eng.]

snigg.c: Snigg Snig { Snig, Snigg, } n. [Cf. Sneak.] (Zool.) A small eel. [Prov. Eng.]

snigger.c: Snigger Snig"ger (?), v. i. See Snicker. Thackeray.

sniggle.c: Sniggle Snig"gle (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Sniggled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Sniggling(?).] [See Snig a kind of eel.] To fish for eels by thrusting the baited hook into their holes or hiding places. Walton.
Sniggle Snig"gle, v. t. To catch, as an eel, by sniggling; hence, to hook; to insnare. Beau. & Fl.

snip.c: Snip Snip (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Snipped (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Snipping.] [D. snippen; akin to G. schnippen.] To cut off the nip or neb of, or to cut off at once with shears or scissors; to clip off suddenly; to nip; hence, to break off; to snatch away.
Snip Snip (?), n. 1. A single cut, as with shears or scissors; a clip. Shak.

snipe.c: Snipe Snipe (?), n. [OE. snipe; akin to D. snep, snip, LG. sneppe, snippe, G. schnepfe, Icel. snīpa (in comp.), Dan. sneppe, Sw. snäppa a sanpiper, and possibly to E. snap. See Snap, Snaffle.] 1. (Zool.) Any one of numerous species of limicoline game birds of the family Scolopacidae, having a long, slender, nearly straight beak.
Snipe Snipe (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Sniped (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Sniping (?).] 1. To shoot or hunt snipe.
Snipe Snipe (?), v. t. 1. To shoot at (detached men of an enemy's force) at long range, esp. when not in action.

snipebill.c: Snipebill Snipe"bill` (?), n. 1. A plane for cutting deep grooves in moldings.

snipefish.c: Snipefish Snipe"fish` (?), n. (Zool.) (a) The bellows fish. (b) A long, slender deep-sea fish (Nemichthys scolopaceus) with a slender beak.

snippack.c: Snippack Snip"pack (?), n. [Cf. Snipe.] (Zool.) The common snipe. [Prov. Eng.]

snippersnaper.c: Snipper-snaper Snip"per-snap`er (?), n. A small, insignificant fellow. [Colloq.]

snippet.c: Snippet Snip"pet (?), n. A small part or piece.

snippety.c: Snippety Snip"pet*y (?), a. Ridiculously small; petty. “Snippety facts.” London Spectator.

snipsnap.c: Snip-snap Snip"-snap` (?), n. [Reduplication of snap.] A tart dialogue with quick replies. [R.] Pope.
Snip-snap Snip"-snap`, a. Quick; short; sharp; smart. Shak.

snite.c: Snite Snite (snīt), n. A snipe. [Obs. or Scot.] Carew.
Snite Snite, v. t. [Icel. snīfa. See Snout.] To blow, as the nose; to snuff, as a candle. [Obs. or Scot.]

snithy.c: Snithy Snithe { Snithe (?), Snith"y (?), } a. [AS. snīðan to cut. See Snathe.] Sharp; piercing; cutting; -- applied to the wind. [Prov. Eng.]

snivel.c: Snivel Sniv"el (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Sniveled (?) or Snivelled; p. pr. & vb. n. Sniveling or Snivelling.] [OE. snivelen, snevelen, snuvelen, freg. of sneven. See Sniff, and cf. Snuffle.] 1. To run at the nose; to make a snuffling noise.
Snivel Sniv"el, n. [AS. snofel. Cf. Snivel, v. i.] Mucus from the nose; snot.

sniveler.c: Sniveler Sniv"el*er (?), n. [Written also sniveller.] One who snivels, esp. one who snivels habitually.

snively.c: Snively Sniv"el*y (?), a. Running at the nose; sniveling pitiful; whining.

snob.c: Snob Snob (?), n. [Icel. snāpr a dolt, impostor, charlatan. Cf. Snub.] 1. A vulgar person who affects to be better, richer, or more fashionable, than he really is; a vulgar upstart; one who apes his superiors. Thackeray.

snobbery.c: Snobbery Snob"ber*y (?), n. The quality of being snobbish; snobbishness.

snobbish.c: Snobbish Snob"bish (?), a. Of or pertaining to a snob; characteristic of, or befitting, a snob; vulgarly pretentious. -- Snob"bish*ly, adv.

snobbishness.c: Snobbishness Snob"bish*ness, n. Vulgar affectation or ostentation; mean admiration of mean things; conduct or manners of a snob.

snobby.c: Snobby Snob"by (snŏb"by̆), a. Snobbish. [R.] E. B. Ramsay.

snobling.c: Snobling Snob"ling, n. A little snob. [Jocose] Thackeray.

snobocracy.c: Snobocracy Snob*oc"ra*cy (snŏb*ŏk"rȧ*sy̆), n. [Snob + -cracy, as in aristocracy, mobocracy.] Snobs, collectively. [Hybrid & Recent] C. Kingsley.

snod.c: Snod Snod (snŏd), n. [See Snood.] A fillet; a headband; a snood. [Obs. or Prov. Eng.]
Snod Snod, a. [Scot. snod to prune, put in order.] Trimmed; smooth; neat; trim; sly; cunning; demure. [Prov. Eng. & Scot.]

snoff.c: Snoff Snoff (snŏf; 115), n. [Cf. Snuff.] (Mining) A short candle end used for igniting a fuse. Raymond.

snood.c: Snood Snood (?), n. [AS. snōd. Cf. Snare.] 1. The fillet which binds the hair of a young unmarried woman, and is emblematic of her maiden character. [Scot.]
Snood Snood, v. t. To bind or braid up, as the hair, with a snood. [Scot.]

snooded.c: Snooded Snood"ed, a. Wearing or having a snood. “The snooded daughter.” Whittier.

snook.c: Snook Snook (snōok), v. i. [Prov. E. snook to search out, to follow by the scent; cf. Sw. snoka to lurk, LG. snöggen, snuckern, snökern, to snuffle, to smell about, to search for.] To lurk; to lie in ambush. [Obs.]

Snook Snook, n. [D. snoek.] (Zool.) (a) A large perchlike marine food fish (Centropomus undecimalis) found both on the Atlantic and Pacific coasts of tropical America; -- called also ravallia, and robalo. (b) The cobia. (c) The garfish.

snooze.c: Snooze Snooze (snōoz), n. [Scot. snooze to sleep; cf. Dan. & Sw. snus snuff.] A short sleep; a nap. [Colloq.]
Snooze Snooze, v. i. [imp. & p. p. Snoozed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Snoozing.] To doze; to drowse; to take a short nap; to slumber. [Colloq.]

snore.c: Snore Snore (snōr), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Snored (snōrd); p. pr. & vb. n. Snoring.] [OE. snoren, AS. snora a snoring; akin to LG. snoren, snorken, snurken, to snore, D. snorken, G. schnarchen to snore, schnarren to rattle, MHG. snarren, Sw. snarka to snore, Icel. snarka to sputter, fizzle. Cf. Snarl to growl, Sneer, Snort. See Snoring.] To breathe with a rough, hoarse, nasal voice in sleep.
Snore Snore, n. A harsh nasal noise made in sleep.

snoring.c: Snoring Snor"ing, n. (Physiol.) The act of respiring through the open mouth so that the currents of inspired and expired air cause a vibration of the uvula and soft palate, thus giving rise to a sound more or less harsh. It is usually unvoluntary, but may be produced voluntarily.

snort.c: Snort Snort (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Snorted; p. pr. & vb. n. Snorting.] [OE. snorten; akin to snoren. See Snore.] 1. To force the air with violence through the nose, so as to make a noise, as do high-spirited horsed in prancing and play. Fairfax.
Snort Snort, n. The act of snorting; the sound produced in snorting.
Snort Snort, v. t. To expel throught the nostrils with a snort; to utter with a snort. Keats.

snot.c: Snot Snot (?), n. [AS. snot; akin to D. snot, LG. snotte, Dan. snot, and to E. snout. See Snout.] 1. Mucus secreted in, or discharged from, the nose. [Low]
Snot Snot, v. t. To blow, wipe, or clear, as the nose.

snotter.c: Snotter Snot"ter (?), v. i. [From Snot.] To snivel; to cry or whine. [Prov. Eng.] Grose.

Snotter Snot"ter, n. [Etymol. uncertain.] (Naut.) A rope going over a yardarm, used to bend a tripping line to, in sending down topgallant and royal yards in vessels of war; also, the short line supporting the heel of the sprit in a small boat.

snotty.c: Snotty Snot"ty (?), a. Foul with snot; hence, mean; dirty.

snout.c: Snout Snout (snout), n. [OE. snoute, probably of Scand, or Low German origin; cf. LG. snute, D. snuit, G. schnauze, Sw. snut, snyte, Dan. snude, Icel. sn?ta to blow the nose; probably akin to E. snuff, v.t. Cf. Snite, Snot, Snuff.] 1. The long, projecting nose of a beast, as of swine.
Snout Snout, v. t. To furnish with a nozzle or point.

snouty.c: Snouty Snout"y (?), a. Resembling a beast's snout.

snow.c: Snow Snow (?), n. [LG. snaue, or D. snaauw, from LG. snau a snout, a beak.] (Naut.) A square-rigged vessel, differing from a brig only in that she has a trysail mast close abaft the mainmast, on which a large trysail is hoisted.

Snow Snow, n. [OE. snow, snaw, AS. snāw; akin to D. sneeuw, OS. & OHG. snēo, G. schnee, Icel. snær, snjōr, snajār, Sw. snö, Dan. snee, Goth. snaiws, Lith. snëgas, Russ. snieg', Ir. & Gael. sneachd, W. nyf, L. nix, nivis, Gr. acc. ni`fa, also AS. snīwan to snow, G. schneien, OHG. snīwan, Lith. snigti, L. ningit it snows, Gr. ni`fei, Zend snizh to snow; cf. Skr. snih to be wet or sticky. √172.] 1. Watery particles congealed into white or transparent crystals or flakes in the air, and falling to the earth, exhibiting a great variety of very beautiful and perfect forms.
Snow Snow (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Snowed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Snowing.] To fall in or as snow; -- chiefly used impersonally; as, it snows; it snowed yesterday.
Snow Snow, v. t. To scatter like snow; to cover with, or as with, snow. Donne. Shak.
Snow banner Snow banner. A bannerlike stream of snow blown into the air from a mountain peak, often having a pinkish color and extending horizontally for several miles across the sky.

snowball.c: Snowball Snow"ball` (?), n. 1. A round mass of snow pressed or roller together, or anything resembling such a mass.
Snowball Snow"ball`, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Snowballed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Snowballing.] To pelt with snowballs; to throw snowballs at.
Snowball Snow"ball`, v. i. 1. To throw snowballs.

snowberry.c: Snowberry Snow"ber`ry (?), n. (Bot.) A name of several shrubs with white berries; as, the Symphoricarpus racemosus of the Northern United States, and the Chiococca racemosa of Florida and tropical America.

snowbird.c: Snowbird Snow"bird (?), n. (Zool.) (a) An arctic finch (Plectrophenax nivalis syn. Plectrophanes nivalis) common, in winter, both in Europe and the United States, and often appearing in large flocks during snowstorms. It is partially white, but variously marked with chestnut and brown. Called also snow bunting, snowflake, snowfleck, and snowflight. (b) Any finch of the genus Junco which appears in flocks in winter time, especially Junco hyemalis in the Eastern United States; -- called also blue snowbird. See Junco. (c) The fieldfare. [Prov. Eng.]

snowblind.c: Snow-blind Snow"-blind` (?), a. Affected with blindness by the brilliancy of snow. -- Snow"-blind`ness, n.

snowbound.c: Snow-bound Snow"-bound` (?), a. Enveloped in, or confined by, snow. Whittier.

snowbroth.c: Snow-broth Snow"-broth` (?), n. Snow and water mixed, or snow just melted; very cold liquor. Shak.

snowcap.c: Snowcap Snow"cap` (?), n. (Zool.) A very small humming bird (Microchaera albocoronata) native of New Grenada.

snowcapped.c: Snow-capped Snow"-capped` (?), a. Having the top capped or covered with snow; as, snow-capped mountains.

snowdrift.c: Snowdrift Snow"drift` (?), n. A bank of drifted snow.

snowdrop.c: Snowdrop Snow"drop` (?), n. (Bot.) A bulbous plant (Galanthus nivalis) bearing white flowers, which often appear while the snow is on the ground. It is cultivated in gardens for its beauty.

snowflake.c: Snowflake Snow"flake` (?), n. 1. A flake, or small filmy mass, of snow.

snowl.c: Snowl Snowl (?), n. (Zool.) The hooded merganser. [Local, U.S.]

snowplough.c: Snowplough Snowplow { Snow"plow`, Snow"plough` } (?), n. An implement operating like a plow, but on a larger scale, for clearing away the snow from roads, railways, etc.

snowshed.c: Snowshed Snow"shed (?), n. A shelter to protect from snow, esp. a long roof over an exposed part of a railroad.

snowshoe.c: Snowshoe Snow"shoe` (?), n. A slight frame of wood three or four feet long and about one third as wide, with thongs or cords stretched across it, and having a support and holder for the foot; -- used by persons for walking on soft snow.

snowshoer.c: Snowshoer Snow"sho`er (?), n. One who travels on snowshoes; an expert in using snowshoes. W. G. Beers.

snowslip.c: Snowslip Snow"slip` (?), n. A large mass or avalanche of snow which slips down the side of a mountain, etc.

snowstorm.c: Snowstorm Snow"storm` (?), n. A storm with falling snow.

snowwhite.c: Snow-white Snow"-white` (?), a. White as snow; very white. “Snow-white and rose-red” Chaucer.

snowy.c: Snowy Snow"y (?), a. 1. White like snow. “So shows a snowy dove trooping with crows.” Shak.

snub.c: Snub Snub (?), v. i. [Cf. D. snuiven to snort, to pant, G. schnauben, MHG. snūben, Prov. G. schnupfen, to sob, and E. snuff, v.t.] To sob with convulsions. [Obs.] Bailey.

Snub Snub, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Snubbed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Snubbing.] [Cf. Icel. ssnubba to snub, chide, Sw. snubba, Icel. snubbōttr snubbed, nipped, and E. snib.] 1. To clip or break off the end of; to check or stunt the growth of; to nop.
Snub Snub, n. 1. A knot; a protuberance; a song. [Obs.]

snubnosed.c: Snub-nosed Snub"-nosed` (?), a. Having a short, flat nose, slightly turned up; as, the snub-nosed eel.

snudge.c: Snudge Snudge (?), v. i. [Cf. Snug.] To lie snug or quiet. [Obs.] Herbert.
Snudge Snudge, n. A miser; a sneaking fellow. [Obs.]

snuff.c: Snuff Snuff (?), n. [Cf. G. schnuppe candle snuff, schnuppen to snuff a candle (see Snuff, v. t., to snuff a candle), or cf. Snub, v. t.] The part of a candle wick charred by the flame, whether burning or not.
Snuff Snuff, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Snuffed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Snuffing.] [OE. snuffen. See Snuff of a candle Snuff to sniff.] To crop the snuff of, as a candle; to take off the end of the snuff of.

Snuff Snuff (?), v. t.[Akin to D. snuffen, G. schnupfen, schnuppen, to snuff, schnupfen a cold in the head, schnuppen to snuff (air), also, to snuff (a candle). Cf. Sniff, Snout, Snub, v. i.] 1. To draw in, or to inhale, forcibly through the nose; to sniff.
Snuff Snuff, v. i. 1. To inhale air through the nose with violence or with noise, as do dogs and horses. Dryden.
Snuff Snuff, n. 1. The act of snuffing; perception by snuffing; a sniff.

snuffbox.c: Snuffbox Snuff"box` (?), n. A small box for carrying snuff about the person.

snuffers.c: Snuffers Snuff"ers (?), n. pl. An instrument for cropping and holding the snuff of a candle.

snuffingly.c: Snuffingly Snuff"ing*ly, adv. In a snuffing manner.

snuffle.c: Snuffle Snuf"fle (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Snuffled(?); p. pr. & vb. n. Snuffling (?).] [Freq. of snuff, v.i.; akin to LG. snuffeln, G. schnüffeln, D. snuffeln, Dan. snövle. Cf. Sniffle.] To speak through the nose; to breathe through the nose when it is obstructed, so as to make a broken sound.
Snuffle Snuf"fle, n. 1. The act of snuffing; a sound made by the air passing through the nose when obstructed.

snuffler.c: Snuffler Snuf"fler (?), n. One who snuffles; one who uses cant.

snug.c: Snug Snug (?), a. [Compar. Snugger (?); superl. Snuggest (?).] [Prov. E. snug tight, handsome; cf. Icel. snöggr smooth, ODan. snög neat, Sw. snugg.] 1. Close and warm; as, an infant lies snug.
Snug Snug, n. (Mach.) Same as Lug, n., 3.
Snug Snug, v. i. [imp. & p. p. Snugged (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Snugging(?).] To lie close; to snuggle; to snudge; -- often with up, or together; as, a child snugs up to its mother.
Snug Snug, v. t. 1. To place snugly. [R.] Goldsmith.

snuggery.c: Snuggery Snug"ger*y (?), n.; pl. Snuggeries (?). A snug, cozy place. [Colloq.] Dickens.

snuggle.c: Snuggle Snug"gle (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Snuggled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Snuggling (?).] [Freq. of snug.] To move one way and the other so as to get a close place; to lie close for comfort; to cuddle; to nestle.

snugly.c: Snugly Snug"ly, adv. In a snug manner; closely; safely.

snugness.c: Snugness Snug"ness, n. The quality or state of being snug.

sny.c: Sny Sny (?), n. [Cf. Icel. snūa to turn.] An upward bend in a piece of timber; the sheer of a vessel.

snying.c: Snying Sny"ing, n. (Naut.) A curved plank, placed edgewise, to work in the bows of a vessel. R. H. Dana, Jr.

so.c: So So (?), adv. [OE. so, sa, swa, AS. swā; akin to OFries, sā, s?, D. zoo, OS. & OHG. s?, G. so, Icel. svā, sv?, svo, so, Sw. s?, Dan. saa, Goth. swa so, sw? as; cf. L. suus one's own, Skr. sva one's own, one's self. √192. Cf. As, Custom, Ethic, Idiom, Such.] 1. In that manner or degree; as, indicated (in any way), or as implied, or as supposed to be known.
So So (?), conj. Provided that; on condition that; in case that; if.
So So, interj. Be as you are; stand still; stop; that will do; right as you are; -- a word used esp. to cows; also used by sailors.

soak.c: Soak Soak (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Soaked (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Soaking.] [OE. soken, AS. socian to sioak, steep, fr. s?can, s?gan, to suck. See Suck.] 1. To cause or suffer to lie in a fluid till the substance has imbibed what it can contain; to macerate in water or other liquid; to steep, as for the purpose of softening or freshening; as, to soak cloth; to soak bread; to soak salt meat, salt fish, or the like.
Soak Soak, v. i. 1. To lie steeping in water or other liquid; to become sturated; as, let the cloth lie and soak.

soakage.c: Soakage Soak"age (?), n. The act of soaking, or the state of being soaked; also, the quantity that enters or issues by soaking.

soaker.c: Soaker Soak"er (?), n. 1. One who, or that which, soaks.

soaking.c: Soaking Soak"ing, a. Wetting thoroughly; drenching; as, a soaking rain. -- Soak"ing*ly, adv.

soaky.c: Soaky Soak"y (?), a. Full of moisture; wet; soppy.

soal.c: Soal Soal (?), n. 1. The sole of a shoe. [Obs. or R.]
Soal Soal, n. [AS. sol mire. Cf. Sully.] A dirty pond. [Prov. Eng.] Halliwell.

soam.c: Soam Soam (?), n. A chain by which a leading horse draws a plow. Knight.

soap.c: Soap Soap (?), n. [OE. sope, AS. sāpe; akin to D. zeep, G. seife, OHG. seifa, Icel. sāpa, Sw. s?pa, Dan. s?be, and perhaps to AS. sīpan to drip, MHG. sīfen, and L. sebum tallow. Cf. Saponaceous.] A substance which dissolves in water, thus forming a lather, and is used as a cleansing agent. Soap is produced by combining fats or oils with alkalies or alkaline earths, usually by boiling, and consists of salts of sodium, potassium, etc., with the fatty acids (oleic, stearic, palmitic, etc.). See the Note below, and cf. Saponification. By extension, any compound of similar composition or properties, whether used as a cleaning agent or not.
Soap Soap (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Soaped (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Soaping.] 1. To rub or wash over with soap.

soapberry.c: Soapberry tree Soap"ber`ry tree` (?). (Bot.) Any tree of the genus Sapindus, esp. Sapindus saponaria, the fleshy part of whose fruit is used instead of soap in washing linen; -- also called soap tree.

soapfish.c: Soapfish Soap"fish` (?), n. (Zool.) Any serranoid fish of the genus Rhypticus; -- so called from the soapy feeling of its skin.

soapiness.c: Soapiness Soap"i*ness (?), n. Quality or state of being soapy.

soaproot.c: Soaproot Soap"root` (?), n. (Bot.) A perennial herb (Gypsophila Struthium) the root of which is used in Spain as a substitute for soap.

soapstone.c: Soapstone Soap"stone` (?), n. See Steatite, and Talc.

soapsuds.c: Soapsuds Soap"suds` (?), n. pl. Suds made with soap.

soapwort.c: Soapwort Soap"wort` (?), n. (Bot.) A common plant (Saponaria officinalis) of the Pink family; -- so called because its bruised leaves, when agitated in water, produce a lather like that from soap. Called also Bouncing Bet.

soapy.c: Soapy Soap"y (?), a. [Compar. Soapier (?); superl. Soapiest.] 1. Resembling soap; having the qualities of, or feeling like, soap; soft and smooth.

soar.c: Soar Soar (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Soared (#); p. pr. & vb. n. Soaring.] [F. s'essorer to soar, essorer to dry (by exposing to the air), fr. L. ex out + aura the air, a breeze; akin to Gr.?????.] 1. To fly aloft, as a bird; to mount upward on wings, or as on wings. Chaucer.
Soar Soar, n. The act of soaring; upward flight.
Soar Soar, a. See Sore, reddish brown.

soaring.c: Soaring Soar"ing, a. & n. from Soar. -- Soar"ing*ly, adv.

sob.c: Sob Sob (sŏb), v. t. [See Sop.] To soak. [Obs.] Mortimer.

Sob Sob, v. i. [imp. & p. p. Sobbed (sŏbd); p. pr. & vb. n. Sobbing.] [OE. sobben; akin to AS. seófian, siófian, to complain, bewail, seófung, siófung, sobbing, lamentation; cf. OHG. sūftōn, sūftjōn, to sigh, MHG. siuften, siufzen, G. seufzen, MHG. sūft a sigh, properly, a drawing in of breath, from sūfen to drink, OHG. sūfan. Cf. Sup.] To sigh with a sudden heaving of the breast, or with a kind of convulsive motion; to sigh with tears, and with a convulsive drawing in of the breath.
Sob Sob, n. 1. The act of sobbing; a convulsive sigh, or inspiration of the breath, as in sorrow.

sobbing.c: Sobbing Sob"bing (?), n. A series of short, convulsive inspirations, the glottis being suddenly closed so that little or no air enters into the lungs.

sober.c: Sober Sober (?), a. [Compar. Soberer (?); superl. Soberest.] [OE. sobre, F. sobre, from L. sobrius, probably from a prefix so- expressing separation + ebrius drunken. Cf. Ebriety.] 1. Temperate in the use of spirituous liquors; habitually temperate; as, a sober man.
Sober So"ber (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Sobered (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Sobering.] To make sober.
Sober So"ber, v. i. To become sober; -- often with down.

soberize.c: Soberize So"ber*ize (?), v. t. & i. To sober. [R.] Crabbe.

soberly.c: Soberly So"ber*ly, adv. In a sober manner; temperately; cooly; calmly; gravely; seriously.
Soberly So"ber*ly, a. Grave; serious; solemn; sad. [Obs.]

soberminded.c: Sober-minded So"ber-mind`ed (?), a. Having a disposition or temper habitually sober. -- So"ber-mind`ed*ness, n.

soberness.c: Soberness So"ber*ness, n. The quality or state of being sober.

soboles.c: Soboles Sob"o*les (?), n. [L., a short.] (Bot.) (a) A shoot running along under ground, forming new plants at short distances. (b) A sucker, as of tree or shrub.

soboliferous.c: Soboliferous Sob`o*lif"er*ous (?), a. [L. soboles + -ferous.] (Bot.) Producing soboles. See Illust. of Houseleek.

sobranje.c: Sobranje ‖So*bran"je (?), n. [Bulgarian, lit., assembly.] The unicameral national assembly of Bulgaria, elected for a term of five years by universal suffrage of adult males.

sobriety.c: Sobriety So*bri"e*ty (?), n. [L. sobrietas: cf. F. sobriété. See Sober.] 1. Habitual soberness or temperance as to the use of spirituous liquors; as, a man of sobriety.

sobriquet.c: Sobriquet ‖So`bri`quet" (so`bre`ka"), n.[F. sobriquet, OF. soubzbriquet, soubriquet, a chuck under the chin, hence, an affront, a nickname; of uncertain origin; cf. It. sottobecco a chuck under the chin.] An assumed name; a fanciful epithet or appellation; a nickname. [Sometimes less correctly written soubriquet.]

soc.c: Soc Soc (sŏk), n. [AS. sōc the power of holding court, sway, domain, properly, the right of investigating or seeking; akin to E. sake, seek. Sake, Seek, and cf. Sac, and Soke.] [Written also sock, and soke.] 1. (O. Eng. Law) (a) The lord's power or privilege of holding a court in a district, as in manor or lordship; jurisdiction of causes, and the limits of that jurisdiction. (b) Liberty or privilege of tenants excused from customary burdens.

socage.c: Socage Soc"age (?), n.[From Soc; cf. LL. socagium.] (O.Eng. Law) A tenure of lands and tenements by a certain or determinate service; a tenure distinct from chivalry or knight's service, in which the obligations were uncertain. The service must be certain, in order to be denominated socage, as to hold by fealty and twenty shillings rent. [Written also soccage.]

socager.c: Socager Soc"a*ger (?), n. (O. Eng. Law) A tennant by socage; a socman.

socalled.c: So-called So"-called` (?), a. So named; called by such a name (but perhaps called thus with doubtful propriety).

sociability.c: Sociability So`cia*bil"i*ty (?), n.[Cf. F. sociabilité.] The quality of being sociable; sociableness.

sociable.c: Sociable So"cia*ble (?), a.[F., fr. L. sociabilis, fr. sociare to associate, fr. socius a companion. See Social.] 1. Capable of being, or fit to be, united in one body or company; associable. [R.]
Sociable So"cia*ble, n. 1. A gathering of people for social purposes; an informal party or reception; as, a church sociable. [Colloq. U. S.]

sociableness.c: Sociableness So"cia*ble*ness, n. The quality of being sociable.

sociably.c: Sociably So"cia*bly, adv. In a sociable manner.

social.c: Social So"cial (?), a. [L. socialis, from socius a companion; akin to sequi to follow: cf. F. social. See Sue to follow.] 1. Of or pertaining to society; relating to men living in society, or to the public as an aggregate body; as, social interest or concerns; social pleasure; social benefits; social happiness; social duties. “Social phenomena.” J. S. Mill.

socialism.c: Socialism So"cial*ism (?), n. [Cf. F. socialisme.] A theory or system of social reform which contemplates a complete reconstruction of society, with a more just and equitable distribution of property and labor. In popular usage, the term is often employed to indicate any lawless, revolutionary social scheme. See Communism, Fourierism, Saint-Simonianism, forms of socialism.

socialist.c: Socialist So"cial*ist, n. [Cf. F. socialiste.] One who advocates or practices the doctrines of socialism.

socialistic.c: Socialistic Socialist { So"cial*ist, So`cial*is"tic, } a. Pertaining to, or of the nature of, socialism.

sociality.c: Sociality So`ci*al"i*ty (?), n. [Cf. F. socialisté, L. socialitas.] The quality of being social; socialness.

socialize.c: Socialize So"cial*ize (?), v. t. 1. To render social.

socially.c: Socially So"cial*ly, adv. In a social manner; sociably.

socialness.c: Socialness So"cial*ness, n. The quality or state of being social.

sociate.c: Sociate So"ci*ate (?), a. [L. sociatus, p. p. of sociare to associate, fr. socius companion.] Associated. [Obs.]
Sociate So"ci*ate (?), v. i. To associate. [Obs.] Shelford.

societarian.c: Societarian So*ci`e*ta"ri*an (?), a. Of or pertaining to society; social.

society.c: Society So*ci"e*ty (?), n.; pl. Societies (#). [L. societas, fr. socius a companion: cf. F. société. See Social.] 1. The relationship of men to one another when associated in any way; companionship; fellowship; company. “Her loved society.” Milton.

socinian.c: Socinian So*cin"i*an (?), a. Of or pertaining to Socinus, or the Socinians.
Socinian So*cin"i*an, n. One of the followers of Socinus; a believer in Socinianism.

socinianism.c: Socinianism So*cin"i*an*ism (?), n. (Eccl. Hist.) The tenets or doctrines of Faustus Socinus, an Italian theologian of the sixteenth century, who denied the Trinity, the deity of Christ, the personality of the Devil, the native and total depravity of man, the vicarious atonement, and the eternity of future punishment. His theory was, that Christ was a man divinely commissioned, who had no existence before he was conceived by the Virgin Mary; that human sin was the imitation of Adam's sin, and that human salvation was the imitation and adoption of Christ's virtue; that the Bible was to be interpreted by human reason; and that its language was metaphorical, and not to be taken literally.

socinianize.c: Socinianize So*cin"i*an*ize (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Socinianized (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Socinianizing (?).] To cause to conform to Socinianism; to regulate by, or imbue with, the principles of Socinianism.

sociological.c: Sociological Sociologic { So`ci*o*log"ic (?), So`ci*o*log"ic*al (?) } a. Of or pertaining to sociology, or social science. -- So`ci*o*log"ic*al*ly, adv.

sociologist.c: Sociologist So`ci*ol"o*gist (?), n. One who treats of, or devotes himself to, the study of sociology. J. S. Mill.

sociology.c: Sociology So`ci*ol"o*gy (?), n. [L. socius a companion + -logy.] That branch of philosophy which treats of the constitution, phenomena, and development of human society; social science. H. Spencer.

sock.c: Sock Sock (?), n. [F. soc, LL. soccus, perhaps of Celtic origin.] A plowshare. Edin. Encyc.

Sock Sock, n. [OE. sock, AS. socc, fr. L. soccus a kind of low-heeled, light shoe. Cf. Sucket.] 1. The shoe worn by actors of comedy in ancient Greece and Rome, -- used as a symbol of comedy, or of the comic drama, as distinguished from tragedy, which is symbolized by the buskin.
Sock Sock (sŏk), v. t. [Perh. shortened fr. sockdolager.] To hurl, drive, or strike violently; -- often with it as an object. [Prov. or Vulgar] Kipling.

sockdolager.c: Sockdolager Sock*dol"a*ger (?), n. [A corruption of doxology.] [Written also sockdologer.] 1. That which finishes or ends a matter; a settler; a poser, as a heavy blow, a conclusive answer, and the like. [Slang, U.S.]

socket.c: Socket Sock"et (?), n. [OE. soket, a dim. through OF. fr. L. soccus. See Sock a covering for the foot.] 1. An opening into which anything is fitted; any hollow thing or place which receives and holds something else; as, the sockets of the teeth.

socketed.c: Socketed Sock"et*ed (?), a. Having a socket. Dawkins.

sockless.c: Sockless Sock"less, a. Destitute of socks or shoes. B. & Fl.

socle.c: Socle So"cle (?), n. [F., fr. L. socculus, dim. of soccus. See Sock a covering for the foot. Cf. Zocco.] (Arch.) (a) A plain block or plinth forming a low pedestal; any base; especially, the base of a statue, column, or the like. See Plinth. (b) A plain face or plinth at the lower part of a wall. Oxf. Gloss.

socman.c: Socman Soc"man (?), n.; pl. Socmen (#). [See Socage.] (O. Eng. Law) One who holds lands or tenements by socage; a socager. Cowell.

socmanry.c: Socmanry Soc"man*ry (?), n. (O.E. Law) Tenure by socage.

socome.c: Socome Soc"ome (?), n. [AS. sōcen, sōcn, searching, or the right of searching, the lord's court. See Soc.] (O.Eng. Law) A custom of tenants to grind corn at the lord's mill. Cowell.

socotrine.c: Socotrine Soc"o*trine (?), a. Of or pertaining to Socotra, an island in the Indian Ocean, on the east coast of Africa. -- n. A native or inhabitant of Socotra.

socratical.c: Socratical Socratic { So*crat"ic (?), So*crat"ic*al (?), } a. [L. Socraticus, Gr.????.] Of or pertaining to Socrates, the Grecian sage and teacher. (b. c. 469-399), or to his manner of teaching and philosophizing.

socratically.c: Socratically So*crat"ic*al*ly, adv. In the Socratic method.

socratism.c: Socratism Soc"ra*tism (?), n. The philosophy or the method of Socrates.

socratist.c: Socratist Soc"ra*tist (?), n. [Gr.????.] A disciple or follower of Socrates.

sod.c: Sod Sod (?), n. (Zool.) The rock dove. [Prov. Eng.]

Sod Sod, n. [Akin to LG. sode, D. zode, OD. sode, soode, OFries. satha, and E. seethe. So named from its sodden state in wet weather. See Seethe.] That stratum of the surface of the soil which is filled with the roots of grass, or any portion of that surface; turf; sward.
Sod Sod, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Sodden; p. pr. & vb. n. Sodding.] To cover with sod; to turf.

soda.c: Soda So"da (?), n. [It., soda, in OIt., ashes used in making glass, fr. L. solida, fem. of solidus solid; solida having probably been a name of glasswort. See Solid.] 1. (Chem.) (a) Sodium oxide or hydroxide. (b) Popularly, sodium carbonate or bicarbonate. Sodium bicarbonate is also called baking soda

sodaic.c: Sodaic So*da"ic (?), a. Pertaining to, or containing, soda. “Sodaic powder.” Ure.

sodalite.c: Sodalite So"da*lite (?), n. [Soda + -lite: cf. F. sodalithe.] (Min.) A mineral of a white to blue or gray color, occuring commonly in dodecahedrons, also massive. It is a silicate of alumina and soda with some chlorine.

sodality.c: Sodality So*dal"i*ty (?), n.; pl. Sodalities (#). [L. sodalitas, fr. sodalis a comrade.] 1. A fellowship or fraternity; a brotherhood.

sodamide.c: Sodamide Sod*am"ide (?), n. (Chem.) A greenish or reddish crystalline substance, NaNH2, obtained by passing ammonia over heated sodium.

sodden.c: Sodden Sod"den (?), a. [p. p. of Seethe.] Boiled; seethed; also, soaked; heavy with moisture; saturated; as, sodden beef; sodden bread; sodden fields.
Sodden Sod"den, v. i. To be seethed; to become sodden.
Sodden Sod"den, v. t. To soak; to make heavy with water.

soddy.c: Soddy Sod"dy (?), a. [From Sod.] Consisting of sod; covered with sod; turfy. Cotgrave.

soder.c: Soder Sod"er (?), n. & v. t. See Solder.

sodger.c: Sodger So"dger (sō"jẽr), n. & v. i. Variant of Soldier. [Dial. or Slang]

sodic.c: Sodic So"dic (?), a. (Chem.) Of or pertaining to sodium; containing sodium.

sodio.c: Sodio- So"di*o- (?). (Chem.) A combining form (also used adjectively) denoting the presence of sodium or one of its compounds.

sodium.c: Sodium So"di*um (?), n. [NL., fr.E. soda.] (Chem.) A common metallic element of the alkali group, in nature always occuring combined, as in common salt, in albite, etc. It is isolated as a soft, waxy, white, unstable metal, so highly reactive that it combines violently with water, and to be preserved must be kept under petroleum or some similar liquid. Sodium is used combined in many salts, in the free state as a reducer, and as a means of obtaining other metals (as magnesium and aluminium) is an important commercial product. Symbol Na (Natrium). Atomic weight 22.990. Specific gravity 0.97.

Sodium bicarbonate Sodium bicarbonate, a white crystalline substance, HNaCO3, with a slight alkaline taste resembling that of sodium carbonate. It is found in many mineral springs and also produced artificially,. It is used in cookery, in baking powders, and as a source of carbonic acid gas (carbon dioxide) for soda water. Called also baking soda, cooking soda, bicarbonate of soda, bicarb, saleratus, and technically, acid sodium carbonate, sodium acid carbonate, primary sodium carbonate, sodium dicarbonate, etc.
Sodium sulphate So"di*um sul"phate. A salt well known as a catharic under the name of Glauber's salt, which term is properly applied to the hydrate, Na2SO4.10H2O.

sodomite.c: Sodomite Sod"om*ite (?), n. 1. An inhabitant of Sodom.

sodomitical.c: Sodomitical Sod`om*it"ic*al (?), a. Pertaining to, or of the nature of, sodomy. -- Sod`om*it"ic*al*ly, adv.

sodomy.c: Sodomy Sod"om*y (?), n. [From Sodom. a country mentioned in the Bible: cf. F. sodomite.] Carnal copulation in a manner against nature; buggery. Gen. xix. 5.

soe.c: Soe Soe (?), n. [Scot. sae, say, saye; cf. Icel. sār a large cask, Sw. s? a tub.] A large wooden vessel for holding water; a cowl. [Obs. or Prov. Eng.] Dr. H. More.

soever.c: Soever So*ev"er (?). A word compounded of so and ever, used in composition with who, what, where, when, how, etc., and indicating any out of all possible or supposable persons, things, places, times, ways, etc. It is sometimes used separate from the pronoun or adverb.

sofa.c: Sofa So"fa (?), n.; pl. Sofas (#). [Ar. soffah, from saffa to dispose in order: cf. F. sofa, It. sofà.] A long seat, usually with a cushioned bottom, back, and ends; -- much used as a comfortable piece of furniture.

soffit.c: Soffit Sof"fit (?), n. [It. soffitta, soffitto, fr. soffiggere to hide, properly, to fix or fasten under, L. suffigere to fasten beneath or below; sub under, beneath + figere to fix, faste: cf. F. soffite.] (Arch.) The under side of the subordinate parts and members of buildings, such as staircases, entablatures, archways, cornices, or the like. See Illust. of Lintel.

sofi.c: Sofi So"fi (?), n.; pl. Sofis (?). Same as Sufi.

soft.c: Soft Soft (sŏft; 115), a. [Compar. Softer (sŏft"ẽr); superl. Softest.] [OE. softe, AS. sōfte, properly adv. of sēfte, adj.; akin to OS. sāfto, adv., D. zacht, OHG. samfto, adv., semfti, adj., G. sanft, LG. sacht; of uncertain origin.] 1. Easily yielding to pressure; easily impressed, molded, or cut; not firm in resisting; impressible; yielding; also, malleable; -- opposed to hard; as, a soft bed; a soft peach; soft earth; soft wood or metal.
Soft Soft (?), n. A soft or foolish person; an idiot. [Colloq.] G. Eliot.
Soft Soft, adv. Softly; without roughness or harshness; gently; quietly. Chaucer.
Soft Soft, interj. Be quiet; hold; stop; not so fast.
Soft steel Soft steel. Steel low in carbon; mild steel; ingot iron.

softa.c: Softa Sof"ta (?), n. [Corruption of Per. sōkhtah one who burns, is ardent or zealous.] Any one attached to a Mohammedan mosque, esp. a student of the higher branches of theology in a mosque school. [Written also sophta.]

soften.c: Soften Sof"ten (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Softened (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Softening.] To make soft or more soft. Specifically: --
Soften Sof"ten, v. i. To become soft or softened, or less rude, harsh, severe, or obdurate.

softener.c: Softener Sof"ten*er (?), n. One who, or that which, softens. [Written also, less properly, softner.]

softening.c: Softening Sof"ten*ing, a. & n. from Soften, v.

softfinned.c: Soft-finned Soft"-finned` (?), a. (Zool.) Having the fin rays cartilaginous or flexible; without spines; -- said of certain fishes.

softhearted.c: Soft-hearted Soft"-heart`ed (?), a. Having softness or tenderness of heart; susceptible of pity or other kindly affection; gentle; meek. -- Soft"-heart`ed*ness, n.

softish.c: Softish Soft"ish (?), a. Somewhat soft. De Witt Clinton.

softling.c: Softling Soft"ling (?), n. A soft, effeminate person; a voluptuary. [R.] Bp. Woolton..

softly.c: Softly Soft"ly, adv. In a soft manner.

softness.c: Softness Soft"ness (?), n. [AS. s?ftness, s?ftnyss.] The quality or state of being soft; -- opposed to hardness, and used in the various specific senses of the adjective.

softshelled.c: Soft-shelled Soft-shell Soft"-shell` (?), Soft"-shelled` (?), } a. Having a soft or fragile shell.

softspoken.c: Soft-spoken Soft"-spo`ken (?), a. Speaking softly; having a mild or gentle voice; hence, mild; affable.

soger.c: Soger So"ger (sō"jẽr), n. & v. i. Var. of Soldier. [Dial. or Slang] R. H. Dana, Jr.

sogginess.c: Sogginess Sog"gi*ness (?), n. The quality or state of being soggy; soddenness; wetness.

soggy.c: Soggy Sog"gy (?), a. [Compar. Soggier (?); superl. Soggiest.] [Cf. Icel. söggr damp, wet, or E. soak.] Filled with water; soft with moisture; sodden; soaked; wet; as, soggy land or timber.

soho.c: Soho So*ho" (?), interj. Ho; -- a word used in calling from a distant place; a sportsman's halloo. Shak.

soidisant.c: Soi-disant ‖Soi`-di*sant" (swä"de`zäN"), a. [F.; soi one's self + disant, p. pr. of dire to say.] Self-named; self-styled; pretended; would-be.

soil.c: Soil Soil (soil), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Soiled (soild); p. pr. & vb. n. Soiling.] [OF. saoler, saouler, to satiate, F. soûler, L. satullare, fr. satullus, dim. of satur sated. See Satire.] To feed, as cattle or horses, in the barn or an inclosure, with fresh grass or green food cut for them, instead of sending them out to pasture; hence (such food having the effect of purging them), to purge by feeding on green food; as, to soil a horse.

Soil Soil, n. [OE. soile, F. sol, fr. L. solum bottom, soil; but the word has probably been influenced in form by soil a miry place. Cf. Saloon, Soil a miry place, Sole of the foot.] 1. The upper stratum of the earth; the mold, or that compound substance which furnishes nutriment to plants, or which is particularly adapted to support and nourish them.
Soil Soil, v. t. To enrich with soil or muck; to manure.

Soil Soil, n. [OF. soil, souil, F. souille, from OF. soillier, F. souiller. See Soil to make dirty.] A marshy or miry place to which a hunted boar resorts for refuge; hence, a wet place, stream, or tract of water, sought for by other game, as deer.

Soil Soil, v. t.[OE. soilen, OF. soillier, F. souiller, (assumed) LL. suculare, fr. L. sucula a little pig, dim. of sus a swine. See Sow, n.] 1. To make dirty or unclean on the surface; to foul; to dirty; to defile; as, to soil a garment with dust.
Soil Soil, v. i. To become soiled; as, light colors soil sooner than dark ones.
Soil Soil, n. [See Soil to make dirty, Soil a miry place.] That which soils or pollutes; a soiled place; spot; stain.
Soil pipe Soil pipe. A pipe or drain for carrying off night soil.

soilless.c: Soilless Soil"less, a. Destitute of soil or mold.

soilure.c: Soilure Soil"ure (?), n. [OF. soillure, F. souillure. See Soil to make dirty.] Stain; pollution. Shak.

soiree.c: Soiree ‖Soi`ree" (?), n. [F., fr. soir evening, fr. L. serus late, serum late time. Cf. Serenade.] An evening party; -- distinguished from levee, and matinée.

soja.c: Soja So"ja (sō"jȧ or sō"yȧ), n. (Bot.) An Asiatic leguminous herb (Glycine max, formerly Glycine Soja) the seeds of which (called soy beans) are used in preparing the sauce called soy. Called also soya.

sojer.c: Sojer So"jer (sō"jẽr), n. & v. i. Var. of Soldier. [Dial. or Slang]

sojourn.c: Sojourn So"journ (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Sojourned (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Sojourning.] [OE. sojornen, sojournen, OF. sojorner, sejorner, F. séjourner, fr. L. sub under, about + diurnus belonging to the day. See Journal, Diurnal.] To dwell for a time; to dwell or live in a place as a temporary resident or as a stranger, not considering the place as a permanent habitation; to delay; to tarry.
Sojourn So"journ, n. [Cf. OF. sujurn, sujur, sejor, F. séjour. See Sojourn, v. i.] A temporary residence, as that of a traveler in a foreign land.

sojourning.c: Sojourning So"journ*ing, n. The act or state of one who sojourns.

sojournment.c: Sojournment So"journ*ment (?), n. Temporary residence, as that of a stranger or a traveler. [R.]

soken.c: Soken Sok"en (?), n. [Cf. Socome.] 1. A toll. See Soc, n., 2. [Obs.]

soko.c: Soko So"ko (?), n. (Zool.) An African anthropoid ape, supposed to be a variety of the chimpanzee.

sol.c: Sol Sol (?), n. [It.] (Mus.) (a) A syllable applied in solmization to the note G, or to the fifth tone of any diatonic scale. (b) The tone itself.

sole.c: Sole Sol { Sol Sole } (?), n. [From hydrosol an aqueous colloidal solution, confused with G. sole, soole, salt water from which salt is obtained.] (Chem.) A fluid mixture of a colloid and a liquid; a liquid colloidal solution or suspension.

Sole Sole (?), n. [F. sole, L. solea; -- so named from its flat shape. See Sole of the foot.] (Zool.)
