sourde.c: Sourde Sourde (?), v. i. [F. sourdre. See Source.] To have origin or source; to rise; to spring. [Obs.]

sourish.c: Sourish Sour"ish, a. Somewhat sour; moderately acid; as, sourish fruit; a sourish taste.

sourly.c: Sourly Sour"ly, adv. In a sour manner; with sourness.

sourness.c: Sourness Sour"ness, n. The quality or state of being sour.

sours.c: Sours Sours (?), n. Source. See Source. [Obs.] Chaucer.

soursop.c: Soursop Sour"sop` (?), n. (Bot.) The large succulent and slightly acid fruit of a small tree (Anona muricata) of the West Indies; also, the tree itself. It is closely allied to the custard apple.

souse.c: Souse Sous { Sous, Souse } (F. sōo; colloq. Eng. sous), n. A corrupt form of Sou. [Obs.] Colman, the Elder.
Souse Souse (?), n. [OF. sausse. See Sauce.] [Written also souce, sowce, and sowse.] 1. Pickle made with salt.
Souse Souse, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Soused (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Sousing.] [Cf. F. saucer to wet with sauce. See Souse pickle.] 1. To steep in pickle; to pickle. “A soused gurnet.” Shak.

Souse Souse, v. i. [Probably fr. OF. sors, p. p. of sordre to rise, and first used of an upward swood, then of a swoop in general, but also confused with Souse, v. t. See Source.] To swoop or plunge, as a bird upon its prey; to fall suddenly; to rush with speed; to make a sudden attack.
Souse Souse, v. t. To pounce upon. [R.]
Souse Souse, n. The act of sousing, or swooping.
Souse Souse, adv. With a sudden swoop; violently. Young.

soutache.c: Soutache ‖Sou`tache" (?), n. [F.] A kind of narrow braid, usually of silk; -- also known as Russian braid.

soutage.c: Soutage Sout"age (? or?; 48), n. [Etymol. uncertain.] That in which anything is packed; bagging, as for hops. [Obs.] Halliwell.

soutane.c: Soutane ‖Sou`tane" (?), n. [F., fr. Sp. sotana, or It. sottana, LL. subtana, fr. L. subtus below, beneath, fr. sub under.] (Eccl. Costume) A close garnment with straight sleeves, and skirts reaching to the ankles, and buttoned in front from top to bottom; especially, the black garment of this shape worn by the clergy in France and Italy as their daily dress; a cassock.

souter.c: Souter Sou"ter (?), n. [AS. s?t?re, fr. It. sutor, fr. suere to sew.] A shoemaker; a cobbler. [Obs.] Chaucer.

souterly.c: Souterly Sou"ter*ly, a. Of or pertaining to a cobbler or cobblers; like a cobbler; hence, vulgar; low. [Obs.]

souterrain.c: Souterrain Sou"ter*rain (?), n. [F. See Subterranean.] A grotto or cavern under ground. [Obs.] Arbuthnot.

south.c: South South (?; by sailors sou), n. [OE. south, suþ, AS. sūð for sunð; akin to D. zuid, OHG. sund, G. süd, süden, Icel. suðr, sunnr, Dan. syd, sönden, Sw. syd, söder, sunnan; all probably akin to E. sun, meaning, the side towards the sun. √297. See Sun.] 1. That one of the four cardinal points directly opposite to the north; the region or direction to the right or direction to the right of a person who faces the east.

South South, a. Lying toward the south; situated at the south, or in a southern direction from the point of observation or reckoning; proceeding toward the south, or coming from the south; blowing from the south; southern; as, the south pole. “At the south entry.” Shak.
South South, adv. 1. Toward the south; southward.
South South (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Southed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Southing.] 1. To turn or move toward the south; to veer toward the south.
South southerly South` south"er*ly (?). (Zool.) the old squaw; -- so called in imitation of its cry. Called also southerly, and southerland. See under Old.

southcottian.c: Southcottian South*cot"ti*an (?), n. (Eccl. Hist.) A follower of Joanna Southcott (1750-1814), an Englishwoman who, professing to have received a miraculous calling, preached and prophesied, and committed many impious absurdities.

southdown.c: Southdown South"down` (?), a. Of or pertaining to the South Downs, a range of pasture hills south of the Thames, in England.

southeast.c: Southeast South`east" (?; by sailors sou"-), n. The point of the compass equally distant from the south and the east; the southeast part or region.
Southeast South`east (?; by sailors sou"-), a. Of or pertaining to the southeast; proceeding toward, or coming from, the southeast; as, a southeast course; a southeast wind.

southeaster.c: Southeaster South`east"er (?), n. A storm, strong wind, or gale coming from the southeast.

southeastern.c: Southeastern South`east"ern (?), a. Of or pertaining to the southeast; southeasterly.

southeastwardly.c: Southeastwardly Southeastward { South`east"ward (?), South`east"ward*ly }, adv. Toward the southeast.

souther.c: Souther South"er (?), n. A strong wind, gale, or storm from the south.

southerliness.c: Southerliness South"er*li*ness (?), n. The quality or state of being southerly; direction toward the south.

southern.c: Southern South"ern (?; 277), a. [AS. sūðern. See South.] Of or pertaining to the south; situated in, or proceeding from, the south; situated or proceeding toward the south.

southerner.c: Southerner South"ern*er (?), n. An inhabitant or native of the south, esp. of the Southern States of North America; opposed to Northerner.

southernly.c: Southernly South"ern*ly (?), a. Somewhat southern. -- adv. In a southerly manner or course; southward.

southernwood.c: Southernwood South"ern*wood` (?), n. (Bot.) A shrubby species of wormwood (Artemisia Abrotanum) having aromatic foliage. It is sometimes used in making beer.

southing.c: Southing South"ing (?; 277), n. 1. Tendency or progress southward; as, the southing of the sun. Emerson.

southmost.c: Southmost South"most` (?), a. Farthest toward the south; southernmost. [R.] Milton.

southness.c: Southness South"ness, n. A tendency in the end of a magnetic needle to point toward the south pole. Faraday.

southpaw.c: Southpaw South"paw` (?), a. (Baseball) Using the left hand in pitching; said of a pitcher. [Cant]
Southpaw South"paw`, n. A pitcher who pitches with the left hand. [Cant]

southren.c: Southren South"ren (?), a. Southern. [Obs.] “I am a Southren man.” Chaucer.

southron.c: Southron South"ron (?), n. An inhabitant of the more southern part of a country; formerly, a name given in Scotland to any Englishman.

southwards.c: Southwards Southward { South"ward (?; colloq.?), South"wards (?; colloq.?), } adv. Toward the south, or toward a point nearer the south than the east or west point; as, to go southward.

southward.c: Southward South"ward, n. The southern regions or countries; the south. Sir W. Raleigh.

southwardly.c: Southwardly South"ward*ly, adv. In a southern direction.

southwest.c: Southwest South`west (?; colloq. sou"-.), n. The point of the compass equally from the south and the west; the southwest part or region.
Southwest South`west", a. Pertaining to, or in the direction of, the southwest; proceeding toward the southwest; coming from the southwest; as, a southwest wind.

southwester.c: Southwester South`west"er (?; colloq.?), n. 1. A storm, gale, or strong wind from the southwest.

southwesterly.c: Southwesterly South`west"er*ly, a. To ward or from the southwest; as, a southwesterly course; a southwesterly wind.

southwestern.c: Southwestern South`west"ern (?), a. Of or pertaining to the southwest; southwesterly; as, to sail a southwestern course.

southwestwardly.c: Southwestwardly Southwestward { South`west"ward (?), South`west"ward*ly }, adv. Toward the southwest.

sovenaunce.c: Sovenaunce Souvenance { Sou"ve*nance (?), So"ve*naunce (?), } n. [F. souvenance.] Remembrance. [Obs.]

souvenir.c: Souvenir Sou`ve*nir (? or?), n. [F., fr. souvenir to remember, fr. L. subvenire to come up, come to mind; sub under + venire to come, akin to E. come. See Come, and cf. Subvention.] That which serves as a reminder; a remembrancer; a memento; a keepsake.

sovereign.c: Sovereign Sov"er*eign (? or?; 277), a. [OE. soverain, sovereyn, OF. soverain, suvrain, F. souverain, LL. superanus, fr. L. superus that is above, upper, higher, fr. super above. See Over, Super, and cf. Soprano. The modern spelling is due to a supposed connection with reign.] 1. Supreme or highest in power; superior to all others; chief; as, our sovereign prince.
Sovereign Sov"er*eign (? or?; 277), n. 1. The person, body, or state in which independent and supreme authority is vested; especially, in a monarchy, a king, queen, or emperor.

sovereignize.c: Sovereignize Sov"er*eign*ize (?), v. i. To exercise supreme authority. [Obs.] Sir T. Herbert.

sovereignly.c: Sovereignly Sov"er*eign*ly, adv. In a sovereign manner; in the highest degree; supremely. Chaucer.

sovereignty.c: Sovereignty Sov"er*eign*ty (?), n.; pl. Sovereignties (#). [OE. soverainetee, OF. sovraineté, F. souveraineté.] The quality or state of being sovereign, or of being a sovereign; the exercise of, or right to exercise, supreme power; dominion; sway; supremacy; independence; also, that which is sovereign; a sovereign state; as, Italy was formerly divided into many sovereignties.

sovran.c: Sovran Sov"ran (?), a. A variant of Sovereign. [Poetic]

sow.c: Sow Sow (?), v. i. To sew. See Sew. [Obs.] Chaucer.

Sow Sow (?), n. [OE. sowe, suwe, AS. sugu, akin to sū, D. zog, zeug, OHG. sū, G. sau, Icel. sȳr, Dan. so, Sw. sugga, so, L. sus. Gr. "y^s, sy^s, Zend. hu boar; probably from the root seen in Skr. sū to beget, to bear; the animal being named in allusion to its fecundity. √294. Cf. Hyena, Soil to stain, Son, Swine.] 1. (Zool.) The female of swine, or of the hog kind.

Sow Sow (?), v. t. [imp. Sowed (?); p. p. Sown (?) or Sowed; p. pr. & vb. n. Sowing.] [OE. sowen, sawen, AS. sāwan; akin to OFries. s?a, D. zaaijen, OS. & HG. sājan, G. säen, Icel. sā, Sw. så, Dan. saae, Goth. saian, Lith. sēti, Russ. sieiate, L. serere, sevi. Cf. Saturday, Season, Seed, Seminary.] 1. To scatter, as seed, upon the earth; to plant by strewing; as, to sow wheat. Also used figuratively: To spread abroad; to propagate. “He would sow some difficulty.” Chaucer.
Sow Sow, v. i. To scatter seed for growth and the production of a crop; -- literally or figuratively.

sowans.c: Sowans Sow"ans (? or?), n. pl. See Sowens.

sowar.c: Sowar Sow"ar (?), n. [Per. sawār a horseman.] In India, a mounted soldier.

sowbane.c: Sowbane Sow"bane` (?), n. (Bot.) The red goosefoot (Chenopodium rubrum), -- said to be fatal to swine.

sowdan.c: Sowdan Sow"dan (?), n. [F. soudan. See Soldan.] Sultan. [Obs.] Chaucer.

sowens.c: Sowens Sow"ens (? or?), n. pl. [Scottish; cf. AS. seáw juice, glue, paste.] A nutritious article of food, much used in Scotland, made from the husk of the oat by a process not unlike that by which common starch is made; -- called flummery in England. [Written also sowans, and sowins.]

sower.c: Sower Sow"er (?), n. One who, or that which, sows.

sowins.c: Sowins Sow"ins (? or?), n. pl. See Sowens.

sowle.c: Sowle Sowl { Sowl, Sowle } (?), v. t. [Cf. prov. G. zaulen, zauseln, G. zausen to tug, drag.] To pull by the ears; to drag about. [Obs.] Shak.

sowl.c: Sowl Sowl, v. i. See Soul, v. i. [Obs.]

sowne.c: Sowne Sowne (?), v. t. & i. To sound. [Obs.] Chaucer.

sowse.c: Sowse Sowse (?), n. & v. See Souse. [Obs.] ryden.

sowter.c: Sowter Sow"ter (?), n. See Souter. [Obs.] B. Jonson.

soya.c: Soya Soy Soy (soi), Soy"a (soi"ȧ), n. [Chinese shōyū.] 1. A Chinese and Japanese liquid sauce for fish, etc., made by subjecting boiled beans (esp. soybeans), or beans and meal, to long fermentation and then long digestion in salt and water.

soybean.c: Soybean Soy"bean (soi"bēn`), n. 1. (Bot.) An Asiatic leguminous herb (Glycine max, formerly Glycine Soja) the seeds of which (also called soy beans) are used in preparing the sauce called soy. Called also soya bean and soya.

soyle.c: Soyle Soyle (?), v. t. [Aphetic form of assoil.] To solve, to clear up; as, to soyl all other texts. [Obs.] Tyndate.
Soyle Soyle, n. [Cf. Soil to feed.] Prey. [Obs.] Spenser.

soyned.c: Soyned Soyn"ed (? or?), a. [F. soigner to care.] Filled with care; anxious. [Obs.] Mir. for Mag.

sozzle.c: Sozzle Soz"zle (?), v. t. [Freq. from soss, v.] 1. To splash or wet carelessly; as, to sozzle the feet in water. [Local, U.S.] Bartlett.
Sozzle Soz"zle, n. 1. One who spills water or other liquids carelessly; specifically, a sluttish woman. [Local, U.S.]

spa.c: Spa Spa (?; 277), n. A spring or mineral water; -- so called from a place of this name in Belgium.

spaad.c: Spaad Spaad (?), n. [Cf. G. spath spar. See Spar the mineral.] (Min.) A kind of spar; earth flax, or amianthus. [Obs.] oodward.

space.c: Space Space (spās), n. [OE. space, F. espace, from L. spatium space; cf. Gr. spa^n to draw, to tear; perh. akin to E. span. Cf. Expatiate.] 1. Extension, considered independently of anything which it may contain; that which makes extended objects conceivable and possible.
Space Space, v. i. [Cf. OF. espacier, L. spatiari. See Space, n.] To walk; to rove; to roam. [Obs.]

Space Space, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Spaced (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Spacong (?).] [Cf. F. espacer. See Space, n.] (Print.) To arrange or adjust the spaces in or between; as, to space words, lines, or letters.

space key space bar { space bar or space key }. (Mach., Computers) A bar or key, in a typewriter, typesetting machine, or other keyboard (as a computer keyboard), used to insert a space between letters.

spacially.c: Spacially Spa"cial*ly, adv. See Spatially. Sir W. Hamilton.

spacious.c: Spacious Spa"cious (?), a. [L. spatiousus: cf. F. spacieux. See Space, n.] 1. Extending far and wide; vast in extent. “A spacious plain outstretched in circuit wide.” Milton.

spad.c: Spad Spad (spăd), n. (Mining) A nail one or two inches long, of iron, brass, tin, or tinner iron, with a hole through the flattened head, used to mark stations in underground surveying.

spadassin.c: Spadassin ‖Spa`das`sin" (?), n. [F., fr. It. spadaccino a swordsman, from spada a sword.] A bravo; a bully; a duelist. Ld. Lytton.

spade.c: Spade Spade (?), n. [Cf. Spay, n.] 1. (Zool.) A hart or stag three years old. [Written also spaid, spayade.]

Spade Spade, n. [AS. spaed; spada; akin to D. spade, G. spaten, Icel. spaði, Dan. & Sw. spade, L. spatha a spatula, a broad two-edged sword, a spathe, Gr. spa`qh. Cf. Epaulet, Spade at cards, Spathe, Spatula.] 1. An implement for digging or cutting the ground, consisting usually of an oblong and nearly rectangular blade of iron, with a handle like that of a shovel. “With spade and pickax armed.” Milton.
Spade Spade (spād), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Spaded; p. pr. & vb. n. Spading.] To dig with a spade; to pare off the sward of, as land, with a spade.

spadefish.c: Spadefish Spade"fish` (spād"fĭsh`), n. (Zool.) An American market fish (Chaetodipterus faber) common on the southern coasts; -- called also angel fish, moonfish, and porgy.

spadefoot.c: Spadefoot Spade"foot` (spād"fŏot`), n. (Zool.) Any species of burrowing toads of the genus Scaphiopus, esp. Scaphiopus Holbrookii, of the Eastern United States; -- called also spade toad.

spadeful.c: Spadeful Spade"ful (spād"fụl), n.; pl. Spadefuls (spād"fụlz). [Spade + full.] As much as a spade will hold or lift.

spader.c: Spader Spad"er (?), n. One who, or that which, spades; specifically, a digging machine.

spadiceous.c: Spadiceous Spa*di"ceous (?), a. [L. spadix, -icis, a date-brown or nut-brown color. See Spadix.] 1. Of a bright clear brown or chestnut color. Sir T. Browne.

spadille.c: Spadille Spa*dille" (?), n. [F., fr. Sp. espadilla, dim. of espada. See Spade a card.] (Card Playing) The ace of spades in omber and quadrille.

spadix.c: Spadix Spa"dix (?), n.; pl. L. Spadices (#), E. Spadixes (#). [L., a palm branch broken off, with its fruit, Gr.?.] 1. (Bot.) A fleshy spike of flowers, usually inclosed in a leaf called a spathe.

spado.c: Spado ‖Spa"do (?), n.; pl. Spadones (#). [L., fr. Gr.?.] 1. Same as Spade, 2.

spadroon.c: Spadroon Spa*droon" (?), n. [Cf. F. & Sp. espadon, It. spadone. See Espadon, Spade.] A sword, especially a broadsword, formerly used both to cut and thrust.

spae.c: Spae Spae (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Spaed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Spaeing.] [Scot. spae, spay, to foretell, to divine, Icel. spā.] To foretell; to divine. [Scot.]

spaeman.c: Spaeman Spae"man (?), n. A prophet; a diviner. [Scot.]

spaewife.c: Spaewife Spae"wife` (?), n. A female fortune teller. [Scot.]

spaghetti.c: Spaghetti ‖Spa*ghet"ti (?), n. [It.] A variety or macaroni made in tubes of small diameter.

spagyrical.c: Spagyrical Spagyric { Spa*gyr"ic (?), Spa*gyr"ic*al (?), } a. [LL. sparygicus, fr. Gr.? to draw, to separate +? to assemble; cf. F. spagirique.] Chemical; alchemical. [Obs.]

spagyric.c: Spagyric Spa*gyr"ic, n. A spagyrist. [Obs.] Bp. Hall.

spagyrist.c: Spagyrist Spag"y*rist (?), n. [Cf. F. spagiriste.] 1. A chemist, esp. one devoted to alchemistic pursuits. [Obs.]

spahee.c: Spahee Spahi { ‖Spa"hi (?), ‖Spa"hee }, n. [Per., Turk., & Hind. sipāhī: cf. F. spahi. See Seroy.] 1. Formerly, one of the Turkish cavalry.

spakenet.c: Spakenet Spake"net` (?), n. [Etymol. uncertain.] A net for catching crabs. Halliwell.

spalding.c: Spalding knife Spald"ing knife` (?). A spalting knife.

spale.c: Spale Spale (?), n. [Cf. Spell a splinter.] 1. A lath; a shaving or chip, as of wood or stone. [Prov. Eng. & Scot.]

spall.c: Spall Spall (?), n. [OF. espaule; cf. It. spalla. See Epaule.] The shoulder. [Obs.] Spenser.
Spall Spall, n. [Prov. E. spall, spell. See Spale, Spell a splinter.] A chip or fragment, especially a chip of stone as struck off the block by the hammer, having at least one feather-edge.
Spall Spall, v. t. 1. (Mining) To break into small pieces, as ore, for the purpose of separating from rock. Pryce.
Spall Spall, v. i. To give off spalls, or wedge-shaped chips; -- said of stone, as when badly set, with the weight thrown too much on the outer surface.

spalpeen.c: Spalpeen Spal"peen (?), n. [Ir. spailpin, fr. spailp a beau, pride, self-conceit.] A scamp; an Irish term for a good-for-nothing fellow; -- often used in good-humored contempt or ridicule. [Colloq.]

spalt.c: Spalt Spalt (?), n. [Cf. G. spaltstein, from spalten to split. See 1st Spell.] (Metal.) Spelter. [Colloq.]
Spalt Spalt, a. [See 1st Spell.] 1. Liable to break or split; brittle; as, spalt timber. [Prov. Eng.] Halliwell.
Spalt Spalt, v. t. & i. [Cf. OE. spalden. See Spalt, a.] To split off; to cleave off, as chips from a piece of timber, with an ax. [Prov. Eng. & Local, U.S.]

spalting.c: Spalting knife Spalt"ing knife` (?). A knife used in splitting codfish. [Written also spalding knife.]

span.c: Span Span (?), archaic imp. & p. p. of Spin.

Span Span, n. [AS. spann; akin to D. span, OHG. spanna, G. spanne, Icel. spönn. √170. See Span, v. t. ] 1. The space from the thumb to the end of the little finger when extended; nine inches; eighth of a fathom.

Span Span (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Spanned (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Spanning.] [AS. pannan; akin to D. & G. spannen, OHG. spannan, Sw. spänna, Dan. spaende, Icel. spenna, and perh. to Gr.? to draw, to drag, L. spatium space. √170. Cf. Spin, v. t., Space, Spasm.] 1. To measure by the span of the hand with the fingers extended, or with the fingers encompassing the object; as, to span a space or distance; to span a cylinder.
Span Span, v. i. To be matched, as horses. [U. S.]

spanaemia.c: Spanaemia ‖Spa*nae"mi*a (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr.? scarce +? blood.] (Med.) A condition of impoverishment of the blood; a morbid state in which the red corpuscles, or other important elements of the blood, are deficient.

spanaemic.c: Spanaemic Spa*nae"mic (? or?), a. (Med.) Of or pertaining to spanaemia; having impoverished blood.

spancel.c: Spancel Span"cel (?), n. [Perhaps span + AS. sāl a rope.] A rope used for tying or hobbling the legs of a horse or cow. [Prov. Eng. & Local, U.S.] Grose.
Spancel Span"cel, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Spanceled (?) or Spancelled; p. pr. & vb. n. Spanceling or Spancelling.] To tie or hobble with a spancel. [Prov. Eng. & Local, U.S.] Malone.

spandogs.c: Spandogs Span"dogs` (?), n. pl. A pair of grappling dogs for hoisting logs and timber.

spandrel.c: Spandrel Span"drel (?), n. [From Span.] 1. (Arch.) The irregular triangular space between the curve of an arch and the inclosing right angle; or the space between the outer moldings of two contiguous arches and a horizontal line above them, or another arch above and inclosing them.

spane.c: Spane Spane (?), v. t. [Akin to G. spänen, LG. & D. spennen, AS. spanu a teat.] To wean. [Obs. or Prov. Eng.]

spang.c: Spang Spang, v. i. To spring; to bound; to leap. [Scot.]
Spang Spang, n. A bound or spring. [Scot.] Sir W. Scott.
Spang Spang, n. [AS. spange a clasp or fastening; akin to D. spang, G. spange, OHG. spanga, Icel. spöng a spangle.] A spangle or shining ornament. [Obs.]

spangle.c: Spangle Span"gle (?), n. [OE. spangel, dim. of AS. spange. See Spang a spangle.] 1. A small plate or boss of shining metal; something brilliant used as an ornament, especially when stitched on the dress.

Spangle Span"gle, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Spangled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Spangling (?).] To set or sprinkle with, or as with, spangles; to adorn with small, distinct, brilliant bodies; as, a spangled breastplate. Donne.
Spangle Span"gle, v. i. To show brilliant spots or points; to glisten; to glitter.

spangler.c: Spangler Span"gler (?), n. One who, or that which, spangles.

spangly.c: Spangly Span"gly (?), a. Resembling, or consisting of, spangles; glittering; as, spangly light.

spaniard.c: Spaniard Span"iard (?), n. A native or inhabitant of Spain.

spaniel.c: Spaniel Span"iel (?), n. [OF. espagneul, F. épagneul, espagnol Spanish, Sp. españnol, fr. España Spain, from L. Hispania.] 1. (Zool.) One of a breed of small dogs having long and thick hair and large drooping ears. The legs are usually strongly feathered, and the tail bushy. See Illust. under Clumber, and Cocker.
Spaniel Span"iel, v. i. To fawn; to cringe; to be obsequious. [R.] Churchill.
Spaniel Span"iel, v. t. To follow like a spaniel. [R.]

spanish.c: Spanish Span"ish (?), a. Of or pertaining to Spain or the Spaniards.
Spanish Span"ish, n. The language of Spain.

spank.c: Spank Spank (spăṉk), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Spanked (spăṉkt); p. pr. & vb. n. Spanking.] [Of unknown origin; cf. LG. spakken, spenkern, to run and spring about quickly.] To strike, as the breech, with the open hand; to slap.
Spank Spank, n. A blow with the open hand; a slap.
Spank Spank, v. i. To move with a quick, lively step between a trot and gallop; to move quickly. Thackeray.

spanker.c: Spanker Spank"er (spăṉk"ẽr), n. 1. One who spanks, or anything used as an instrument for spanking.
Spanker Spank"er, n. A small coin. [Obs. or Prov. Eng.]

spanking.c: spanking spank"ing, a. 1. Moving with a quick, lively pace, or capable of so doing; dashing.
spanking breeze spanking breeze (Naut.), a strong breeze.

spanless.c: spanless span"less (spăn"lĕs), a. Incapable of being spanned.

spanner.c: spanner span"ner (spăn"nẽr), n. 1. One who, or that which, spans.

spannew.c: span-new span"-new` (spăn"nū`), a. [Icel. spānnȳr, properly, new as a ship just split; spānn chip + nȳr new. See Spoon, and New.] Quite new; brand-new; fire-new. “A span-new archbishop's chair.” Fuller.

spannishing.c: spannishing span"nish*ing (spăn"nĭsh*ĭng), n. [From OF. espanir to spread, F. épanouir. See Expand.] The full blooming of a flower. [Obs.] Rom. of R.

spanpiece.c: spanpiece span"piece (spăn"pēs`), n. (Arch.) The collar of a roof; sparpiece.

spanworm.c: spanworm span"worm` (spăn"wûrm`), n. (Zool.) The larva of any geometrid moth, as the cankerworm; a geometer; a measuring worm.

spar.c: spar spar (spär), n. [AS. spaer in spaerstān chalkstone; akin to MHG. spar, G. sparkalk plaster.] (Min.) An old name for a nonmetallic mineral, usually cleavable and somewhat lustrous; as, calc spar, or calcite, fluor spar, etc. It was especially used in the case of the gangue minerals of a metalliferous vein.

Spar Spar, n. [OE. sparre; akin to D. spar, G. sparren, OHG. sparro, Dan. & Sw. sparre, Icel. sparri; of uncertain origin. √171. Cf. Spar, v. t. ] 1. (Naut.) A general term any round piece of timber used as a mast, yard, boom, or gaff.
Spar Spar, v. t. [OE. sparren, AS. sparrian; akin to G. sperren, Icel. sperra; from the noun. √171. See Spara beam, bar.] 1. To bolt; to bar. [Obs.] Chaucer.

Spar Spar, v. i. [imp. & p. p. Sparred (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Sparring.] [Of uncertain origin; cf. OF. esparer to kick, F. éparer, or Icel. sperra to stretch out the legs, to struggle.] 1. To strike with the feet or spurs, as cocks do.
Spar Spar, n. 1. A contest at sparring or boxing.

sparable.c: Sparable Spar"a*ble (?), n. [Corrupted from sparrow bill.] A kind of small nail used by shoemakers.

sparada.c: Sparada Spar"a*da (?), n. (Zool.) A small California surf fish (Micrometrus aggregatus); -- called also shiner.

sparadrap.c: Sparadrap Spar"a*drap (?), n. [F. sparadrap; cf. It. sparadrappo, NL. sparadrapa.] 1. A cerecloth. [Obs.]

sparagrass.c: Sparagrass Sparagus Sparage { Spar"age (?; 48), Spar"a*gus (?), Spar"a*grass` (?), } n. Obs. or corrupt forms of Asparagus.

sparble.c: Sparble Spar"ble (?), v. t. [OF. esparpiller to scatter, F. éparpiller.] To scatter; to disperse; to rout. [Obs.]

spare.c: Spare Spare (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Spared (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Sparing.] [AS. sparian, fr. spaer spare, sparing, saving; akin to D. & G. sparen, OHG. spar?n, Icel. & Sw. spara, Dan. spare See Spare, a.] 1. To use frugally or stintingly, as that which is scarce or valuable; to retain or keep unused; to save. “No cost would he spare.” Chaucer.
Spare Spare (?), v. i. 1. To be frugal; not to be profuse; to live frugally; to be parsimonious.
Spare Spare, a. [Compar. Sparer (?); superl. Sparest; -- not used in all the senses of the word.] [AS. spaer sparing. Cf. Spare, v. t. ] 1. Scanty; not abundant or plentiful; as, a spare diet.
Spare Spare (?), n. 1. The act of sparing; moderation; restraint. [Obs.]

sparely.c: Sparely Spare"ly, adv. In a spare manner; sparingly.

spareness.c: Spareness Spare"ness, n. [Cf. AS. spaernis frugality.] The quality or state of being lean or thin; leanness.

sparerib.c: Sparerib Spare"rib` (?), n. [Spare, a. + rib.] A piece of pork, consisting or ribs with little flesh on them.

sparge.c: Sparge Sparge (?), v. t. [L. spargere; cf. F. asperger.] To sprinkle; to moisten by sprinkling; as, to sparge paper.

spargefaction.c: Spargefaction Spar`ge*fac"tion (?), n. [L. spargere to strew + facere, factum, to make.] The act of sprinkling. [Obs.] Swift.

sparger.c: Sparger Spar"ger (?), n. [Cf. F. asperger to sprinkle, L. aspergere, spargere.] A vessel with a perforated cover, for sprinkling with a liquid; a sprinkler.

sparhawk.c: Sparhawk Spar"hawk` (?), n. [OE. sperhauke.] (Zool.) The sparrow hawk. [Prov. Eng.]

sparhung.c: Spar-hung Spar"-hung` (?), a. Hung with spar, as a cave.

sparing.c: Sparing Spar"ing (?), a. Spare; saving; frugal; merciful. Bacon.

spark.c: Spark Spark (?), n. [OE. sparke, AS. spearca; akin to D. spark, sperk; cf. Icel. spraka to crackle, Lith. spragëti, Gr.? a bursting with a noise, Skr. sph?rj to crackle, to thunder. Cf. Speak.] 1. A small particle of fire or ignited substance which is emitted by a body in combustion.
Spark Spark, n. [Icel. sparkr lively, sprightly.] 1. A brisk, showy, gay man.
Spark Spark, v. i. 1. To sparkle. [Obs.] Spenser.
Spark Spark, v. i. To play the spark, beau, or lover.

Spark coil Spark coil. (Elec.) (a) An induction coil used for producing sparks, esp. in an internal-combustion engine, wireless telegraph apparatus, etc. (b) A self-induction coil used to increase the spark in an electric gas-lighting apparatus.

Spark gap Spark gap. (Elec.) The space filled with air or other dielectric between high potential terminals (as of an electrostatic machine, induction coil, or condenser), through which the discharge passes; the air gap of a jump spark.

Spark plug Spark plug. In internal-combustion engines with electric ignition, a plug, screwed into the cylinder head, connected with the induction coil or magneto circuit on the outside, and used to produce a spark to ignite the fuel-air mixture in the engine.

sparkful.c: Sparkful Spark"ful (?), a. Lively; brisk; gay. [Obs.] “Our sparkful youth.” Camden.

sparkish.c: Sparkish Spark"ish, a. 1. Like a spark; airy; gay. W. Walsh.

sparkle.c: Sparkle Spar"kle (?), n. [Dim. of spark.] 1. A little spark; a scintillation.

Sparkle Spar"kle, v. i. [imp. & p. p. Sparkled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Sparkling (?).] [See Sparkle, n., Spark of fire.] 1. To emit sparks; to throw off ignited or incandescent particles; to shine as if throwing off sparks; to emit flashes of light; to scintillate; to twinkle; as, the blazing wood sparkles; the stars sparkle.
Sparkle Spar"kle, v. t. To emit in the form or likeness of sparks. “Did sparkle forth great light.” Spenser.
Sparkle Spar"kle, v. t. [Cf. Sparble.] 1. To disperse. [Obs.]

sparkler.c: Sparkler Spar"kler (?), n. One who scatters; esp., one who scatters money; an improvident person. [Obs.]
Sparkler Spar"kler, n. One who, or that which, sparkles.

sparkling.c: Sparkling Spar"kling (?), a. Emitting sparks; glittering; flashing; brilliant; lively; as, sparkling wine; sparkling eyes. -- Spar"kling*ly, adv. -- Spar"kling*ness, n.

sparling.c: Sparling Spar"ling (?), n. [Akin to G. spierling, spiering, D. spiering: cf. F. éperlan.] (Zool.) (a) The European smelt (Osmerus eperlanus). (b) A young salmon. (c) A tern. [Scot. & Prov. Eng.]

sparlyre.c: Sparlyre Spar"lyre` (?), n. [AS. spear-lira.] The calf of the leg. [Obs.] Wyclif (Deut. xxviii. 35).

sparoid.c: Sparoid Spa"roid (?; 277), a. [L. sparus the gilthead + -oid: cf. F. sparoïde.] (Zool.) Of or pertaining to the Sparidae, a family of spinous-finned fishes which includes the scup, sheepshead, and sea bream. -- n. One of the Sparidae.

sparpiece.c: Sparpiece Spar"piece` (?), n. (Arch.) The collar beam of a roof; the spanpiece. Gwilt.

sparpoil.c: Sparpoil Spar"poil (?), v. t. [See Sparble.] To scatter; to spread; to disperse. [Obs.]

sparrow.c: Sparrow Spar"row (?), n. [OE. sparwe, AS. spearwa; akin to OHG. sparo, G. sperling, Icel. spörr, Dan. spurv, spurre, Sw. sparf, Goth. sparwa; -- originally, probably, the quiverer or flutterer, and akin to E. spurn. See Spurn, and cf. Spavin.] 1. (Zool.) One of many species of small singing birds of the family Fringilligae, having conical bills, and feeding chiefly on seeds. Many sparrows are called also finches, and buntings. The common sparrow, or house sparrow, of Europe (Passer domesticus) is noted for its familiarity, its voracity, its attachment to its young, and its fecundity. See House sparrow, under House.

sparrowgrass.c: Sparrowgrass Spar"row*grass` (?), n. [Corrupted from asparagus.] Asparagus. [Colloq.] See the Note under Asparagus.

sparrowwort.c: Sparrowwort Spar"row*wort` (?), n. (Bot.) An evergreen shrub of the genus Erica (Erica passerina).

sparry.c: Sparry Spar"ry (?), a. [From Spar.] Resembling spar, or consisting of spar; abounding with spar; having a confused crystalline structure; spathose.

sparse.c: Sparse Sparse (?), a. [Compar. Sparser (?); superl. Sparsest.] [L. sparsus, p. p. of spargere to strew, scatter. Cf. Asperse, Disperse.] 1. Thinly scattered; set or planted here and there; not being dense or close together; as, a sparse population. Carlyle.
Sparse Sparse, v. t. [L. sparsus, p. p. of spargere to scatter.] To scatter; to disperse. [Obs.] Spenser.

sparsely.c: Sparsely Sparse"ly, adv. In a scattered or sparse manner.

sparseness.c: Sparseness Sparse"ness, n. The quality or state of being sparse; as, sparseness of population.

sparsim.c: Sparsim ‖Spar"sim (?), adv. [L., fr. spargere to scatter.] Sparsely; scatteredly; here and there.

spartan.c: Spartan Spar"tan (?), a. [L. Spartanus.] Of or pertaining to Sparta, especially to ancient Sparta; hence, hardy; undaunted; as, Spartan souls; Spartan bravey. -- n. A native or inhabitant of Sparta; figuratively, a person of great courage and fortitude.

sparteine.c: Sparteine Spar"te*ine (?), n. (Chem.) A narcotic alkaloid extracted from the tops of the common broom (Cytisus scoparius, formerly Spartium scoparium), as a colorless oily liquid of aniline-like odor and very bitter taste.

sparterie.c: Sparterie Spar"ter*ie (?), n. [F., from Sp. esparto esparto, L. spartum, Gr.?.] Articles made of the blades or fiber of the Lygeum Spartum and Stipa tenacissima (syn. Macrochloa tenacissima), kinds of grass used in Spain and other countries for making ropes, mats, baskets, nets, and mattresses. Loudon.

sparth.c: Sparth Sparth (?), n. [Cf. Icel. spar?a.] An Anglo-Saxon battle-ax, or halberd. [Obs.]

sparve.c: Sparve Sparve (?), n. (Zool.) The hedge sparrow. [Prov. Eng.]

spasm.c: Spasm Spasm (?), n. [F. spasme, L. spasmus, Gr.?, from?,?, to draw, to cause convulsion. Cf. Span, v. t.] 1. (Med.) An involuntary and unnatural contraction of one or more muscles or muscular fibers.

spasmodic.c: Spasmodic Spas"mod"ic (?), a. [Gr.?;? a convulsion +? likeness: cf. F. spasmotique.] 1. (Med.) Of or pertaining to spasm; consisting in spasm; occuring in, or characterized by, spasms; as, a spasmodic asthma.
Spasmodic Spas*mod"ic, n. (Med.) A medicine for spasm.

spasmodical.c: Spasmodical Spas*mod"ic*al (?), a. Same as Spasmodic, a. -- Spas*mod"ic*al*ly (#), adv.

spastic.c: Spastic Spas"tic (?), a. [L. spasticus, Gr.?, fr.? to draw: cf. F. spastique. See Spasm.] (Med.) Of or pertaining to spasm; spasmodic; especially, pertaining to tonic spasm; tetanic.

spasticity.c: Spasticity Spas*tic"i*ty (?), n. 1. A state of spasm.

spat.c: Spat Spat (?), imp. of Spit. [Obs. or R.]
Spat Spat, n. [From the root of spit; hence, literally, that which is ejected.] A young oyster or other bivalve mollusk, both before and after it first becomes adherent, or such young, collectively.
Spat Spat, v. i. & t. To emit spawn; to emit, as spawn.
Spat Spat, n. [Cf. Pat.] 1. A light blow with something flat. [U.S. & Prov. Eng.]
Spat Spat, v. i. To dispute. [R.] Smart.
Spat Spat, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Spatted; p. pr. & vb. n. Spatting.] To slap, as with the open hand; to clap together; as the hands. [Local, U.S.]
Spat Spat, n. [Short for Spatterdash.] 1. A legging; a gaiter. [Scot. & Dial. Eng.]

spatangoid.c: Spatangoid Spa*tan"goid (?), a. (Zool.) Of or pertaining to the Spatangoidea. -- n. One of the Spatangoidea.

spatangoidea.c: Spatangoidea ‖Spat`an*goi"de*a (?), n. pl. [NL. See Spatangus, and -oid.] (Zool.) An order of irregular sea urchins, usually having a more or less heart-shaped shell with four or five petal-like ambulacra above. The mouth is edentulous and situated anteriorly, on the under side.

spatangus.c: Spatangus ‖Spa*tan"gus (?), n. [NL., fr. L. spatangius a kind of sea urchin, Gr.?.] (Zool.) A genus of heart-shaped sea urchins belonging to the Spatangoidea.

spate.c: Spate Spate (?), n. [Of Celtic origin; cf. Ir. speid.] A river flood; an overflow or inundation. Burns.

spathaceous.c: Spathaceous Spa*tha"ceous (?), a. (Bot.) Having a spathe; resembling a spathe; spathal.

spathal.c: Spathal Spa"thal (?), a. (Bot.) Furnished with a spathe; as, spathal flowers. Howitt.

spathe.c: Spathe Spathe (?), n. [L. spatha, Gr.?: cf. F. spathe. See Spade for digging.] (Bot.) A special involucre formed of one leaf and inclosing a spadix, as in aroid plants and palms. See the Note under Bract, and Illust. of Spadix.

spathed.c: Spathed Spathed (?), a. (Bot.) Having a spathe or calyx like a sheath.

spathic.c: Spathic Spath"ic (?), a. [Cf. F. spathique, fr. F. & G. spath spar.] Like spar; foliated or lamellar; spathose.

spathiform.c: Spathiform Spath"i*form (?), a. [F. spathiforme.] Resembling spar in form. “The ocherous, spathiform, and mineralized forms of uranite.” Lavoisier (Trans.).

spathose.c: Spathose Spath"ose`, a. [See Spathe.] (Bot.) Having a spathe; resembling a spathe; spatheceous; spathal.

spatial.c: Spatial Spa"tial (?), a. Of or pertaining to space. “Spatial quantity and relations.” L. H. Atwater.

spatiate.c: Spatiate Spa"ti*ate (?), v. t. [L. spatiatus, p. p. of spatiari, fr. spatiatum. See Space.] To rove; to ramble. [Obs.] Bacon.

spatter.c: Spatter Spat"ter (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Spattered (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Spattering.] [From the root of spit salvia.] 1. To sprinkle with a liquid or with any wet substance, as water, mud, or the like; to make wet of foul spots upon by sprinkling; as, to spatter a coat; to spatter the floor; to spatter boots with mud.
Spatter Spat"ter, v. i. To throw something out of the mouth in a scattering manner; to sputter.

spatterdashes.c: Spatterdashes Spat"ter*dash`es (?), n. pl. [Spatter + dash.] Coverings for the legs, to protect them from water and mud; long gaiters.

spatterdock.c: Spatter-dock Spat`ter-dock` (?), n. (Bot.) The common yellow water lily (Nuphar advena).

spattlingpoppy.c: Spattling-poppy Spat"tling-pop"py (?), n. [Prov. E. spattle to spit + E. poppy.] (Bot.) A kind of catchfly (Silene inflata) which is sometimes frothy from the action of captured insects.

spatula.c: Spatula Spat"u*la (?; 135), n. [L. spatula, spathula, dim. of spatha a spatula: F. spatule. See Spade for digging.] An implement shaped like a knife, flat, thin, and somewhat flexible, used for spreading paints, fine plasters, drugs in compounding prescriptions, etc. Cf. Palette knife, under Palette.

spatulate.c: Spatulate Spat"u*late (?), a. [NL. spatulatus.] (Nat. Hist.) Shaped like spatula, or like a battledoor, being roundish, with a long, narrow, linear base. [Also written spathulate.]

spauld.c: Spauld Spauld (?), n. [See Spall the shoulder.] The shoulder. [Scot.]

spavin.c: Spavin Spav"in (?), n. [OE. spaveyne, OF. esparvain, F. éparvin; akin to OF. espervier a sparrow hawk, F. épervier, fr. OHG. sparwāri (G. sperber), fr. OHG. sparo sparrow, because this disease makes the horse raise the infirm leg in the manner of a sparrow hawk or sparrow. See Sparrow.] (Far.) A disease of horses characterized by a bony swelling developed on the hock as the result of inflammation of the bones; also, the swelling itself. The resulting lameness is due to the inflammation, and not the bony tumor as popularly supposed. Harbaugh.

spawl.c: Spawl Spawl (?), n. A splinter or fragment, as of wood or stone. See Spall.
Spawl Spawl, n. [Cf. AS. spātl, fr. spǣtan to spit; probably akin to spīwan, E. spew. Cf. Spew.] Scattered or ejected spittle.
Spawl Spawl, v. i. & t. [imp. & p. p. Spawled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Spawling.] [Cf. AS. spātlian.] To scatter spittle from the mouth; to spit, as saliva.

spawling.c: Spawling Spawl"ing, n. That which is spawled, or spit out.

spawn.c: Spawn Spawn (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Spawned (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Spawning.] [OE. spanen, OF. espandre, properly, to shed, spread, L. expandere to spread out. See Expand.] 1. To produce or deposit (eggs), as fishes or frogs do.
Spawn Spawn, v. i. 1. To deposit eggs, as fish or frogs do.
Spawn Spawn, n. [√170. See Spawn, v. t.] 1. The ova, or eggs, of fishes, oysters, and other aquatic animals.

spawner.c: Spawner Spawn"er (?), n. 1. (Zool.) A mature female fish.

spay.c: Spay Spay (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Spayed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Spaying.] [Cf. Armor. spac'hein, spaza to geld, W. dyspaddu to geld, L. spado a eunuch, Gr.?.] To remove or extirpate the ovaries of, as a sow or a bitch; to castrate (a female animal).
Spay Spay, n. [Cf. Spade a spay, Spay, v. t.] (Zool.) The male of the red deer in his third year; a spade.

spayade.c: Spayade Spayad { Spay"ad (?), Spay"ade (?), } n. (Zool.) A spay.

speak.c: Speak Speak (?), v. i. [imp. Spoke (?) (Spake (?) Archaic); p. p. Spoken (?) (Spoke, Obs. or Colloq.); p. pr. & vb. n. Speaking.] [OE. speken, AS. specan, sprecan; akin to OF.ries. spreka, D. spreken, OS. spreken, G. sprechen, OHG. sprehhan, and perhaps to Skr. sphūrj to crackle, to thunder. Cf. Spark of fire, Speech.] 1. To utter words or articulate sounds, as human beings; to express thoughts by words; as, the organs may be so obstructed that a man may not be able to speak.
Speak Speak (?), v. t. 1. To utter with the mouth; to pronounce; to utter articulately, as human beings.

speakable.c: Speakable Speak"a*ble (?), a. 1. Capable of being spoken; fit to be spoken. Ascham.

speaker.c: Speaker Speak"er (?), n. 1. One who speaks. Specifically: (a) One who utters or pronounces a discourse; usually, one who utters a speech in public; as, the man is a good speaker, or a bad speaker. (b) One who is the mouthpiece of others; especially, one who presides over, or speaks for, a delibrative assembly, preserving order and regulating the debates; as, the Speaker of the House of Commons, originally, the mouthpiece of the House to address the king; the Speaker of a House of Representatives.

speakership.c: Speakership Speak"er*ship, n. The office of speaker; as, the speakership of the House of Representatives.

speaking.c: Speaking Speak"ing, a. 1. Uttering speech; used for conveying speech; as, man is a speaking animal; a speaking tube.
Speaking Speak"ing, n. 1. The act of uttering words.

spear.c: Spear Spear (?), n. [OE. spere, AS. spere; akin to D. & G. speer, OS. & OHS. sper, Icel. spjör, pl., Dan. spaer, L. sparus.] 1. A long, pointed weapon, used in war and hunting, by thrusting or throwing; a weapon with a long shaft and a sharp head or blade; a lance. “A sharp ground spear.” Chaucer.
Spear Spear, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Speared (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Spearing.] To pierce with a spear; to kill with a spear; as, to spear a fish.
Spear Spear, v. i. To shoot into a long stem, as some plants. See Spire. Mortimer.

spearer.c: Spearer Spear"er (?), n. One who uses a spear; as, a spearer of fish.

spearfish.c: Spearfish Spear"fish` (?), n. (Zool.) (a) A large and powerful fish (Tetrapturus albidus) related to the swordfish, but having scales and ventral fins. It is found on the American coast and the Mediterranean. (b) The carp sucker.

spearhead.c: Spearhead Spear"head` (?), n. The pointed head, or end, of a spear.

spearman.c: Spearman Spear"man (?), n.; pl. Spearmen (?). One who is armed with a spear. Acts xxiii. 23.

spearmint.c: Spearmint Spear"mint` (?), n. [So named from its spiry, not capitate, inflorescence. Dr. Prior.] (Bot.) A species of mint (Mentha viridis) growing in moist soil. It vields an aromatic oil. See Mint, and Mentha.

spearwood.c: Spearwood Spear"wood` (?), n. (Bot.) An Australian tree (Acacia Doratoxylon), and its tough wood, used by the natives for spears.

spearwort.c: Spearwort Spear"wort` (?), n. [AS. sperewyrt.] (Bot.) A name given to several species of crowfoot (Ranunculus) which have spear-shaped leaves.

speary.c: Speary Spear"y (?), a. Having the form of a spear.

specht.c: Specht Specht (?), n. [See Speight.] (Zool.) A woodpecker. [Obs. or prov. Eng.] Sherwood.

special.c: Special Spe"cial (?), a. [L. specialis, fr. species a particular sort, kind, or quality: cf. F. spécial. See Species, and cf. Especial.] 1. Of or pertaining to a species; constituting a species or sort.

specialism.c: Specialism Spe"cial*ism (?), n. Devotion to a particular and restricted part or branch of knowledge, art, or science; as, medical specialism.

specialist.c: Specialist Spe"cial*ist (?), n. One who devotes himself to some specialty; as, a medical specialist, one who devotes himself to diseases of particular parts of the body, as the eye, the ear, the nerves, etc.

speciality.c: Speciality Spe`ci*al"i*ty (?), n.; pl. Specialities (#). [See Special, and Specialty.] 1. A particular or peculiar case; a particularity. Sir M. Hale.

specialization.c: Specialization Spe`cial*i*za"tion (?), n. 1. The act of specializing, or the state of being spezialized.

specialize.c: Specialize Spe"cial*ize (?), v. t. 1. To mention specially; to particularize.

specially.c: Specially Spe"cial*ly, adv. 1. In a special manner; particularly; especially. Chaucer.

specialty.c: Specialty Spe"cial*ty (?), n.; pl. Specialties (#). [F. spécialité. Cf. Speciality.] 1. Particularity.

specie.c: Specie ‖Spe"ci*e (?), abl. of L. species sort, kind. Used in the phrase in specie, that is, in sort, in kind, in (its own) form.
Specie Spe"cie (?), n. [Formed as a singular from species, in sense 5.] Coin; hard money.

species.c: Species Spe"cies (?), n. sing. & pl. [L., a sight, outward appearance, shape, form, a particular sort, kind, or quality, a species. See Spice, n., and cf. Specie, Special.] 1. Visible or sensible presentation; appearance; a sensible percept received by the imagination; an image. [R.] “The species of the letters illuminated with indigo and violet.” Sir I. Newton.

specifiable.c: Specifiable Spec"i*fi`a*ble (?), a. Admitting specification; capable of being specified.

specific.c: specific spe*cif"ic (spe*sĭf"ĭk), a. [F. spécifique, or NL. spesificus; L. species a particular sort or kind + facere to make. Cf. specify.] 1. Of or pertaining to a species; characterizing or constituting a species; possessing the peculiar property or properties of a thing which constitute its species, and distinguish it from other things; as, the specific form of an animal or a plant; the specific qualities of a drug; the specific distinction between virtue and vice.
Specific Spe*cif"ic, n. 1. (Med.) A specific remedy. See Specific, a., 3.

specifically.c: Specifically Spe*cif"ic*al*ly (?), adv. In a specific manner.

specificalness.c: Specificalness Spe*cif"ic*al*ness, n. The quality of being specific.

specificate.c: Specificate Spe*cif"i*cate (spe*sĭf"ĭ*kāt), v. t. [See Specify.] To show, mark, or designate the species, or the distinguishing particulars of; to specify. [Obs.] ir M. Hale.

specification.c: specification spec`i*fi*ca"tion (spĕs`ĭ*fĭ*kā"shŭn), n. [Cf. F. spécification, LL. specificatio.] 1. The act of specifying or determining by a mark or limit; notation of limits.

specificness.c: Specificness Spe*cif"ic*ness (?), n. The quality or state of being specific.

specify.c: Specify Spec"i*fy (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Specified (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Specifying (?).] [F. spécifier, or OF. especifier, fr. LL. specificare. See Species, -fy.] To mention or name, as a particular thing; to designate in words so as to distinguish from other things; as, to specify the uses of a plant; to specify articles purchased.

specimen.c: Specimen Spec"i*men (?), n. [L., fr. specere to look, to behold. See Spy.] A part, or small portion, of anything, or one of a number of things, intended to exhibit the kind and quality of the whole, or of what is not exhibited; a sample; as, a specimen of a man's handwriting; a specimen of a person's blood; a specimen of painting; aspecimen of one's art.

speciosity.c: Speciosity Spe`ci*os"i*ty (?), n.; pl. Speciocities (#). [Cf. LL. speciositas.] 1. The quality or state of being specious; speciousness.

specious.c: Specious Spe"cious (?), a. [L. speciosusgood-looking, beautiful, specious, fr. species look, show, appearance; cf. F. spécoeux. See Species.] 1. Presenting a pleasing appearance; pleasing in form or look; showy.

speck.c: Speck Speck (?), n. [Cf. Icel. spik blubber, AS. spic, D. spek, G. speck.] The blubber of whales or other marine mammals; also, the fat of the hippopotamus.

Speck Speck, n. [OE. spekke, AS. specca; cf. LG. spaak.] 1. A small discolored place in or on anything, or a small place of a color different from that of the main substance; a spot; a stain; a blemish; as, a speck on paper or loth; specks of decay in fruit. “Gray sand, with black specks.” Anson.

Speck Speck, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Specked (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Specking.] To cause the presence of specks upon or in, especially specks regarded as defects or blemishes; to spot; to speckle; as, paper specked by impurities in the water used in its manufacture.

speckle.c: Speckle Spec"kle (?), n. [Dim. of speck; cf. D. spikkel.] A little or spot in or anything, of a different substance or color from that of the thing itself.

Speckle Spec"kle, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Speckled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Speckling (?).] To mark with small spots of a different color from that of the rest of the surface; to variegate with spots of a different color from the ground or surface.

speckled.c: Speckled Spec"kled (?), a. Marked or variegated with small spots of a different color from that of the rest of the surface.

speckledbill.c: Speckled-bill Spec"kled-bill" (?), n. (Zool.) The American white-fronted goose (Anser albifrons).

speckledness.c: Speckledness Spec"kled*ness, n. The quality of being speckled.

specksioneer.c: Specksioneer Speck`sion*eer" (?), n. The chief harpooner, who also directs in cutting up the speck, or blubber; -- so called among whalers.

speckt.c: Speckt Speckt (?), n. A woodpecker. See Speight.

spectacle.c: Spectacle Spec"ta*cle (?), n. [F., fr. L. spectaculum, fr. spectare to look at, to behold, v. intens. fr. specere. See Spy.] 1. Something exhibited to view; usually, something presented to view as extraordinary, or as unusual and worthy of special notice; a remarkable or noteworthy sight; a show; a pageant; a gazingstock.

spectacled.c: Spectacled Spec"ta*cled (?), a. 1. Furnished with spectacles; wearing spectacles.

spectacular.c: Spectacular Spec*tac"u*lar (?), a. 1. Of or pertaining to a shows; of the nature of a show. “Spectacular sports.” G. Hickes.

spectant.c: Spectant Spec"tant (?), a. [L. spectans, p. pr. of spectare to look at.] Looking forward.

spectation.c: Spectation Spec*ta"tion (?), n. [L. spectatio.] Regard; aspect; appearance. Harvey.

spectator.c: Spectator Spec*ta"tor (?), n. [L. spectator: cf. F. spectateur. See Spectacle.] One who on; one who sees or beholds; a beholder; one who is personally present at, and sees, any exhibition; as, the spectators at a show. “Devised and played to take spectators.” Shak.

spectatorial.c: Spectatorial Spec`ta*to"ri*al (?), a. Of or pertaining to a spectator. Addison.

spectatorship.c: Spectatorship Spec*ta"tor*ship (?), n. 1. The office or quality of a spectator. [R.] Addison.

spectatrix.c: Spectatrix Spectatress { Spec*ta"tress (?), Spec*ta"trix (?), } n. [L. spectatrix.] A female beholder or looker-on. “A spectatress of the whole scene.” Jeffrey.

spectre.c: Spectre Specter { Spec"ter, Spec"tre } (?), n. [F. spectre, fr. L. spectrum an appearance, image, specter, fr. specere to look. See Spy, and cf. Spectrum.] 1. Something preternaturally visible; an apparition; a ghost; a phantom.

spectral.c: Spectral Spec"tral (?), a. 1. Of or pertaining to a specter; ghosty.

spectrally.c: Spectrally Spec"tral*ly, adv. In the form or manner of a specter.

spectrobolometer.c: Spectrobolometer Spec`tro*bo*lom"e*ter (?), n. (Physics) A combination of spectroscope and bolometer for determining the distribution of energy in a spectrum. -- Spec`tro*bo`lo*met"ric (#), a.

spectroelectric.c: Spectroelectric Spec`tro*e*lec"tric (?), a. Pert. to or designating any form of spark tube the electric discharge within which is used in spectroscopic observations.

spectrogram.c: Spectrogram Spec"tro*gram (?), n. [Spectrum + -gram.] (Physics) A photograph, map, or diagram of a spectrum.

spectrograph.c: Spectrograph Spec"tro*graph (?), n. [Spectrum + graph.] (Physics) (a) An apparatus for photographing or mapping a spectrum. (b) A photograph or picture of a spectrum. -- Spec`tro*graph"ic (#), a. -- Spec`tro*graph"ic*al*ly (#), adv. -- Spec*trog"ra*phy (#), n.

spectroheliogram.c: Spectroheliogram Spec`tro*he"li*o*gram` (?), n. [Spectrum + heloi- + -gram.] (Astrophysics) A photograph of the sun made by monochromatic light, usually of the calcium line (k), and showing the sun's faculae and prominences.

spectroheliograph.c: Spectroheliograph Spec`tro*he"li*o*graph (?), n. (Astrophysics) An apparatus for making spectroheliograms, consisting of a spectroscopic camera used in combination with a telescope, and provided with clockwork for moving the sun's image across the slit. -- Spec`tro*he`li*o*graph"ic (#), a.

spectrological.c: Spectrological Spec`tro*log"ic*al (?), a. Of or pertaining to spectrology; as, spectrological studies or experiments. -- Spec`tro*log"ic*al*ly, adv.

spectrology.c: Spectrology Spec*trol"o*gy (?), n. [Spectrum + -logy.] (Chem.Phys.) The science of spectrum analysis in any or all of its relations and applications.

spectrometer.c: Spectrometer Spec*trom"e*ter (?), n. [Spectrum + -meter.] (Physics) A spectroscope fitted for measurements of the luminious spectra observed with it.

spectrometry.c: Spectrometry Spec*trom"e*try (?), n. (Physics) Art or process of using a spectrometer, of any type; -- when used alone, it usually refers to the use of a spectrometer using light in the visible, infrared, or ultraviolet region. -- Spec`tro*met"ric (#), a.

spectrophone.c: Spectrophone Spec"tro*phone (?), n. [Spectrum + Gr.? sound.] An instrument constructed on the principle of the photophone and used in spectrum analysis as an adjunct to the spectroscope. -- Spec`tro*phon"ic (#), a.

spectrophotometer.c: Spectrophotometer Spec`tro*pho*tom"e*ter (?), n. [Spectrum + photometer.] 1. (Opt.) An instrument for measuring or comparing the intensities of the colors of the spectrum.

spectrophotometry.c: Spectrophotometry Spec`tro*pho*tom"e*try (?), n. 1. The art of comparing, photometrically, the brightness of two spectra, wave length by wave length; the use of the spectrophotometer.

spectroscope.c: Spectroscope Spec"tro*scope (?), n. [Spectrum + -scope.] (Physics) An optical instrument for forming and examining spectra (as that of solar light, or those produced by flames in which different substances are volatilized), so as to determine, from the position of the spectral lines, the composition of the substance.

spectroscopical.c: Spectroscopical Spectroscopic { Spec`tro*scop"ic (?), Spec`tro*scop"ic*al (?), } a. Of or pertaining to a spectroscope, or spectroscopy. -- Spec`tro*scop"ic*al*ly, adv.

spectroscopist.c: Spectroscopist Spec*tros"co*pist (? or?), n. One who investigates by means of a spectroscope; one skilled in the use of the spectroscope.

spectroscopy.c: Spectroscopy Spec*tros"co*py (?), n. the art and science dealing with the use of a spectroscope, and the production and analysis of spectra; the action of using a spectroscope.

spectrum.c: Spectrum Spec"trum (?), n.; pl. Spectra (#). [L. See Specter.] 1. An apparition; a specter. [Obs.]

specular.c: Specular Spec"u*lar (?), a. [L. specularis (cf., from the same root, specula a lookout, watchtower): cf. F. spéculaire. See Speculum.] 1. Having the qualities of a speculum, or mirror; having a smooth, reflecting surface; as, a specular metal; a specular surface.

speculate.c: Speculate Spec"u*late (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Speculated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Speculating.] [L. speculatus, p. p. of speculari to spy out, observe, fr. specula a lookout, fr. specere to look. See Spy.] 1. To consider by turning a subject in the mind, and viewing it in its different aspects and relations; to meditate; to contemplate; to theorize; as, to speculate on questions in religion; to speculate on political events.
Speculate Spec"u*late, v. t. To consider attentively; as, to speculate the nature of a thing. [R.] Sir W. Hamilton.

speculation.c: Speculation Spec`u*la"tion (?), n. [L. speculatio a spying out, observation: cf. F. spéculation.] 1. The act of speculating. Specifically: --

speculatist.c: Speculatist Spec"u*la*tist (spĕk"u*lȧ*tĭst), n. One who speculates, or forms theories; a speculator; a theorist.

speculative.c: Speculative Spec"u*la*tive (spĕk"u*lȧ*tĭv), a. [Cf. F. spéculatif, L. speculativus.] 1. Given to speculation; contemplative.

speculator.c: Speculator Spec"u*la`tor (spĕk"u*lā`tẽr), n. [L., a spy, explorer, investigator: cf. F. spéculateur.] One who speculates. Specifically: (a) An observer; a contemplator; hence, a spy; a watcher. [Obs.] Sir T. Browne.

speculatory.c: Speculatory Spec"u*la*to*ry (spĕk"u*lȧ*to*ry̆), a. [L. speculatorius belonging to spies or scouts.] 1. Intended or adapted for viewing or espying; having oversight. T. Warton.

speculist.c: Speculist Spec"u*list (?), n. One who observes or considers; an observer. [R.] Goldsmith.

speculum.c: Speculum Spec"u*lum (?), n.; pl. L. Specula (#), E. Speculum (#). [L., fr. specere to look, behold. See Spy.] 1. A mirror, or looking-glass; especially, a metal mirror, as in Greek and Roman archaeology.

sped.c: Sped Sped (?), imp. & p. p. of Speed.

speech.c: Speech Speech (?), n. [OE. speche, AS. sp?c, spr?, fr. specan, sprecan, to speak; akin to D. spraak speech, OHG. sprāhha, G. sprache, Sw. spr?k, Dan. sprog. See Speak.] 1. The faculty of uttering articulate sounds or words; the faculty of expressing thoughts by words or articulate sounds; the power of speaking.
Speech Speech, v. i. & t. To make a speech; to harangue. [R.]

speechful.c: Speechful Speech"ful (?), a. Full of speech or words; voluble; loquacious. [R.]

speechification.c: Speechification Speech`i*fi*ca"tion (?), n.[See Spechify.] The act of speechifying. [Used humorously or in contempt.]

speechifier.c: Speechifier Speech"i*fi`er (?), n. One who makes a speech or speeches; an orator; a declaimer. [Used humorously or in contempt.] G. Eliot.

speechify.c: Speechify Speech"i*fy (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Speechified (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Speechifying (?).] [Speech + -fy.] To make a speech; to harangue. [Used derisively or humorously.]

speechifying.c: Speechifying Speech"i*fy`ing, n. The act of making a speech or speeches. [Used derisively or humorously.]

speeching.c: Speeching Speech"ing, n. The act of making a speech. [R.]

speechless.c: Speechless Speech"less, a. 1. Destitute or deprived of the faculty of speech.

speechmaker.c: Speechmaker Speech"mak`er (?), n. One who makes speeches; one accustomed to speak in a public assembly.

speed.c: Speed Speed (?), n. [AS. sp?d success, swiftness, from sp?wan to succeed; akin to D. spoedd, OHG. spuot success, spuot to succees, Skr. sphā to increase, grow fat. √170b.] 1. Prosperity in an undertaking; favorable issue; success. “For common speed.” Chaucer.
Speed Speed (spēd), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Sped (spĕd), Speeded; p. pr. & vb. n. Speeding.] [AS. spēdan, fr. spēd, n.; akin to D. spoeden, G. sich sputen. See Speed, n.] 1. To go; to fare. [Obs.]
Speed Speed, v. t. 1. To cause to be successful, or to prosper; hence, to aid; to favor. “Fortune speed us!” Shak.
Speed counter Speed counter. (Mach.) A device for automatically counting the revolutions or pulsations of an engine or other machine; -- called also simply counter.

speeder.c: Speeder Speed"er (?), n. 1. One who, or that which, speeds.

speedful.c: Speedful Speed"ful (?), a. Full of speed (in any sense). [Obs.]

speedfully.c: Speedfully Speed"ful*ly, adv. In a speedful manner. [Obs.]

speedily.c: Speedily Speed"i*ly (?), adv. In a speedy manner.

speediness.c: Speediness Speed"i*ness, n. The quality or state of being speedy.

speedwell.c: Speedwell Speed"well (?), n. (Bot.) Any plant of the genus Veronica, mostly low herbs with pale blue corollas, which quickly fall off.

speedy.c: Speedy Speed"y (-y̆), a. [Compar. Speedier (?); superl. Speediest.] [AS. spēdyg.] Not dilatory or slow; quick; swift; nimble; hasty; rapid in motion or performance; as, a speedy flight; on speedy foot.

speer.c: Speer Speer, v. t. To ask. [Scot.] See Spere.

speet.c: Speet Speet (?), v. t. [Cf. D. speten. See Spit an iron prong.] To stab. [Obs.] Gammer Gurton's Needle.

speight.c: Speight Speight (?), n. [G. specht, probably akin to L. picus: cf. D. specht. √169. See Pie a magpie.] (Zool.) A woodpecker; -- called also specht, spekt, spight. [Obs. or Prov. Eng.]

speir.c: Speir Speir (?), v. i. To ask. See Spere. Sir W. Scott.

speiss.c: Speiss Speiss (?), n. [Cf. G. speise food, mixed metal for bells, etc.] 1. (Metal.) A regulus consisting essentially of nickel, obtained as a residue in fusing cobalt and nickel ores with silica and sodium carbonate to make smalt.

spekboom.c: Spekboom Spek"boom (?), n. [D., lit. fat tree.] (Bot.) The purslane tree of South Africa, -- said to be the favorite food of elephants. Balfour (Cyc. of India).

speke.c: Speke Speke (?), v. i. & t. To speak. [Obs.] Chaucer.

spekehouse.c: Spekehouse Speke"house` (?), n. The parlor or reception room of a convent. [Obs.]

spelding.c: Spelding Spel"ding (?), n. [Scot. speld to spread out, spelder to split. spread open; cf. G. spalten split.] A haddock or other small fish split open and dried in the sun; -- called also speldron. [Scot.]

spelk.c: Spelk Spelk (?), n. [AS. spelc, spilc, a little rod by which a thing is kept straight, a splint for binding up broken bones, akin to Icel. spelkur, pl., a splint. Cf. Spell a splinter.] A small stick or rod used as a spike in thatching; a splinter. [Prov. Eng.] Grose.

spell.c: Spell Spell (?), n. [OE. speld, AS. speld a spill to light a candle with; akin to D. speld a pin, OD. spelle, G. spalten to split, OHG. spaltan, MHG. spelte a splinter, Icel. spjald a square tablet, Goth. spilda a writing tablet. Cf. Spillsplinter, roll of paper, Spell to tell the letters of.] A spelk, or splinter. [Obs.] Holland.

Spell Spell, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Spelled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Spelling.] [AS. spelian to supply another's place.] To supply the place of for a time; to take the turn of, at work; to relieve; as, to spell the helmsman.

Spell Spell, n. 1. The relief of one person by another in any piece of work or watching; also, a turn at work which is carried on by one person or gang relieving another; as, a spell at the pumps; a spell at the masthead.

Spell Spell (?), n.[AS. spell a saying, tale, speech; akin to OS. & OHG. spel, Icel. spjall,Goth. spill. Cf. Gospel, Spell to tell the letters of.] 1. A story; a tale. [Obs.] “Hearken to my spell.” Chaucer.

Spell Spell, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Spelled (?) or Spelt (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Spelling.] [OE. spellen, spellien, tell, relate, AS. spellian, fr. spell a saying, tale; akin to MHG. spellen to relate, Goth. spill?n.e Spell a tale. In sense 4 and those following, OE. spellen, perhaps originally a different word, and from or influenced by spell a splinter, from the use of a piece of wood to point to the letters in schools: cf. D. spellen to spell. Cf. Spell splinter.] 1. To tell; to relate; to teach. [Obs.]
Spell Spell, v. i. 1. To form words with letters, esp. with the proper letters, either orally or in writing.

spellable.c: Spellable Spell"a*ble (?), a. Capable of being spelt. Carlyle.

spellbind.c: Spellbind Spell"bind` (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Spellbound (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Spellbinding.] To bind or hold by, or as if by, a spell or charm; to entrance or fascinate, esp. by eloquence of speech, as in a political campaign. -- Spell"bind`er (#), n.

spellbound.c: Spellbound Spell"bound` (?), a. Bound by, or as by, a spell.

spellful.c: Spellful Spell"ful (?), a. Abounding in spells, or charms.

spelling.c: Spelling Spell"ing, n. The act of one who spells; formation of words by letters; orthography.
Spelling Spell"ing, a. Of or pertaining to spelling.

spellwork.c: Spellwork Spell"work` (?), n. Power or effect of magic; that which is wrought by magic; enchantment.

spelt.c: Spelt Spelt (?), imp. & p. p. of Spell. Spelled.
Spelt Spelt, n. [AS. spelt, fr. L. spelta.] (Bot.) A species of grain (Triticum Spelta) much cultivated for food in Germany and Switzerland; -- called also German wheat.
Spelt Spelt, v. t. & i. [See Spell a splinter.] To split; to break; to spalt. [Obs.] Mortimer.

spelter.c: Spelter Spel"ter (?), n. [Cf. LG. spialter, G. & D. spiauter. Cf. Pewter.] (Metal.) Zinc; -- especially so called in commerce and arts.

spelunc.c: Spelunc Spe*lunc" (?), n. [L. spelunca cave.] A cavern; a cave. [Obs.] Piers Plowman.

spence.c: Spence Spence (?), n. [OF. despense, F. dépense, buffet, buttery, fr. OF. despendre to spend, distribute, L. dispendere, dispensum. See Dispense, Spend.] 1. A place where provisions are kept; a buttery; a larder; a pantry. Chiefly Brit. dial. [MW10] -->

spencer.c: Spencer Spen"cer (?), n. [OF. despensier. See Spence, and cf. Dispenser.] One who has the care of the spence, or buttery. [Obs.] Promptorium Parvulorum.
Spencer Spen"cer, n. [From the third Earl Spencer, who first wore it, or brought it into fashion.] A short jacket worn by men and by women. Ld. Lutton.

Spencer Spen"cer, n. (Naut.) A fore-and-aft sail, abaft the foremast or the mainmast, hoisted upon a small supplementary mast and set with a gaff and no boom; a trysail carried at the foremast or mainmast; -- named after its inventor, Knight Spencer, of England [1802].

spend.c: Spend Spend (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Spent (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Spending.] [AS. spendan (in comp.), fr. L. expendere or dispendere to weigh out, to expend, dispense. See Pendant, and cf. Dispend, Expend, Spence, Spencer.] 1. To weigh or lay out; to dispose of; to part with; as, to spend money for clothing.
Spend Spend (?), v. i. 1. To expend money or any other possession; to consume, use, waste, or part with, anything; as, he who gets easily spends freely.

spender.c: Spender Spen"der (?), n. One who spends; esp., one who spends lavishly; a prodigal; a spendthrift.

spending.c: Spending Spend"ing, n. The act of expending; expenditure.

spendthrift.c: Spendthrift Spend"thrift` (?), n. One who spends money profusely or improvidently; a prodigal; one who lavishes or wastes his estate. Also used figuratively.

spenserian.c: Spenserian Spen*se"ri*an (?), a. Of or pertaining to the English poet Spenser; -- specifically applied to the stanza used in his poem “The Faërie Queene.”

spent.c: Spent Spent (spĕnt), a. 1. Exhausted; worn out; having lost energy or motive force.

sperre.c: Sperre Sper { Sper (?), Sperre }, v. t. [See Spar bar.] To shut in; to support; to inclose; to fasten. [Obs.] “To sperre the gate.” Spenser.

sperable.c: Sperable Spe"ra*ble (?), a. [L. spearabilis, fr. sperare to hope.] Within the range of hpe; proper to be hoped for. [Obs.] Bacon.

sperate.c: Sperate Spe"rate (?), a. [L. speratus, p. p. of sperare to hope.] Hoped for, or to be hoped for. [R.] Bouvier.

spere.c: Spere Spere (?), v. i. [AS. spyrian to inquire, properly, to follow the track; akin to D. speuren, G. spüren, Icel. spyrja. √171. See Spoor.] To search; to pry; to ask; to inquire. [Prov. Eng. & Scot.] [Written also speer, speir.] Jamieson.
Spere Spere, n. [See Sphere.] A sphere. [Obs.] Chaucer.

sperge.c: Sperge Sperge (?), n. (Distilling) A charge of wash for the still. Knight.

sperling.c: Sperling Sper"ling (?), n. [See Sparling.] (Zool.) (a) A smelt; a sparling. [Prov. Eng.] (b) A young herring. [Local, U.S.]

sperm.c: Sperm Sperm (?), n.[F. sperme, L. sperma, Gr.???,???, from???? to sow. Cf. Spore.] (Physiol.) The male fecundating fluid; semen. See Semen.

Sperm whale Sperm" whale` (?). (Zool.) A very large toothed whale (Physeter macrocephalus), having a head of enormous size. The upper jaw is destitute of teeth. In the upper part of the head, above the skull, there is a large cavity, or case, filled with oil and spermaceti. This whale sometimes grows to the length of more than eighty feet. It is found in the warmer parts of all the oceans. Called also cachalot, and spermaceti whale.

spermaceti.c: Spermaceti Sper`ma*ce"ti (?), n. [L. sperma sperm + cetus,gen. ceti, any large sea animal, a whale, Gr.???. See Sperm, Cetaceous.] A white waxy substance obtained from cavities in the head of the sperm whale, and used making candles, oilments, cosmetics, etc. It consists essentially of ethereal salts of palmitic acid with ethal and other hydrocarbon bases. The substance of spermaceti after the removal of certain impurities is sometimes called cetin.

spermaphore.c: Spermaphore Sper"ma*phore (?), n. [Gr.???? sperm + fe`rein to bear.] (Bot.) That part of the ovary from which the ovules arise; the placenta.

spermary.c: Spermary Sper"ma*ry (?), n. (Anat.) An organ in which spermatozoa are developed; a sperm gland; a testicle.

spermatheca.c: Spermatheca ‖Sper`ma*the"ca (?), n.; pl. Spermathecae (#). [NL., from Gr.???? seed +???? case, or receptacle.] (Zool.) A small sac connected with the female reproductive organs of insects and many other invertebrates, serving to receive and retain the spermatozoa.

spermatic.c: Spermatic Sper*mat"ic (?), a. [L. spermaticus, Gr.????: cf. F. spermatique. See Sperm.] (Physiol.) Of or pertaining to semen; as, the spermatic fluid, the spermatic vessels, etc.

spermatin.c: Spermatin Sper"ma*tin (?), n. (Physiol. Chem.) A substance allied to alkali albumin and to mucin, present in semen, to which it is said to impart the mucilaginous character.

spermatism.c: Spermatism Sper"ma*tism (?), n. (Physiol.) The emission of sperm, or semen.

spermatium.c: Spermatium ‖Sper*ma"ti*um (?), n.; pl. Spermatia (#). [NL.] (Bot.) One of the motionless spermatozoids in the conceptacles of certain fungi. J. H. Balfour.

spermatize.c: Spermatize Sper"ma*tize (?), v. i. [Gr.???. See Sperm.] To yield seed; to emit seed, or sperm. [Obs.] Sir T. Browne.

spermo.c: Spermo- Spermato- { Sper"ma*to- (?), Sper"mo- (?) }. Combining forms from Gr. spe`rma, -atos, seed, sperm, semen (of plants or animals); as, spermatoblast, spermoblast.

spermatocyte.c: Spermatocyte Sper"ma*to*cyte (?), n. [Spermato- + Gr.???? a hollow vessel.] (Physiol.) Same as Spermoblast.

spermatogemma.c: Spermatogemma Sper`ma*to*gem"ma (?), n. [NL. See Spermato-, and Gemma.] (Physiol.) Same as Spermosphere.

spermatogenesis.c: Spermatogenesis Sper`ma*to*gen"e*sis (?), n. [Spermato- + genesis.] (Biol.) The development of the spermatozoids.

spermatogenetic.c: Spermatogenetic Sper`ma*to*ge*net"ic (?), a. (Physiol.) Relating to, or connected with, spermatogenesis; as, spermatogenetic function.

spermatogonium.c: Spermatogonium ‖Sper`ma*to*go"ni*um (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr.????,???, sperm +??? offspring.] (Physiol.) A primitive seminal cell, occuring in masses in the seminal tubules. It divides into a mass (spermosphere) of small cells (spermoblast), which in turn give rise to spermatozoids.

spermatoid.c: Spermatoid Sper"ma*toid (?), a. [Spermato- + -oid.] (Physiol.) Spermlike; resembling sperm, or semen.

spermatoon.c: Spermatoon ‖Sper`ma*to"on (?), n.; pl. Spermatoa (#). [NL., fr. Gr. spe`rma, -atos, seed +??? an egg.] (Anat.) A spermoblast. -- Sper`ma*to"al (#), a. Owen.

spermatophore.c: Spermatophore Sper"ma*to*phore (?), n. [Spermato- + Gr. fe`rein to bear.] 1. (Physiol.) Same as Spermospore.

spermatophorous.c: Spermatophorous Sper`ma*toph"o*rous (?), a. (Physiol.) Producing seed, or sperm; seminiferous; as, the so-called spermatophorous cells.

spermatophyta.c: Spermatophyta ‖Sper`ma*toph"y*ta (?), n. pl. [NL.; spermato- + Gr.? plant.] (Bot.) A phylum embracing the highest plants, or those that produce seeds; the seed plants, or flowering plants. They form the most numerous group, including over 120,000 species. In general, the group is characterized by the marked development of the sporophyte, with great differentiation of its parts (root, stem, leaves, flowers, etc.); by the extreme reduction of the gametophyte; and by the development of seeds. All the Spermatophyta are heterosporous; fertilization of the egg cell is either through a pollen tube emitted by the microspore or (in a few gymnosperms) by spermatozoids.

spermatophyte.c: Spermatophyte Sper"ma*to"phyte` (?), n. Any plant of the phylum Spermatophyta. -- Sper`ma*to*phyt"ic (#), a.

spermatorrhoea.c: Spermatorrhoea Spermatorrhea {Sper`ma*tor*rhe"a, Sper`ma*tor*rhoe"a, (?), } n. [NL., fr. Gr. spe`rma, -atos, seed +??? to flow.] (Med.) Abnormally frequent involuntary emission of the semen without copulation.

spermatozoid.c: Spermatozoid Sper`ma*to*zo"id (?), n. [Spermatozoon + Gr. e'i^dos form.] (Biol.) The male germ cell in animals and plants, the essential element in fertilization; a microscopic animalcule-like particle, usually provided with one or more cilia by which it is capable of active motion. In animals, the familiar type is that of a small, more or less ovoid head, with a delicate threadlike cilium, or tail. Called also spermatozoon. In plants the more usual term is antherozoid.

spermatozoon.c: Spermatozoon ‖Sper`ma*to*zo"'ön (?), n.; pl. Spermatozoa (#). [NL., fr. Gr.???, sperm + zw^,on an animal.] (Biol.) Same as Spermatozoid.

spermic.c: Spermic Sper"mic (?), a. Of or pertaining to sperm, or semen.

spermidium.c: Spermidium ‖Sper*mid"i*um (?), n.; pl. Spermidia (#). [Nl., fr. Gr. spe`rma seed.] (Bot.) An achenium.

spermism.c: Spermism Sperm"ism (?), n. [Gr.? seed, sperm + -ism.] (Biol.) The theory, formerly held by many, that the sperm or spermatozoon contains the germ of the future embryo; animalculism.

spermist.c: Spermist Sperm"ist (?), n. (Biol.) A believer in the doctrine, formerly current, of encasement in the male (see Encasement), in which the seminal thread, or spermatozoid, was considered as the real animal germ, the head being the true animal head and the tail the body.

spermoblast.c: Spermoblast Sper"mo*blast (?), n. [Spermo- + -blast.] (Physiol.) One of the cells formed by the division of the spermospore, each of which is destined to become a spermatozoid; a spermatocyte; a spermatoblast.

spermococcus.c: Spermococcus ‖Sper`mo*coc"cus (?), n. [NL. See Spermo-, and Coccus.] (Physiol.) The nucleus of the sperm cell.

spermoderm.c: Spermoderm Sper"mo*derm (?), n. [Spermo- + derm: cf. F. spermoderme.] (Bot.) The covering of a seed; -- sometimes limited to the outer coat or testa. Lindley.

spermogonium.c: Spermogonium ‖Sper`mo*go"ni*um (?), n. [NL.; spermo- + Gr.??? offspring.] (Bot.) A conceptacle of certain lichens, which contains spermatia.

spermologist.c: Spermologist Sper*mol"o*gist (?), n. [Gr.????? picking up seeds; spe`rma sperm, seed +???? to gather.] One who treats of, or collects, seeds. Bailey.

spermophile.c: Spermophile Sper"mo*phile (?), n. [Gr. spe`rma a seed + fi`los loving, fond.] (Zool.) Any ground squirrel of the genus Spermophilus; a gopher. See Illust. under Gopher.

spermophyta.c: Spermophyta ‖Sper*moph"y*ta (?), n. pl. [Nl., from Gr. spe`rma a seed + fyto`n a plant.] Plants which produce seed; phaenogamia. These plants constitute the highest grand division of the vegetable kingdom.

spermophyte.c: Spermophyte Sper"mo*phyte (?), n. (Bot.) Any plant which produces true seeds; -- a term recently proposed to replace phænogam.

spermophytic.c: Spermophytic Sper`mo*phyt"ic (?), a. (Bot.) Capable of producing seeds; phænogamic.

spermoplasma.c: Spermoplasma ‖Sper`mo*plas"ma (?), n. [NL. See Spermo-, and Plasma.] (Physiol.) The protoplasm of the sperm cell. Haeckel.

spermosphere.c: Spermosphere Sper"mo*sphere (?), n. [Spermo- + sphere.] (Physiol.) A mass or ball of cells formed by the repeated division of a male germinal cell (spermospore), each constituent cell (spermoblast) of which is converted into a spermatozoid; a spermatogemma.

spermospore.c: Spermospore Sper"mo*spore (?), n. [Spermo- + spore.] (Physiol.) The male germinal or seminal cell, from the breaking up of which the spermoblasts are formed and ultimately the spermatozoids; a spermatospore. Balfour.

spermule.c: Spermule Sper"mule (?), n. [Dim. fr. sperm.] (Physiol.) A sperm cell. Haeckel.

sperrylite.c: Sperrylite Sper"ry*lite (?), n.[Named after F. L. Sperry, who discovered it.] (Min.) An arsenide of platinum occuring in grains and minute isometric crystals of tin-white color. It is found near Sudbury, Ontario Canada, and is the only known compound of platinum occuring in nature.

sperse.c: Sperse Sperse (?), v. t. To disperse. [Obs.] Spenser.

spessartite.c: Spessartite Spes"sart*ite (?), n.[From Spessart, in Germany.] (Min.) A manganesian variety of garnet.

spet.c: Spet Spet (?), v. t. [AS. sp?tan. See Spit.] To spit; to throw out. [Obs.]

spetches.c: Spetches Spetch"es (?), n. pl. Parings and refuse of hides, skins, etc., from which glue is made.

spew.c: Spew Spew (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Spewed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Spewing.] [OE. spewen, speowen, AS. spīwan;n to D. spuwen to spit. OS & OHG. spīwan, G. speien, Icel. sp?ja to spew, Sw. spy, Dan. spye, Goth. spiewan, th. spjauti, L. spuere to split, Gr.???, Skr. shtiv, shthīv. Cf. Pyke, Spit.] [Written also spue.] 1. To eject from the stomach; to vomit.
Spew Spew, v. i. 1. To vomit. Chaucer.
Spew Spew, n. That which is vomited; vomit.

spewiness.c: Spewiness Spew"i*ness (?), n. The state of being spewy.

spewy.c: Spewy Spew"y (?), a. Wet; soggy; inclined to spew.

sphacel.c: Sphacel Sphac"el (?), n. [Gr.???: cf. F. sphacèle.] (Med.) Gangrene.

sphacelate.c: Sphacelate Sphac"e*late (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Sphacelated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Sphacelating.] [NL. sphacelare, sphacelatum, mortify: cf. F. sphacéler. See Sphacelus.] (Med.) To die, decay, or become gangrenous, as flesh or bone; to mortify.
Sphacelate Sphac"e*late, v. t. (Med.) To affect with gangrene.

sphacelated.c: Sphacelated Sphacelate { Sphac"e*late (?), Sphac"e*la`ted (?), } a. (Med.) Affected with gangrene; mortified.

sphacelation.c: Sphacelation Sphac`e*la"tion (?), n. (Med.) The process of becoming or making gangrenous; mortification.

sphacelus.c: Sphacelus ‖Sphac"e*lus (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr.????.] (Med.) Gangrenous part; gangrene; slough.

sphaerenchyma.c: Sphaerenchyma ‖Sphae*ren"chy*ma (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr.??? sphere + -enchyma as in parenchima.] (Bot.) Vegetable tissue composed of thin-walled rounded cells, -- a modification of parenchyma.

sphaeridium.c: Sphaeridium ‖Sphae*rid"i*um (?), n.; pl. Sphaeridia (#). [NL., fr. Gr.??? a sphere.] (Zool.) A peculiar sense organ found upon the exterior of most kinds of sea urchins, and consisting of an oval or sherical head surmounting a short pedicel. It is generally supposed to be an olfactory organ.

sphaerospore.c: Sphaerospore Sphae"ro*spore (?), n. [Gr.???? sphere + E. spore.] (Bot.) One of the nonsexual spores found in red algae; a tetraspore.

sphagnicolous.c: Sphagnicolous Sphag*nic"o*lous (?), a. [Sphagnum + L. colere to inhabit.] (Bot.) Growing in moss of the genus Sphagnum.

sphagnous.c: Sphagnous Sphag"nous (?), a. (Bot.) Pertaining to moss of the genus Sphagnum, or bog moss; abounding in peat or bog moss.

sphagnum.c: Sphagnum ‖Sphag"num (?), n. [NL., fr/ Gr.??? a kind of moss.] (Bot.) A genus of mosses having white leaves slightly tinged with red or green and found growing in marshy places; bog moss; peat moss.

sphalerite.c: Sphalerite Sphal"er*ite (?), n. [Gr.??? slippery, uncertain. See Blende.] (Min.) Zinc sulphide; -- called also blende, black-jack, false galena, etc. See Blende (a).

sphene.c: Sphene Sphene (?), n. [F. sphène, fr. Gr. sfh`n a wedge.] (Min.) A mineral found usually in thin, wedge-shaped crystals of a yellow or green to black color. It is a silicate of titanium and calcium; titanite.

sphenethmoid.c: Sphenethmoid Sphe*neth"moid (?), a. [Sphenoid + ethmoid.] (Anat.) Of or pertaining to both the sphenoidal and the ethmoidal regions of the skull, or the sphenethmoid bone; sphenethmoidal.

sphenethmoidal.c: Sphenethmoidal Sphe`neth*moid"al (?), a. (Anat.) Relating to the sphenoethmoid bone; sphenoethmoid.

spheniscan.c: Spheniscan Sphe*nis"can (?), n. (Zool.) Any species of penguin.

spheno.c: Spheno- Sphe"no- (?). A combining form used in anatomy to indicate connection with, or relation to, the sphenoid bone; as in sphenomaxillary, sphenopalatine.

sphenodon.c: Sphenodon Sphe"no*don (?), n. [Gr. sfh`n a wedge +???,???, a tooth.] (Zool.) Same as Hatteria.

sphenogram.c: Sphenogram Sphe"no*gram (?), n. [Gr. sfh`n a wedge + -gram.] A cuneiform, or arrow-headed, character.

sphenographer.c: Sphenographer Sphe*nog"ra*pher, n. One skilled in sphenography; a sphenographist.

sphenographic.c: Sphenographic Sphe`no*graph"ic (?), a. Of or pertaining to sphenography.

sphenography.c: Sphenography Sphe*nog"ra*phy (?), n. [Gr. sfh`n a wedge + -graphy.] The art of writing in cuneiform characters, or of deciphering inscriptions made in such characters.

sphenoid.c: Sphenoid Sphe"noid (?), a. [Gr.???; sfh`n a wedge + e'i^dos form: cf. F. sphénoïde.] 1. Wedge-shaped; as, a sphenoid crystal.
