stupendous.c: Stupendous Stu*pen"dous (?), a. [L. stupendus astonishing, p. future pass. of stupere to be astonished at. Cf. Stupid.] Astonishing; wonderful; amazing; especially, astonishing in magnitude or elevation; as, a stupendous pile. “A stupendous sum.” Macaulay.

stupeous.c: Stupeous Stu"pe*ous (?), a. [L. stupa, or better stuppa, tow; cf. L. stuppeus made of tow. Cf. Stupose.] Resembling tow; having long, loose scales, or matted filaments, like tow; stupose.

stupid.c: Stupid Stu"pid (?), a. [L. stupidus, fr. stupere to be stupefied: cf. F. stupide.] 1. Very dull; insensible; senseless; wanting in understanding; heavy; sluggish; in a state of stupor; -- said of persons.

stupidity.c: Stupidity Stu*pid"i*ty (?), n. [L. stupiditas: cf. F. stupidité.] 1. The quality or state of being stupid; extreme dullness of perception or understanding; insensibility; sluggishness.

stupor.c: Stupor Stu"por (?), n. [L., from stupere to be struck senseless.] 1. Great diminution or suspension of sensibility; suppression of sense or feeling; lethargy.

stupose.c: Stupose Stu*pose (?), a. [L. stupa, or better stuppa, tow. Cf. Stupeous.] (Bot.) Composed of, or having, tufted or matted filaments like tow; stupeous.

stuprate.c: Stuprate Stu"prate (?), v. t. [L. stupratus, p. p. of stuprare to ravish, fr. stuprum defilement.] To ravish; to debauch. [R.] Heywood.

stupration.c: Stupration Stu*pra"tion (?), n. Violation of chastity by force; rape. [R.] Sir T. Browne.

sturb.c: Sturb Sturb (?), v. t. To disturb. [Obs.] Chaucer.

sturdily.c: Sturdily Stur"di*ly (?), adv. In a sturdy manner.

sturdiness.c: Sturdiness Stur"di*ness, n. Quality of being sturdy.

sturdy.c: Sturdy Stur"dy (?), a. [Compar. Sturdier (?); superl. Sturdiest.] [OE. sturdi inconsiderable, OF. estourdi stunned, giddy, thoughtless, rash, F. étourdi, p. p. of OF. estourdir to stun, to render giddy, to amaze, F. étourdir; of uncertain origin. The sense has probably been influenced by E. stout.] 1. Foolishly obstinate or resolute; stubborn; unrelenting; unfeeling; stern.
Sturdy Stur"dy (?), n. [OF. estourdi giddiness, stupefaction.] (Vet.) A disease in sheep and cattle, marked by great nervousness, or by dullness and stupor.

sturgeon.c: Sturgeon Stur"geon (?), n. [F. esturgeon, LL. sturio, sturgio, OHG. sturjo, G. stör; akin to AS. styria, styriga.] (Zool.) Any one of numerous species of large cartilaginous ganoid fishes belonging to Acipenser and allied genera of the family Acipenseridae. They run up rivers to spawn, and are common on the coasts and in the large rivers and lakes of North America, Europe, and Asia. Caviar is prepared from the roe, and isinglass from the air bladder.

sturiones.c: Sturiones ‖Stu`ri*o"nes (?), n. pl. [NL., from LL. sturio. See Sturgeon.] (Zool.) An order of fishes including the sturgeons.

sturionian.c: Sturionian Stu`ri*o"ni*an (?), n. (Zool.) One of the family of fishes of which the sturgeon is the type.

sturk.c: Sturk Sturk (?), n. See Stirk. [Prov. Eng. & Scot.]

sturnoid.c: Sturnoid Stur"noid (?), a. [L. sturnus a starling + -oid.] (Zool.) Like or pertaining to the starlings.

sturt.c: Sturt Sturt (?), v. t. [Cf. Start, v. i.] To vex; to annoy; to startle. [Obs. or Prov. Eng. & Scot.]
Sturt Sturt, n. 1. Disturbance; annoyance; care. [Obs. or Prov. Eng. & Scot.] “Sturt and care.” J. Rolland.

sturtion.c: Sturtion Stur"tion (?), n. A corruption of Nasturtion.

stut.c: Stut Stut (?), v. i. To stutter. [Obs.] Skelton.

stutter.c: Stutter Stut"ter (?), v. t. & i. [imp. & p. p. Stuttered (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Stuttering.] [Freq. of stut, OE. stoten; probably of Dutch or Low German origin; cf. D. & LG. stotteren, G. stottern, D. stooten to push, to strike; akin to G. stossen, Icel. stauta, Sw. stöta, Dan. stöde, Goth. stautan, L. tundere, Skr. tud to thrust. Cf. Contuse, Obtuse.] To hesitate or stumble in uttering words; to speak with spasmodic repetition or pauses; to stammer.
Stutter Stut"ter, n. 1. The act of stuttering; a stammer. See Stammer, and Stuttering.

stutterer.c: Stutterer Stut"ter*er (?), n. One who stutters; a stammerer.

stuttering.c: Stuttering Stut"ter*ing, n. The act of one who stutters; -- restricted by some physiologists to defective speech due to inability to form the proper sounds, the breathing being normal, as distinguished from stammering.
Stuttering Stut"ter*ing, a. Apt to stutter; hesitating; stammering. -- Stut"ter*ing*ly, adv.

sty.c: Sty Sty (stī), n.; pl. Sties (stīz). [Written also stigh.] [AS. stigu, fr. stīgan to rise; originally, probably, a place into which animals climbed or went up. √164. See Sty, v. i., and cf. Steward.] 1. A pen or inclosure for swine.
Sty Sty, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Stied (stīd); p. pr. & vb. n. Stying (stī"ĭng).] To shut up in, or as in, a sty. Shak.

Sty Sty, v. i. [OE. stien, stiȝen, AS. stīgan to rise; akin to D. stijgen, OS. & OHG. stīgan, G. steigen, Icel. stīga, Sw. stiga, Dan. stige, Goth. steigan, L. vestigium footstep, Gr.? to walk, to go, Skr. stigh to mount. Cf. Distich, Stair steps, Stirrup, Sty a boil, a pen for swine, Vestige.] To soar; to ascend; to mount. See Stirrup. [Obs.]

Sty Sty, n. [For older styan, styanye, understood as sty on eye, AS. stīgend (sc. eáge eye), properly, rising, or swelling (eye), p. p. of stīgan to rise. See Sty, v. i.] (Med.) An inflamed swelling or boil on the edge of the eyelid. [Written also stye.]

styan.c: Styan Sty"an (?), n. See Sty, a boil. [R.] De quincey.

styca.c: Styca Sty"ca (?), n. [LL., fr. AS. stic, styc, stycge.] An anglo-Saxon copper coin of the lowest value, being worth half a farthing. S. M. Leake.

stycerin.c: Stycerin Sty"cer*in (?), n. [Styryl + glycerin.] (Chem.) A triacid alcohol, related to glycerin, and obtained from certain styryl derivatives as a yellow, gummy, amorphous substance; -- called also phenyl glycerin.

stye.c: Stye Stye, n. See Sty, a boil.

stygian.c: Stygian Styg"i*an (stĭj"ĭ*ain), a. [L. Stygius, fr. Styx, Stygis, Gr. Sty`x, Stygo`s, the Styx.] Of or pertaining to the river Styx; hence, hellish; infernal. See Styx.

stylagalmaic.c: Stylagalmaic Sty`la*gal*ma"ic (stī`lȧ*găl*mā"ĭk), a. [Gr. sty^los a column + 'a`galma an image.] (Arch.) Performing the office of columns; as, Atlantes and Caryatides are stylagalmaic figures or images. [Written also stylogalmaic.]

stylaster.c: Stylaster ‖Sty*las"ter (?), n. [NL., from Gr. sty^los pillar + 'asth`r star.] (Zool.) Any one of numerous species of delicate, usually pink, calcareous hydroid corals of the genus Stylaster.

style.c: Style Style (?), n. [OE. stile, F. style, Of. also stile, L. stilus a style or writing instrument, manner or writing, mode of expression; probably for stiglus, meaning, a pricking instrument, and akin to E. stick. See Stick, v. t., and cf. Stiletto. The spelling with y is due to a supposed connection with Gr. sty^los a pillar.] 1. An instrument used by the ancients in writing on tablets covered with wax, having one of its ends sharp, and the other blunt, and somewhat expanded, for the purpose of making erasures by smoothing the wax.
Style Style, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Styled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Styling.] To entitle; to term, name, or call; to denominate. “Styled great conquerors.” Milton.

stylet.c: Stylet Sty"let (?), n. [F., dim. of style; cf. It. stiletto. See Stiletto.] A small poniard; a stiletto.

styliferous.c: Styliferous Sty*lif"er*ous (?), a. [Style + -ferous.] (Bot.) Bearing one or more styles.

styliform.c: Styliform Sty"li*form (?), a. [Style + -form: cf. F. styliforme.] Having the form of, or resembling, a style, pin, or pen; styloid.

stylish.c: Stylish Styl"ish (?), a. Having style or artistic quality; given to, or fond of, the display of style; highly fashionable; modish; as, a stylish dress, house, manner. -- Styl"ish*ly, adv. -- Styl"ish*ness, n.

stylist.c: Stylist Styl"ist, n. One who is a master or a model of style, especially in writing or speaking; a critic of style.

stylistic.c: Stylistic Sty*lis"tic (?), a. Of or pertaining to style in language. [R.] “Stylistic trifles.” J. A. Symonds.

stylite.c: Stylite Sty"lite (stī"līt), n. [Gr. styli`ths, fr. sty^los a pillar.] (Eccl. Hist.) One of a sect of anchorites in the early church, who lived on the tops of pillars for the exercise of their patience; -- called also pillarist and pillar saint.

stylo.c: Stylo- Sty"lo- (stī"lo-). A combining form used in anatomy to indicate connection with, or relation to, the styloid process of the temporal bone; as, stylohyal, stylomastoid, stylomaxillary.

stylobate.c: Stylobate Sty"lo*bate (stī"lo*bat), n. [L. stylobates, stylobata, Gr. styloba`ths; sty^los a pillar + ba`ths one that treads, fr. bai`nein to go.] (Arch.) The uninterrupted and continuous flat band, coping, or pavement upon which the bases of a row of columns are supported. See Sub-base.

styloglossal.c: Styloglossal Sty`lo*glos"sal (?), a. [Stylo- + glossal.] (Anat.) Of or pertaining to styloid process and the tongue.

stylographic.c: Stylographic Sty`lo*graph"ic (?), a. 1. Of or pertaining to stylography; used in stylography; as, stylographic tablets.

stylographical.c: Stylographical Sty`lo*graph"ic*al (?), a. Same as Stylographic, 1. -- Sty`lo*graph"ic*al*ly, adv.

stylography.c: Stylography Sty*log"ra*phy (?), n. [Style + -graphy.] A mode of writing or tracing lines by means of a style on cards or tablets.

stylohyal.c: Stylohyal Sty`lo*hy"al (?), n. [Stylo- + the Gr. letter?.] (Anat.) A segment in the hyoidean arch between the epihyal and tympanohyal.

stylohyoid.c: Stylohyoid Sty`lo*hy"oid (?), a. (Anat.) Of or pertaining to the styloid process and the hyoid bone.

styloid.c: Styloid Sty"loid (?), a. [Style + -oid: cf. F. styloïde, Gr.?.] 1. Styliform; as, the styloid process.

stylomastoid.c: Stylomastoid Sty`lo*mas"toid (?), a. (Anat.) Of or pertaining to the styloid and mastoid processes of the temporal bone.

stylomaxillary.c: Stylomaxillary Sty`lo*max"il*la*ry (?), a. (Anat.) Of or pertaining to the styloid process and the maxilla.

stylometer.c: Stylometer Sty*lom"e*ter (?), n. [Gr.? column + -meter.] An instrument for measuring columns.

stylommata.c: Stylommata ‖Sty*lom"ma*ta (?), n. pl. [NL., fr. Gr.? a pillar +?,?, the eye.] Same as Stylommatophora.

stylommatophora.c: Stylommatophora ‖Sty*lom`ma*toph"o*ra (?), n. pl. [NL., fr. Gr.? column +? eye + fe`rein to bear.] (Zool.) A division of Pulmonata in which the eyes are situated at the tips of the tentacles. It includes the common land snails and slugs. See Illust. under Snail.

stylommatophorous.c: Stylommatophorous Sty*lom`ma*toph"o*rous (?), a. (Zool.) Of or pertaining to Stylommatophora.

stylopodium.c: Stylopodium ‖Sty`lo*po"di*um (?), n.; pl. Stylopodia (#). [NL. See Style, and Podium.] (Bot.) An expansion at the base of the style, as in umbelliferous plants.

stylops.c: Stylops ‖Sty"lops (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr.? a pillar +?,?, the eye.] (Zool.) A genus of minute insects parasitic, in their larval state, on bees and wasps. It is the typical genus of the group Strepsiptera, formerly considered a distinct order, but now generally referred to the Coleoptera. See Strepsiptera.

stylus.c: Stylus ‖Sty"lus (?), n. [L. stylus, or better stilus.] 1. An instrument for writing. See Style, n., 1.

stimy.c: Stimy Stymie { Sty"mie (?), n. Also Sti"my }. [Orig. uncertain.] (Golf) The position of two balls on the putting green such that, being more than six inches apart, one ball lies directly between the other and the hole at which the latter must be played; also, the act of bringing the balls into this position.
Stimy Stymie { Sty"mie, v. t. Also Sti"my }. (Golf) To bring into the position of, or impede by, a stymie.

styphnate.c: Styphnate Styph"nate (?), n. (Chem.) A salt of styphnic acid.

styphnic.c: Styphnic Styph"nic (?), a. [Gr. (spurious) sty`fein to contract.] (Chem.) Pertaining to, or designating, a yellow crystalline astringent acid, (NO2)3.C6H.(OH)2, obtained by the action of nitric acid on resorcin. Styphnic acid resembles picric acid, but is not bitter. It acts like a strong dibasic acid, having a series of well defined salts.

styptic.c: Styptic Styp"tic (?), a. [L. stypticus, Gr.?, fr.? to contract.] Producing contraction; stopping bleeding; having the quality of restraining hemorrhage when applied to the bleeding part; astringent. [Written also stiptic.]

stypticity.c: Stypticity Styp*tic"i*ty (?), n. [Cf. F. stypticité.] The quality or state of being styptic; astringency.

styracin.c: Styracin Styr"a*cin (?), n. [See Styrax.] (Chem.) A white crystalline tasteless substance extracted from gum storax, and consisting of a salt of cinnamic acid with cinnamic alcohol.

styrax.c: Styrax Sty"rax (?), n. [L. styrax, storax, Gr.?. See Storax.] 1. (Bot.) A genus of shrubs and trees, mostly American or Asiatic, abounding in resinous and aromatic substances. Styrax officinalis yields storax, and Styrax Benzoin yields benzoin.

styrol.c: Styrol Sty"rol (?), n. [Styrax + L. oleum oil.] (Chem.) See Styrolene.

styrolene.c: Styrolene Sty"ro*lene (?), n. (Chem.) An unsaturated hydrocarbon, C8H8, obtained by the distillation of storax, by the decomposition of cinnamic acid, and by the condensation of acetylene, as a fragrant, aromatic, mobile liquid; -- called also phenyl ethylene, vinyl benzene, styrol, styrene, and cinnamene.

styrone.c: Styrone Sty"rone (?), n. (Chem.) A white crystalline substance having a sweet taste and a hyacinthlike odor, obtained by the decomposition of styracin; -- properly called cinnamic alcohol or styryl alcohol.

styryl.c: Styryl Sty"ryl (?), n. [Styrax + -yl.] (Chem.) A hypothetical radical found in certain derivatives of styrolene and cinnamic acid; -- called also cinnyl, or cinnamyl.

styx.c: Styx ‖Styx (?), n. [L., fr. Gr.?.] (Class. Myth.) The principal river of the lower world, which had to be crossed in passing to the regions of the dead.

suability.c: Suability Su`a*bil"i*ty (?), n. (Law) Liability to be sued; the state of being subjected by law to civil process.

suable.c: Suable Su"a*ble (?), a. (Law) Capable of being sued; subject by law to be called to answer in court. Story.

suade.c: Suade Suade (?), v. t. [L. suadere.] To persuade. [Obs.]

suadible.c: Suadible Suad"i*ble (?), a. [L. suadibilis.] Suasible. [Obs.] Wyclif (James iii. 17).

suage.c: Suage Suage (?), v. t. To assuage. [Obs.] Dryden.

suant.c: Suant Su"ant (?), a. [Cf. Sue to pursue.] Spread equally over the surface; uniform; even. [Written also suent.] [Local, U.S. & Prov. Eng.] -- Su"ant*ly, adv. [Local, U.S. & Prov. Eng.]

suasible.c: Suasible Sua"si*ble (?), a. [L. suadere, suasum, to persuade.] Capable of being persuaded; easily persuaded.

suasion.c: Suasion Sua"sion (?), n. [L. suasio, fr. suadere, suasum, to advise, persuade, fr. suadus persuading, persuasive; akin to suavis sweet: cf. OF. suasion. See Suave, and cf. Dissuade, Persuade.] The act of persuading; persuasion; as, moral suasion.

suasive.c: Suasive Sua"sive (?), a. Having power to persuade; persuasive; suasory. South. “Genial and suasive satire.” Earle. -- Sua"sive*ly, adv.

suasory.c: Suasory Sua"so*ry (?), a. [L. suasorius: cf. F. suasoire.] Tending to persuade; suasive.

suave.c: Suave Suave (?), a. [L. suavis sweet, pleasant: cf. F. suave. See Sweet, and cf. Suasion.] Sweet; pleasant; delightful; gracious or agreeable in manner; bland. -- Suave"ly, adv.

suavify.c: Suavify Suav"i*fy (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Suavified (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Suavifying (?).] [Suave + -fy.] To make affable or suave.

suaviloquent.c: Suaviloquent Sua*vil"o*quent (?), a. [L. suaviloquens; suavis sweet + loquens, p. pr. of loqui to speak.] Sweetly speaking; using agreeable speech. [R.]

suaviloquy.c: Suaviloquy Sua*vil"o*quy (?), n. [L. suaviloquium.] Sweetness of speech. [R.]

suavity.c: Suavity Suav"i*ty (?), n. [L. suavitas: cf. F. suavité.] 1. Sweetness to the taste. [Obs.] Sir T. Browne.

sub.c: Sub- Sub- (?). [L. sub under, below; akin to Gr.?, Skr. upa to, on, under, over. Cf. Hypo-, Super-.] 1. A prefix signifying under, below, beneath, and hence often, in an inferior position or degree, in an imperfect or partial state, as in subscribe, substruct, subserve, subject, subordinate, subacid, subastringent, subgranular, suborn. Sub- in Latin compounds often becomes sum- before m, sur before r, and regularly becomes suc-, suf-, sug-, and sup- before c, f, g, and p respectively. Before c, p, and t it sometimes takes form sus- (by the dropping of b from a collateral form, subs-).
Sub Sub, n. 1. A subordinate; a subaltern. [Colloq.]
Sub judice ‖Sub ju"di*ce (?). [L.] Before the judge, or court; not yet decided; under judicial consideration.

subacetate.c: Subacetate Sub*ac"e*tate (?), n. (Chem.) An acetate containing an excess of the basic constituent.

subacid.c: Subacid Sub*ac"id (?), a. [L. subacidus. See Sub-, Acid.] Moderately acid or sour; as, some plants have subacid juices. -- n. A substance moderately acid.

subacrid.c: Subacrid Sub*ac"rid (?), a. Moderalely acrid or harsh.

subacromial.c: Subacromial Sub`a*cro"mi*al (?), a. (Anat.) Situated beneath the acromial process of the scapula.

subact.c: Subact Sub*act" (?), v. t. [L. subactus, p. p. of subigere to subdue; sub under + agere to lead, bring.] To reduce; to subdue. [Obs.] Bacon.

subaction.c: Subaction Sub*ac"tion (?), n. [Cf. L. subactio a working up, discipline.] The act of reducing to any state, as of mixing two bodies combletely. [Obs.] Bacon.

subaduncate.c: Subaduncate Sub`a*dun"cate (?), a. (Zool.) Somewhat hooked or curved.

subadvocate.c: Subadvocate Sub*ad"vo*cate (?), n. An under or subordinate advocate.

subaerial.c: Subaerial Sub`a*e"ri*al (?), a. Beneath the sky; in the open air; specifically (Geol.), taking place on the earth's surface, as opposed to subaqueous.

subagent.c: Subagent Sub*a"gent (?), n. (Law) A person employed by an agent to transact the whole, or a part, of the business intrusted to the latter. Bouvier. Chitty.

subagitation.c: Subagitation Sub*ag`i*ta"tion (?), n. [L. subagitatio, fr. subagitare to lie with illicity.] Unlawful sexual intercourse. [Obs.]

subah.c: Subah ‖Su"bah (sōo"bȧ), n. [Per. & Hind. sūbah.] A province; a government, as of a viceroy; also, a subahdar. [India]

subahdar.c: Subahdar Su"bah*dar (?), n. [Per. & Hind. sūbah-dār, Per. sūbah a province + dār holding, keeping.] A viceroy; a governor of a subah; also, a native captain in the British native army. [India]

subahship.c: Subahship Subahdary { Su"bah*dar`y (?), Su"bah*ship (?), } n. The office or jurisdiction of a subahdar.

subaid.c: Subaid Sub*aid" (?), v. t. To aid secretly; to assist in a private manner, or indirectly. [R.] Daniel.

subalpine.c: Subalpine Sub*al"pine (?), a. [L. subalpinus.] (Bot. & Zool.) Inhabiting the somewhat high slopes and summits of mountains, but considerably below the snow line.

subaltern.c: Subaltern Sub*al"tern (?), a. [F. subalterne, LL. subalternus, fr. L. sub under + alter the one, the other of two. See Alter.] 1. Ranked or ranged below; subordinate; inferior; specifically (Mil.), ranking as a junior officer; being below the rank of captain; as, a subaltern officer.
Subaltern Sub*al"tern (?), n. 1. A person holding a subordinate position; specifically, a commissioned military officer below the rank of captain.

subalternant.c: Subalternant Sub`al*ter"nant (?), n. (Logic) A universal proposition. See Subaltern, 2. Whately.

subalternate.c: Subalternate Sub`al*ter"nate (?), a. 1. Succeeding by turns; successive.
Subalternate Sub`al*ter"nate, n. (Logic) A particular proposition, as opposed to a universal one. See Subaltern, 2.

subalternation.c: Subalternation Sub*al"ter*na`tion (?), n. The state of being subalternate; succession of turns; subordination.

subapennine.c: Subapennine Sub*ap"en*nine (?), a. Under, or at the foot of, the Apennine mountains; -- applied, in geology, to a series of Tertiary strata of the older Pliocene period.

subapical.c: Subapical Sub*ap"ic*al (?), a. Being under the apex; of or pertaining to the part just below the apex.

subaquaneous.c: Subaquaneous Sub`a*qua"ne*ous (?), a. [L. subaquaneus; sub + aqua water.] Subaqueous. [Obs.]

subaqueous.c: Subaqueous Subaquatic { Sub`a*quat"ic (?), Sub*a"que*ous (?), } a. 1. Being under water, or beneath the surface of water; adapted for use under water; submarine; as, a subaqueous helmet.

subarachnoidal.c: Subarachnoidal Subarachnoid { Sub`a*rach"noid (?), Sub*ar`ach*noid"al (?), } a. (Anat.) Situated under the arachnoid membrane.

subarctic.c: Subarctic Sub*arc"tic (?), a. Approximately arctic; belonging to a region just without the arctic circle.

subarcuated.c: Subarcuated Subarcuate { Sub*ar"cu*ate (?), Sub*ar"cu*a`ted (?), } a. Having a figure resembling that of a bow; somewhat curved or arched.

subarration.c: Subarration Sub`ar*ra"tion (?), n. [Pref. sub- + L. arra, arrha, earnest money. See Earnest a pledge.] The ancient custom of betrothing by the bestowal, on the part of the man, of marriage gifts or tokens, as money, rings, or other presents, upon the woman.

subarytenoid.c: Subarytenoid Sub`a*ryt"e*noid (?), a. (Anat.) Situated under the arytenoid cartilage of the larynx.

subastral.c: Subastral Sub*as"tral (?), a. Beneath the stars or heavens; terrestrial. Bp. Warburton.

subatom.c: Subatom Sub*at"om (?), n. (Chem.) A hypothetical component of a chemical atom, on the theory that the elements themselves are complex substances; -- called also atomicule.

subaud.c: Subaud Sub*aud" (?), v. t. [L. subaudire, subauditum; sub under + audire to hear.] To understand or supply in an ellipsis. [R.]

subaudition.c: Subaudition Sub`au*di"tion (?), n. [L. subauditio.] The act of understanding, or supplying, something not expressed; also, that which is so understood or supplied. Trench.

subaxillary.c: Subaxillary Sub*ax"il*la*ry (?), a. 1. (Anat.) Situated under the axilla, or armpit.

subbase.c: Sub-base Sub"-base` (?), n. (Arch.) The lowest member of a base when divided horizontally, or of a baseboard, pedestal, or the like.

subbass.c: Sub-bass Sub"-bass`, n. (Mus.) The deepest pedal stop, or the lowest tones of an organ; the fundamental or ground bass. [Written also sub-base.] Ayliffe.

subbrachial.c: Subbrachial Sub*brach"i*al (?), a. Of or pertaining to the subbrachians.

subbrachiales.c: Subbrachiales ‖Sub*brach`i*a"les (?), n. pl. [NL. See Sub-, and Brachial.] (Zool.) A division of soft-finned fishes in which the ventral fins are situated beneath the pectorial fins, or nearly so.

subbrachian.c: Subbrachian Sub*brach"i*an (?), n. [Pref. sub- + brachium.] (Zool.) One of the Subbrachiales.

subbreed.c: Subbreed Sub"breed` (?), n. (Zool.) A race or strain differing in certain characters from the parent breed; an incipient breed.

subbronchial.c: Subbronchial Sub*bron"chi*al (?), a. (Anat.) Situated under, or on the ventral side of, the bronchi; as, the subbronchial air sacs of birds.

subcaliber.c: Subcaliber Sub*cal"i*ber (?), a. Smaller than the caliber of a firearm. [Written also subcalibre.]

subcarbonate.c: Subcarbonate Sub*car"bon*ate (?), n. (Chem.) A carbonate containing an excess of the basic constituent.

subcarboniferous.c: Subcarboniferous Sub*car`bon*if"er*ous (?), a. (Geol.) Of or pertaining to the lowest division of the Carboniferous formations underlying the proper coal measures. It was a marine formation characterized in general by beds of limestone. -- n. The Subcarboniferous period or formation.

subcarbureted.c: Subcarbureted Sub*car"bu*ret`ed (?), a. (Chem.) United with, or containing, carbon in less than the normal proportion. [Written also subcarburetted.] [Obsoles.]

subcartilaginous.c: Subcartilaginous Sub*car`ti*lag"i*nous (?), a. (Anat.) (a) Situated under or beneath a cartilage or cartilages. (b) Partially cartilaginous.

subcaudal.c: Subcaudal Sub*cau"dal (?), a. (Anat.) Situated under, or on the ventral side of, the tail; as, the subcaudal, or chevron, bones.

subcelestial.c: Subcelestial Sub`ce*les"tial (?), a. Being beneath the heavens; as, subcelestial glories. Barrow.

subcellar.c: Subcellar Sub*cel"lar (?), n. A cellar beneath another story wholly or partly underground; usually, a cellar under a cellar.

subchanter.c: Subchanter Sub*chant"er (?), n. (Eccl.) An underchanter; a precentor's deputy in a cathedral; a succentor.

subclass.c: Subclass Sub"class` (?), n. One of the natural groups, more important than an order, into which some classes are divided; as, the angiospermous subclass of exogens.

subclavian.c: Subclavian Sub*cla"vi*an (?), a. [Pref. sub- + L. clavis a key. See Clavicle.] (Anat.) Situated under the clavicle, or collar bone; as, the subclavian arteries.

subcolumnar.c: Subcolumnar Sub`co*lum"nar (?), a. (Geol.) Having an imperfect or interrupted columnar structure.

subcommittee.c: Subcommittee Sub`com*mit"tee (?), n. An under committee; a part or division of a committee.

subcompressed.c: Subcompressed Sub`com*pressed" (?), a. Not fully compressed; partially or somewhat compressed.

subconjunctival.c: Subconjunctival Sub*con`junc*ti"val (?), a. (Anat.) Situated under the conjunctiva.

subconscious.c: Subconscious Sub*con"scious (?), a. 1. Occurring without the possibility or the fact of an attendant consciousness; -- said of states of the soul.

subconsciousness.c: Subconsciousness Sub*con"scious*ness (?), n. The state or quality of being subconscious; a state of mind in which perception and other mental processes occur without distinct consciousness.

subconstellation.c: Subconstellation Sub*con`stel*la"tion (?), n. (Astron.) A subordinate constellation. Sir T. Browne.

subcontract.c: Subcontract Sub*con"tract (?), n. A contract under, or subordinate to, a previous contract.

subcontracted.c: Subcontracted Sub`con*tract"ed (?), a. 1. Contracted after a former contract.

subcontractor.c: Subcontractor Sub`con*tract"or (?), n. One who takes a portion of a contract, as for work, from the principal contractor.

subcontrary.c: Subcontrary Sub*con"tra*ry (?), a. 1. Contrary in an inferior degree.
Subcontrary Sub*con"tra*ry, n.; pl. Subcontraries (?). (Logic) A subcontrary proposition; a proposition inferior or contrary in a lower degree.

subcoracoid.c: Subcoracoid Sub*cor"a*coid (?), a. (Anat.) Situated under the coracoid process of the scapula; as, the subcoracoid dislocation of the humerus.

subcordate.c: Subcordate Sub*cor"date (?), a. Somewhat cordate; somewhat like a heart in shape.

subcorneous.c: Subcorneous Sub*cor"ne*ous (?), a. (Anat.) (a) Situated under a horny part or layer. (b) Partially horny.

subcostal.c: Subcostal Sub*cos"tal (?), a. (Anat. & Zool.) Situated below the costas, or ribs; as, the subcostal muscles.

subcranial.c: Subcranial Sub*cra"ni*al (?), a. (Anat.) Situated under, or on the ventral side of, the cranium; facial.

subcrustaceous.c: Subcrustaceous Sub`crus*ta"ceous (?), a. Occurring beneath a crust or scab; as, a subcrustaceous cicatrization.

subcultrated.c: Subcultrated Subcultrate { Sub*cul"trate (?), Sub*cul"tra*ted (?), } a. (Zool.) Having a form resembling that of a colter, or straight on one side and curved on the other.

subcutaneous.c: Subcutaneous Sub`cu*ta"ne*ous (?), a. Situated under the skin; hypodermic. -- Sub`cu*ta"ne*ous*ly, adv.

subcuticular.c: Subcuticular Sub`cu*tic"u*lar (?), a. (Anat.) Situated under the cuticle, or scarfskin.

subcylindric.c: Subcylindric Subcylindrical { Sub`cy*lin"dric*al (?), Sub`cy*lin"dric (?), } a. Imperfectly cylindrical; approximately cylindrical.

subdeacon.c: Subdeacon Sub*dea"con (?), n. [Pref. sub- + deacon: cf. L. subdiaconus.] (Eccl.) One belonging to an order in the Roman Catholic Church, next interior to the order of deacons; also, a member of a minor order in the Greek Church.

subdeaconship.c: Subdeaconship Subdeaconry { Sub*dea"con*ry (?), Sub*dea"con*ship, } n. (Eccl.) The order or office of subdeacon.

subdean.c: Subdean Sub"dean` (?), n. [Pref. sub- + dean: cf. F. sousdoyen.] An under dean; the deputy or substitute of a dean. Ayliffe.

subdeanery.c: Subdeanery Sub*dean"er*y (?), n. Office or rank of subdean.

subdecanal.c: Subdecanal Sub*dec"a*nal (?), a. Of or pertaining to a subdean or subdeanery.

subdecuple.c: Subdecuple Sub*dec"u*ple (?), a. Containing one part of ten.

subdelegate.c: Subdelegate Sub*del"e*gate (?), n. A subordinate delegate, or one with inferior powers.
Subdelegate Sub*del"e*gate (?), v. t. To appoint to act as subdelegate, or as a subordinate; to depete.

subdepartment.c: Subdepartment Sub`de*part"ment (?), n. A subordinate department; a bureau. See the Note under Bureau.

subdeposit.c: Subdeposit Sub`de*pos"it (?), n. That which is deposited beneath something else.

subderisorious.c: Subderisorious Sub`der*i*so"ri*ous (?), a. [Pref. sub- + L. derisorius. See Derisory.] Ridiculing with moderation. [R.] Dr. H. More.

subderivative.c: Subderivative Sub`de*riv"a*tive (?), n. A word derived from a derivative, and not directly from the root; as, “friendliness” is a subderivative, being derived from “friendly”, which is in turn a derivative from “friend.”

subdiaconate.c: Subdiaconate Sub`di*ac"o*nate (?), a. Of or pertaining to a subdeacon, or to the office or rank of a subdeacon.
Subdiaconate Sub`di*ac"o*nate, n. The office or rank of a subdeacon.

subdial.c: Subdial Sub*di"al (?), a. [L. subdialis in the open air.] Of or pertaining to the open air; being under the open sky. [R.] N. Bacon.

subdichotomy.c: Subdichotomy Sub`di*chot"o*my (?), n. A subordinate, or inferior, division into parts; a subdivision. [R.]

subdititious.c: Subdititious Sub`di*ti"tious (?), a. [L. subdititius, subditicius, fr. subdere to substitute.] Put secretly in the place of something else; foisted in. [R.]

subdiversify.c: Subdiversify Sub`di*ver"si*fy (?), v. t. To diversify aggain what is already diversified. [R.] Sir M. Hale.

subdivide.c: Subdivide Sub`di*vide" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Subdivided (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Subdividing.] [L. subdividere, sub under + dividere to divide. See Divide.] To divide the parts of (anything) into more parts; to part into smaller divisions; to divide again, as what has already been divided.
Subdivide Sub`di*vide", v. i. To be, or to become, subdivided.

subdivine.c: Subdivine Sub`di*vine" (?), a. Partaking of divinity; divine in a partial or lower degree. Bp. Hall.

subdivision.c: Subdivision Sub`di*vi"sion (?), n. [L. subdivisio: cf. F. subdivision.] 1. The act of subdividing, or separating a part into smaller parts.

subdolous.c: Subdolous Sub"do*lous (?), a. [L. subdolus, sub + dolus deceit.] Sly; crafty; cunning; artful. [R.]

subdominant.c: Subdominant Sub*dom"i*nant (?), n. (Mus.) The fourth tone above, or fifth below, the tonic; -- so called as being under the dominant.

subduable.c: Subduable Sub*du"a*ble (?), a. Able to be subdued.

subdual.c: Subdual Sub*du"al (?), n. Act of subduing. Bp. Warburton.

subduct.c: Subduct Subduce { Sub*duce" (?), Sub*duct" (?), } v. t. [L. subducere, subductum; sub under + ducere to lead, to draw. See Duke, and cf. Subdue.] 1. To withdraw; to take away. Milton.

subduction.c: Subduction Sub*duc"tion (?), n. [L. subductio.] 1. The act of subducting or taking away. Bp. Hall.

subdue.c: Subdue Sub*due" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Subdued (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Subduing.] [OE. soduen, OF. sosduire to seduce, L. subtus below (fr. sub under) + ducere to lead. See Duke, and cf. Subduct.] 1. To bring under; to conquer by force or the exertion of superior power, and bring into permanent subjection; to reduce under dominion; to vanquish.

subdued.c: Subdued Sub*dued" (?), a. 1. Conquered; overpowered; crushed; submissive; mild.

subduer.c: Subduer Sub*du"er (?), n. One who, or that which, subdues; a conqueror. Spenser.

subdulcid.c: Subdulcid Sub*dul"cid (?), a. [Pref. sub + L. dulcis sweet.] Somewhat sweet; sweetish. [R.]

subduple.c: Subduple Sub"du*ple (?), a. (Math.) Indicating one part of two; in the ratio of one to two.

subduplicate.c: Subduplicate Sub*du"pli*cate (?), a. (Math.) Expressed by the square root; -- said of ratios.

subdural.c: Subdural Sub*du"ral (?), a. (Anat.) Situated under the dura mater, or between the dura mater and the arachnoid membrane.

subeditor.c: Subeditor Sub*ed"i*tor (?), n. An assistant editor, as of a periodical or journal.

subelongate.c: Subelongate Sub`e*lon"gate (?), a. Not fully elongated; somewhat elongated.

subendocardial.c: Subendocardial Sub*en`do*car"di*al (?), a. (Anat.) Situated under the endocardium.

subendymal.c: Subendymal Sub*en"dy*mal (?), a. [Pref. sub + endyma.] Situated under the endyma.

subepidermal.c: Subepidermal Sub*ep`i*der"mal (?), a. Situated immediately below the epidermis.

subepiglottic.c: Subepiglottic Sub*ep`i*glot"tic (?), a. (Anat.) Situated under the epiglottis.

subepithelial.c: Subepithelial Sub*ep`i*the"li*al (?), a. (Anat.) Situated under the epithelium.

suberate.c: Suberate Su"ber*ate (?), n. [Cf. F. subérate.] (Chem.) A salt of suberic acid.

subereous.c: Subereous Su*be"re*ous (?), a. [L. subereus of the cork tree.] Of or pertaining to cork; of the nature of cork; suberose.

suberic.c: Suberic Su*ber"ic (?), a. [L. suber the cork tree: cf. F. subéreque.] (Chem.) Of or pertaining to cork; specifically, designating an acid, C6H12.(CO2H)2, homologous with oxalic acid, and obtained from cork and certain fatty oils, as a white crystalline substance.

suberin.c: Suberin Su"ber*in (?), n. [L. suber the cork tree: cf. F. subérine.] (Bot.) A material found in the cell walls of cork. It is a modification of lignin.

suberite.c: Suberite Su"ber*ite (?), n. [L. suber the cork tree.] (Zool.) Any sponge of the genus Suberites and allied genera. These sponges have a fine and compact texture, and contain minute siliceous spicules.

suberization.c: Suberization Su`ber*i*za"tion (?), n. (Bot.) Conversion of the cell walls into cork tissue by development of suberin; -- commonly taking place in exposed tissues, as when a callus forms over a wound. Suberized cell walls are impervious to water.

suberize.c: Suberize Su"ber*ize (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. -ized (?); p. pr. & vb. n. -izing (?).] [L. suber cork.] (Bot.) To effect suberization of.

suberone.c: Suberone Su"ber*one (?), n. (Chem.) (a) The hypothetical ketone of suberic acid. (b) A colorless liquid, analogous suberone proper, having a pleasant peppermint odor. It is obtained by the distillation of calcium suberate.

suberous.c: Suberous Suberose { Su"ber*ose` (?), Su"ber*ous (?), } a. [L. suber the cork tree: cf. F. subéreux.] (Bot.) Having a corky texture.

subesophageal.c: Subesophageal Sub*e`so*phag"e*al (?), a. (Zool.) Situated beneath the esophagus. [Written also suboesophageal.]

subfamily.c: Subfamily Sub*fam"i*ly (?), n. (Biol.) One of the subdivisions, of more importance than genus, into which certain families are divided.

subfuscous.c: Subfuscous Sub*fus"cous (?), a. [L. subfuscus, suffuscus. See Sub-, and Fuscous.] Duskish; dusky; moderately dark; brownish; tawny.

subgelatinous.c: Subgelatinous Sub`ge*lat"i*nous (?), a. Imperfectly or partially gelatinous.

subgeneric.c: Subgeneric Sub`ge*ner"ic (?), a. Of or pertaining to a subgenus.

subgenus.c: Subgenus Sub*ge"nus (?), n.; pl. Subgenera (?). (Biol.) A subdivision of a genus, comprising one or more species which differ from other species of the genus in some important character or characters; as, the azaleas now constitute a subgenus of Rhododendron.

subglacial.c: Subglacial Sub*gla"cial (?), a. Pertaining or belonging to the under side of a glacier; being beneath a glacier; as, subglacial streams.

subglossal.c: Subglossal Sub*glos"sal (?), a. (Anat.) Situated under the tongue; sublingual.

subglottic.c: Subglottic Sub*glot"tic (?), a. (Anat.) Situated below the glottis; -- applied to that part of the cavity of the larynx below the true vocal cords.

subgovernor.c: Subgovernor Sub*gov"ern*or (?), n. A subordinate or assistant governor.

subgroup.c: Subgroup Sub"group` (?), n. (Biol.) A subdivision of a group, as of animals. Darwin.

subhastation.c: Subhastation Sub`has*ta"tion (?), n. [L. subhastatio.] A public sale or auction. [R.] Bp. Burnet.

subhepatic.c: Subhepatic Sub`he*pat"ic (?), a. (Anat.) Situated under, or on the ventral side of, the liver; -- applied to the interlobular branches of the portal vein.

subhornblendic.c: Subhornblendic Sub`horn*blend"ic (?), a. (Min.) Containing hornblende in a scattered state; of or relating to rocks containing disseminated hornblende.

subhumerate.c: Subhumerate Sub*hu"mer*ate (?), v. t. [See Sub-, Humerus.] To place the shoulders under; to bear. [Obs.]

subhyaloid.c: Subhyaloid Sub*hy"a*loid (?), a. (Anat.) Situated under the hyaliod membrane.

subhyoidean.c: Subhyoidean Sub`hy*oid"e*an (?), a. (Anat. & Med.) Situated or performed beneath the hyoid bone; as, subhyoidean laryngotomy.

subimago.c: Subimago ‖Sub`i*ma"go (?), n. [NL. See Sub-, and Imago.] (Zool.) A stage in the development of certain insects, such as the May flies, intermediate between the pupa and imago. In this stage, the insect is able to fly, but subsequently sheds a skin before becoming mature. Called also pseudimago.

subincusation.c: Subincusation Sub*in`cu*sa"tion (?), n. [Pref. sub + L. incusatio accusation, fr. incusare to accuse.] A slight charge or accusation. [Obs.] Bp. Hall.

subindex.c: Subindex Sub*in"dex (?), n.; pl. Subindices (?). (Math.) A number or mark placed opposite the lower part of a letter or symbol to distinguish the symbol; thus, a0, b1, c2, xn, have 0, 1, 2, and n as subindices.

subindicate.c: Subindicate Sub*in"di*cate (?), v. t. [Pref. sub + indicate: cf. L. subindicare.] To indicate by signs or hints; to indicate imperfectly. [R.] Dr. H. More.

subindication.c: Subindication Sub*in`di*ca"tion (?), n. The act of indicating by signs; a slight indication. [R.] “The subindication and shadowing of heavenly things.” Barrow.

subindividual.c: Subindividual Sub*in`di*vid"u*al (?), n. A division of that which is individual.

subinduce.c: Subinduce Sub`in*duce" (?), v. t. To insinuate; to offer indirectly. [Obs.] Sir E. Dering.

subinfer.c: Subinfer Sub`in*fer" (?), v. t. & i. To infer from an inference already made. [Obs.] Bp. Hall.

subinfeudation.c: Subinfeudation Sub*in`feu*da"tion (?), n. (Law) (a) The granting of lands by inferior lords to their dependents, to be held by themselves by feudal tenure. Craig. (b) Subordinate tenancy; undertenancy.

subintestinal.c: Subintestinal Sub`in*tes"ti*nal (?), a. (Anat.) Situated under, or on the ventral side of, the intestine.

subinvolution.c: Subinvolution Sub*in`vo*lu"tion (?), n. Partial or incomplete involution; as, subinvolution of the uterus.

subitaneous.c: Subitaneous Sub`i*ta"ne*ous (?), a. [L. subitaneus. See Sudden.] Sudden; hasty. [Obs.] Bullokar. -- Sub`i*ta"ne*ous*ness, n. [Obs.]

subitany.c: Subitany Sub"i*ta*ny (?), a. Subitaneous; sudden; hasty. [Obs.] Hales.

subito.c: Subito ‖Su"bi*to (?), adv. [It. & L.] (Mus.) In haste; quickly; rapidly.

subjacent.c: Subjacent Sub*ja"cent (?), a. [L. subjacens, p. pr. of subjacere to lie under; sub under + jacere to lie.] 1. Lying under or below.

subject.c: Subject Sub*ject" (?), a. [OE. suget, OF. souzget, sougit (in which the first part is L. subtus below, fr. sub under), subgiet, subject, F. sujet, from L. subjectus lying under, subjected, p. p. of subjicere, subicere, to throw, lay, place, or bring under; sub under + jacere to throw. See Jet a shooting forth.] 1. Placed or situated under; lying below, or in a lower situation. [Obs.] Spenser.
Subject Sub*ject", n. [From L. subjectus, through an old form of F. sujet. See Subject, a.] 1. That which is placed under the authority, dominion, control, or influence of something else.
Subject Sub*ject" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Subjected (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Subjecting.] 1. To bring under control, power, or dominion; to make subject; to subordinate; to subdue.

subjected.c: Subjected Sub*ject"ed (?), a. 1. Subjacent. “Led them direct... to the subjected plain.” [Obs.] Milton.

subjection.c: Subjection Sub*jec"tion (?), n. [L. subjectio: cf. OF. subjection, F. subjétion. See Subject, a.] 1. The act of subjecting, or of bringing under the dominion of another; the act of subduing.

subjectist.c: Subjectist Sub"ject*ist (?), n. (Metaph.) One skilled in subjective philosophy; a subjectivist.

subjective.c: Subjective Sub*jec"tive (?), a. [L. subjectivus: cf. F. subjectif.] 1. Of or pertaining to a subject.

subjectivism.c: Subjectivism Sub*jec"tiv*ism (?), n. (Metaph.) Any philosophical doctrine which refers all knowledge to, and founds it upon, any subjective states; egoism.

subjectivist.c: Subjectivist Sub*jec"tiv*ist, n. (Metaph.) One who holds to subjectivism; an egoist.

subjectivity.c: Subjectivity Sub`jec*tiv"i*ty (?), n. The quality or state of being subjective; character of the subject.

subjectmatter.c: Subject-matter Sub"ject-mat`ter (?), n. The matter or thought presented for consideration in some statement or discussion; that which is made the object of thought or study.

subjectness.c: Subjectness Sub"ject*ness, n. Quality of being subject. [R.]

subjicible.c: Subjicible Sub*jic"i*ble (?), a. Capable of being subjected. [Obs.] Jer. Taylor.

subjoin.c: Subjoin Sub*join" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Subjoined (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Subjoining.] [Cf. OF. subjoindre, L. subjungere. See Sub-, and Join, and cf. Subjective.] To add after something else has been said or written; to ANNEX; as, to subjoin an argument or reason.

subjugate.c: Subjugate Sub"ju*gate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Subjugated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Subjugating.] [L. subjugatus, p. p. of subjugare to subjugate; sub under + jugum a yoke. See Yoke.] To subdue, and bring under the yoke of power or dominion; to conquer by force, and compel to submit to the government or absolute control of another; to vanquish.

subjugation.c: Subjugation Sub`ju*ga"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. subjugation, LL. subjugatio.] The act of subjugating, or the state of being subjugated.

subjugator.c: Subjugator Sub"ju*ga`tor (?), n. [L.] One who subjugates; a conqueror.

subjunction.c: Subjunction Sub*junc"tion (?), n. [See Subjunctive.] 1. Act of subjoining, or state of being subjoined.

subjunctive.c: Subjunctive Sub*junc"tive (?), a. [L. subjunctivus, fr. subjungere, subjunctum, to subjoin: cf. F. subjonctif. See Subjoin.] Subjoined or added to something before said or written.
Subjunctive Sub*junc"tive, n. (Gram.) The subjunctive mood; also, a verb in the subjunctive mood.

subkingdom.c: Subkingdom Sub*king"dom (?), n. One of the several primary divisions of either the animal, or vegetable kingdom, as, in Zoology, the Vertebrata, Tunicata, Mollusca, Articulata, Molluscoidea, Echinodermata, Coelentera, and the Protozoa; in botany, the Phanerogamia, and the Cryptogamia.

sublapsarian.c: Sublapsarian Sub`lap*sa"ri*an (?), n. & a. [Pref. sub + lapse: cf. F. sublapsarien, sublapsarie.] (Eccl. Hist.) Same as Infralapsarian.

sublate.c: Sublate Sub"late (?), v. t. [From sublatus, used as p. p. of tollere to take away. See Tolerate.] To take or carry away; to remove. [R.] E. Hall.

sublation.c: Sublation Sub*la"tion (?), n. [L. sublatio, fr. sublatus, used as p. p. of tollere to take away.] The act of taking or carrying away; removal. [R.] Bp. Hall.

sublative.c: Sublative Sub"la*tive (?), a. Having power, or tending, to take away. [R.] Harris.

sublease.c: Sublease Sub"lease` (?), n. (Law) A lease by a tenant or lessee to another person; an underlease. Bouvier.

sublessee.c: Sublessee Sub`les*see" (?), n. A holder of a sublease.

sublet.c: Sublet Sub*let" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Sublet; p. pr. & vb. n. Subletting.] To underlet; to lease, as when a lessee leases to another person.

sublevation.c: Sublevation Sub`le*va"tion (?), n. [L. sublevare to lift up; sub under + levare to lift, raise: cf. L. sublevatio an allevation.] 1. The act of raising on high; elevation. Sir T. More.

sublibrarian.c: Sublibrarian Sub`li*bra"ri*an (?), n. An under or assistant librarian.

sublieutenant.c: Sublieutenant Sub`lieu*ten"ant (?), n. [Pref. sub + lieutenant: cf. F. sous-lieutenant.] An inferior or second lieutenant; in the British service, a commissioned officer of the lowest rank.

subligation.c: Subligation Sub`li*ga"tion (?), n. [L. subligatio, from subligare to bind below; sub under + ligare to bind.] The act of binding underneath. [R.]

sublimable.c: Sublimable Sub*lim"a*ble (?), a. [Cf. F. sublimable. See Sublime., v. t.] Capable of being sublimed or sublimated. -- Sub*lim"a*ble*ness, n. Boyle.

sublimate.c: Sublimate Sub"li*mate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Sublimated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Sublimating.] [L. sublimatus, p. p. of sublimare to raise, elevate, fr. sublimis high: cf. F. sublimer. See Sublime, a., and cf. Surlime, v. t.] 1. To bring by heat into the state of vapor, which, on cooling, returns again to the solid state; as, to sublimate sulphur or camphor.
Sublimate Sub"li*mate (?), n. [LL. sublimatum.] (Chem.) A product obtained by sublimation; hence, also, a purified product so obtained.
Sublimate Sub"li*mate, a. [LL. sublimatus.] Brought into a state of vapor by heat, and again condensed as a solid.

sublimated.c: Sublimated Sub"li*ma`ted (?), a. Refined by, or as by, sublimation; exalted; purified.

sublimation.c: Sublimation Sub"li*ma`tion (?), n. [LL. sublimatio: cf. F. sublimation.] 1. (Chem.) The act or process of subliming, or the state or result of being sublimed.

sublimatory.c: Sublimatory Sub"li*ma*to*ry (?), a. Used for sublimation; as, sublimatory vessels. Boyle.
Sublimatory Sub"li*ma*to*ry, n. A vessel used for sublimation.

sublime.c: Sublime Sub*lime" (?), a. [Compar. Sublimer (?); superl. Sublimest.] [L. sublimis; sub under + (perhaps) a word akin to limen lintel, sill, thus meaning, up to the lintel: cf. F. sublime. Cf. Eliminate.] 1. Lifted up; high in place; exalted aloft; uplifted; lofty.
Sublime Sub*lime", n. That which is sublime; -- with the definite article; as: (a) A grand or lofty style in speaking or writing; a style that expresses lofty conceptions.

Sublime Sub*lime", v. t. [imp. & p. p. Sublimed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Subliming.] [Cf. L. sublimare, F. sublimer to subject to sublimation. See Sublime, a., and cf. Sublimate, v. t.] 1. To raise on high. [Archaic]

Sublime Sub*lime" (?), v. i. (Chem.) To pass off in vapor, with immediate condensation; specifically, to evaporate or volatilize from the solid state without apparent melting; -- said of those substances, like arsenic, benzoic acid, etc., which do not exhibit a liquid form on heating, except under increased pressure.

sublimed.c: Sublimed Sub*limed" (?), a. (Chem.) Having been subjected to the process of sublimation; hence, also, purified. “Sublimed mercurie.” Chaucer.

sublimely.c: Sublimely Sub*lime"ly (?), adv. In a sublime manner.

sublimeness.c: Sublimeness Sub*lime"ness, n. The quality or state of being sublime; sublimity.

sublimification.c: Sublimification Sub*lim`i*fi*ca"tion (?), n. [L. sublimis sublime + -ficare to make. See -ry.] The act of making sublime, or state of being made sublime.

subliminal.c: Subliminal Sub*lim"i*nal (?), a. [Pref. sub- + L. limen threshold.] 1. (Philos.) Existing in the mind, but below the surface or threshold of consciousness; that is, existing as feeling rather than as clear ideas.

sublimity.c: Sublimity Sub*lim"i*ty (?), n.; pl. Sublimities (#). [L. sublimitas: cf. F. sublimité.] 1. The quality or state of being sublime (in any sense of the adjective).

sublineation.c: Sublineation Sub*lin`e*a"tion (?), n. A mark of a line or lines under a word in a sentence, or under another line; underlining.

sublingua.c: Sublingua ‖Sub*lin"gua (?), n.; pl. Sublinguae (#). [NL.] (Anat.) A process or fold below the tongue in some animals.

sublingual.c: Sublingual Sub*lin"gual (?), a. [Pref. sub + lingual: cf. F. sublingual.] (Anat.) (a) Situated under the tongue; as, the sublingual gland. (b) Of or pertaining to the sublingual gland; as, sublingual salvia.

sublition.c: Sublition Sub*li"tion (?), n. [L. sublinere, sublitum, to smear, to lay on as a ground color.] (Paint.) The act or process of laying the ground in a painting. [R.]

sublittoral.c: Sublittoral Sub*lit"to*ral (?), a. Under the shore. Smart.

sublobular.c: Sublobular Sub*lob"u*lar (?), a. (Anat.) Situated under, or at the bases of, the lobules of the liver.

sublumbar.c: Sublumbar Sub*lum"bar (?), a. (Anat.) Situated under, or on the ventral side of, the lumbar region of the vertebral column.

sublunary.c: Sublunary Sublunar { Sub*lu"nar (?), Sub"lu*na*ry (?), } a. [Pref. sub + lunar, or lunary: cf. F. sublunaire.] Situated beneath the moon; hence, of or pertaining to this world; terrestrial; earthly.

subluxation.c: Subluxation Sub`lux*a"tion (?), n. [Pref. sub + luxation: cf. F. subluxation.] (Surg.) An incomplete or partial dislocation.

submammary.c: Submammary Sub*mam"ma*ry (?), a. Situated under the mammae; as, submammary inflammation.

submarine.c: Submarine Sub`ma*rine" (?), a. Being, acting, or growing, under water in the sea; as, submarine navigators; submarine plants.
Submarine Sub*ma*rine", n. A submarine plant or animal.

Submarine Sub`ma*rine" (?), n. 1. A submarine boat; a ship that can travel under the surface of the water. Most such ships are ships of war, as part of a navy, but submarines are also used for oceanic research. Also called sub and (from the German U-Boot) U-boat. esp., Nav., a submarine torpedo boat; -- called specif. submergible submarine when capable of operating at various depths and of traveling considerable distances under water, and submersible submarine when capable of being only partly submerged, i.e., so that the conning tower, etc., is still above water. The latter type and most of the former type are submerged as desired by regulating the amount of water admitted to the ballast tanks and sink on an even keel; some of the former type effect submersion while under way by means of horizontal rudders, in some cases also with admission of water to the ballast tanks.

submarshal.c: Submarshal Sub*mar"shal (?), n. An under or deputy marshal.

submaxillary.c: Submaxillary Sub*max"il*la*ry (?), a. (Anat.) (a) Situated under the maxilla, or lower jaw; inframaxillary; as, the submaxillary gland. (b) Of or pertaining to submaxillary gland; as, submaxillary salvia.

submedial.c: Submedial Sub*me"di*al (?), a. Lying under the middle.

submedian.c: Submedian Sub*me"di*an (?), a. (Zool.) Next to the median (on either side); as, the submedian teeth of mollusks.

submediant.c: Submediant Sub*me"di*ant (?), n. (Mus.) The sixth tone of the scale; the under mediant, or third below the keynote; the superdominant.

submental.c: Submental Sub*men"tal (?), a. (Anat.) Situated under the chin; as, the submental artery.

submentum.c: Submentum Sub*men"tum (?), n.; pl. Submenta (#). [NL. See Sub-, and Mentum.] (Zool.) The basal part of the labium of insects. It bears the mentum.

submerge.c: Submerge Sub*merge" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Submerged (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Submerging (?).] [L. submergere, submersum; sub under + mergere to plunge: cf. F. submerger. See Merge.] 1. To put under water; to plunge.
Submerge Sub*merge" (?), v. i. To plunge into water or other fluid; to be buried or covered, as by a fluid; to be merged; hence, to be completely included.

submergence.c: Submergence Sub*mer"gence (?), n. [From L. submergens, p. pr.] The act of submerging, or the state of being submerged; submersion.

submersed.c: Submersed Sub*mersed" (?), a. [L. submersus, p. p. of submergere. See Submerge.] Being or growing under water, as the leaves of aquatic plants.

submersion.c: Submersion Sub*mer"sion (?), n. [L. submersio: cf. F. submersion.] 1. The act of submerging, or putting under water or other fluid, or of causing to be overflowed; the act of plunging under water, or of drowning.

submetallic.c: Submetallic Sub`me*tal"lic (?), a. Imperfectly metallic; as, a submetallic luster.

subminister.c: Subminister Sub*min"is*ter (?), v. t. [L. subministrare, subministratum. See Sub-, and Ministre, v. t.] To supply; to afford. [Obs.] Sir M. Hale.
Subminister Sub*min"is*ter, v. i. To be subservient; to be useful. [Obs.] “Our passions... subminister to the best and worst purposes.” L'EStrange.

subministrant.c: Subministrant Sub*min"is*trant (?), a. [L. subministrans, p. pr.] Subordinate; subservient. [Obs.] Bacon.

subministrate.c: Subministrate Sub*min"is*trate (?), v. t. [See Subminister.] To supply; to afford; to subminister. [Obs.] Harvey.

subministration.c: Subministration Sub*min`is*tra"tion (?), n. [L. subministratio.] The act of subministering. [Obs.] Sir H. Wotton.

submiss.c: Submiss Sub*miss" (?), a. [L. submissus, p. p. of submittere to let down, to lower. See Submit.] 1. Submissive; humble; obsequious. [Archaic] “Soft Silence and submiss Obedience.” Spenser. “Stooping and submiss.” R. L. Stevenson.

submission.c: Submission Sub*mis"sion (?), n. [L. submissio a letting down, lowering: cf. F. soumission.] 1. The act of submitting; the act of yielding to power or authority; surrender of the person and power to the control or government of another; obedience; compliance.

submissive.c: Submissive Sub*mis"sive (?), a. 1. Inclined or ready to submit; acknowledging one's inferiority; yielding; obedient; humble.

submissly.c: Submissly Sub*miss"ly (?), adv. In a submissive manner; with a submission. [Archaic] Jer. Taylor.

submit.c: Submit Sub*mit" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Submitted (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Submitting.] [L. submittere; sub under + mittere to send: cf. F. soumettre. See Missile.] 1. To let down; to lower. [Obs.]
Submit Sub*mit", v. i. 1. To yield one's person to the power of another; to give up resistance; to surrender.

submitter.c: Submitter Sub*mit"ter (?), n. One who submits. Whitlock.

submonish.c: Submonish Sub*mon"ish (?), v. t. [L. submonere. See Summon, and -ish.] To suggest; to prompt. [R.] “The submonishing inclinations of my senses.” T. Granger.

submonition.c: Submonition Sub`mo*ni"tion (?), n. [LL. submonitio.] Suggestion; prompting. [R.] T. Granger.

submucous.c: Submucous Sub*mu"cous (?), a. (Anat.) Situated under a mucous membrane.

submultiple.c: Submultiple Sub*mul"ti*ple (?), n. (Math.) A number or quality which is contained in another an exact number of times, or is an aliquot part of it; thus, 7 is the submultiple of 56, being contained in it eight times.
Submultiple Sub*mul"ti*ple, a. (Math.) Of or pertaining to a submultiple; being a submultiple; as, a submultiple number; submultiple ratio.

submuscular.c: Submuscular Sub*mus"cu*lar (?), a. Situated underneath a muscle or muscles.

subnasal.c: Subnasal Sub*na"sal (?), a. (Anat.) Situated under the nose; as, the subnasal point, or the middle point of the inferior border of the anterior nasal aperture.

subnascent.c: Subnascent Sub*nas"cent (?), a. [L. subnascens, p. pr. of subnasci to grow under; sub under + nasci to be born.] Growing underneath. [R.] Evelyn.

subnect.c: Subnect Sub*nect" (?), v. t. [L. subnectere, subnextum; sub under + nectere to tie.] To tie or fasten beneath; to join beneath. [R.] Pope.

subnex.c: Subnex Sub*nex" (?), v. t. [See Subnect.] To subjoin; to subnect. [Obs.] Holland.

subnormal.c: Subnormal Sub*nor"mal (?), n. (Geom.) That part of the axis of a curved line which is intercepted between the ordinate and the normal.

subnotation.c: Subnotation Sub`no*ta"tion (?), n. [L. subnotatio a signing underneath, fr. subnotare to subscribe; sub under + notare to note or mark.] A rescript. Bouvier.

subnotochordal.c: Subnotochordal Sub*no`to*chor"dal (?), a. (Anat.) Situated on the ventral side of the notochord; as, the subnotochordal rod.

subnuvolar.c: Subnuvolar Sub*nu"vo*lar (?), a. [Pref. sub + It. nuvola cloud: cf. L. subnubilus somewhat cloudy.] Under the clouds; attended or partly covered or obscured by clouds; somewhat cloudy. [R. & Poetic]

subobscurely.c: Subobscurely Sub`ob*scure"ly (?), adv. Somewhat obscurely or darkly. [R.] Donne.

suboccipital.c: Suboccipital Sub`oc*cip"i*tal (?), a. (Anat.) Situated under, or posterior to, the occiput; as, the suboccipital, or first cervical, nerve.

suboctuple.c: Suboctuple Suboctave { Sub*oc"tave (?), Sub*oc"tu*ple (?), } a. Containing one part of eight; having the ratio of one to eight. Bp. Wilkins.

subocular.c: Subocular Sub*oc"u*lar (?), a. [Pref. sub + ocular: cf. L. subocularis.] (Anat.) Situated under, or on the ventral side of, the eye.

subofficer.c: Subofficer Sub*of"fi*cer (?), n. [Pref. sub + officer: cf. F. sous-officer.] An under or subordinate officer.

subopercular.c: Subopercular Sub`o*per"cu*lar (?), a. (Anat.) Situated below the operculum; pertaining to the suboperculum. -- n. The suboperculum.

suboperculum.c: Suboperculum Sub`o*per"cu*lum (?), n. [NL. See Sub-, Operculum.] (Anat.) The lower opercular bone in fishes.

suborbiculate.c: Suborbiculate Suborbicular { Sub`or*bic"u*lar (?), Sub`or*bic"u*late (?), } a. Almost orbiculate or orbicular.

suborbitar.c: Suborbitar Suborbital { Sub*or"bit*al (?), Sub*or"bit*ar (?), } a. (Anat.) Situated under or below the orbit.

suborder.c: Suborder Sub*or"der (?), n. (Nat. Hist.) A division of an order; a group of genera of a little lower rank than an order and of greater importance than a tribe or family; as, cichoraceous plants form a suborder of Compositae.

subordinacy.c: Subordinacy Sub*or"di*na*cy (?), n. [See Subordinate.] The quality or state of being subordinate, or subject to control; subordination, as, to bring the imagination to act in subordinacy to reason. Spectator.

subordinancy.c: Subordinancy Subordinance { Sub*or"di*nance (?), Sub*or"di*nan*cy (?), } n. [Pref. sub + L. ordinans, p. pr. of ordinare. See Subordinate, a.] Subordinacy; subordination. [Obs.] Dr. H. More. Sir W. Temple.

subordinary.c: Subordinary Sub*or"di*na*ry (?), n. (Her.) One of several heraldic bearings somewhat less common than an ordinary. See Ordinary.

subordinate.c: Subordinate Sub*or"di*nate (?), a. [Pref. sub + L. ordinatus, p. p. of ordinare to set in order, to arrange. See Ordain.] 1. Placed in a lower order, class, or rank; holding a lower or inferior position.
Subordinate Sub*or"di*nate, n. One who stands in order or rank below another; -- distinguished from a principal. Milton.

Subordinate Sub*or"di*nate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Subordinated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Subordinating.] 1. To place in a lower order or class; to make or consider as of less value or importance; as, to subordinate one creature to another.

subordination.c: Subordination Sub*or`di*na"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. subordination.] 1. The act of subordinating, placing in a lower order, or subjecting.

subordinative.c: Subordinative Sub*or"di*na*tive (?), a. Tending to subordinate; expressing subordination; used to introduce a subordinate sentence; as, a subordinative conjunction.

suborn.c: Suborn Sub*orn" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Suborned (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Suborning.] [F. suborner, L. subornare; sub under, secretly + ornare to furnish, provide, equip, adorn. See Ornament.] 1. (Law) To procure or cause to take a false oath amounting to perjury, such oath being actually taken. Sir W. O. Russell.

subornation.c: Subornation Sub`or*na"tion (?), n. [F. subornation.] 1. (Law) The act of suborning; the crime of procuring a person to take such a false oath as constitutes perjury. Blackstone.

suborner.c: Suborner Sub*orn"er (?), n. One who suborns or procures another to take, a false oath; one who procures another to do a bad action.

suboval.c: Suboval Sub*o"val (?), a. Somewhat oval; nearly oval.

subovate.c: Subovate Sub*o"vate (?), a. Nearly in the form of an egg, or of the section of an egg, but having the inferior extremity broadest; nearly ovate.

suboxide.c: Suboxide Sub*ox"ide (?), n. (Chem.) An oxide containing a relatively small amount of oxygen, and less than the normal proportion; as, potassium suboxide, K4O.

subpeduncular.c: Subpeduncular Sub`pe*dun"cu*lar (?), a. (Anat.) Situated beneath the peduncle; as, the subpeduncular lobe of the cerebellum.

subpedunculate.c: Subpedunculate Sub`pe*dun"cu*late (?), a. (Bot. & Zool.) Supported on, or growing from, a very short stem; having a short peduncle.

subpellucid.c: Subpellucid Sub`pel*lu"cid (?), a. Somewhat pellucid; nearly pellucid.

subpena.c: Subpena Sub*pe"na (?), n. & v. t. See Subpoena.

subpentangular.c: Subpentangular Sub`pen*tan"gu*lar (?), a. Nearly or approximately pentangular; almost pentangular.

subpericardial.c: Subpericardial Sub*per`i*car"di*al (?), a. (Anat.) Situated under the cardiac pericardium.

subperiosteal.c: Subperiosteal Sub*per`i*os"te*al (?), a. (Anat.) Situated under the periosteum.

subperitoneal.c: Subperitoneal Sub*per`i*to"ne*al (?), a. (Anat.) Situated under the peritoneal membrane.

subpetiolar.c: Subpetiolar Sub*pet"i*o*lar (?), a. (Bot.) Concealed within the base of the petiole, as the leaf buds of the plane tree.

subpleural.c: Subpleural Sub*pleu"ral (?), a. (Anat.) Situated under the pleural membrane.

subpodophyllous.c: Subpodophyllous Sub*pod`o*phyl"lous (?), a. (Anat.) Situated under the podophyllous tissue of the horse's foot.

subpoena.c: Subpoena Sub*poe"na (?), n. [NL., fr. L. sub under + poena punishment. See Pain.] (Law) A writ commanding the attendance in court, as a witness, of the person on whom it is served, under a penalty; the process by which a defendant in equity is commanded to appear and answer the plaintiff's bill. [Written also subpena.]

Subpoena Sub*poe"na, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Subpoenaed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Subpoenaing.] (Law) To serve with a writ of subpoena; to command attendance in court by a legal writ, under a penalty in case of disobedience.

subpoenal.c: Subpoenal Sub*poe"nal (?), a. Required or done under penalty. Gauden.

subpolar.c: Subpolar Sub*po"lar (?), a. Situated below the poles.

subpolygonal.c: Subpolygonal Sub`po*lyg"o*nal (?), a. Approximately polygonal; somewhat or almost polygonal.

subprehensile.c: Subprehensile Sub`pre*hen"sile (?), a. Somewhat prehensile; prehensile in an inferior degree.

subprior.c: Subprior Sub*pri"or (?), n. [Pref. sub + prior: cf. F. sous-prieur.] (Eccl.) The vicegerent of a prior; a claustral officer who assists the prior.

subpubic.c: Subpubic Sub*pu"bic (?), a. (Anat.) Situated under, or posterior to, the pubic bones.

subpulmonary.c: Subpulmonary Sub*pul"mo*na*ry (?), a. (Anat.) Situated under, or on the ventral side of, the lungs.

subpurchaser.c: Subpurchaser Sub*pur"chas*er (?), n. A purchaser who buys from a purchaser; one who buys at second hand.

subquadrate.c: Subquadrate Sub*quad"rate (?), a. Nearly or approximately square; almost square.

subquadruple.c: Subquadruple Sub*quad"ru*ple (?), a. Containing one part of four; in the ratio of one to four; as, subquadruple proportion. Bp. Wilkins.

subquinquefid.c: Subquinquefid Sub*quin"que*fid (?), a. Almost quinquefid; nearly quinquefid.

subquintuple.c: Subquintuple Sub*quin"tu*ple (?), a. Having the ratio of one to five; as, subquintuple proportion. Bp. Wilkins.

subreader.c: Subreader Sub*read"er (?), n. (Law) An under reader in the inns of court, who reads the texts of law the reader is to discourse upon. [Eng.] Crabb.

subreligion.c: Subreligion Sub`re*li"gion (?), n. A secondary religion; a belief or principle held in a quasi religious veneration.

subreption.c: Subreption Sub*rep"tion (?), n. [L. subreptio, fr. subripere, subreptum, to snatch or take away secretly: cf. F. subreption. See Surreptitious.] The act of obtaining a favor by surprise, or by unfair representation through suppression or fraudulent concealment of facts. Bp. Hall.

subreptitious.c: Subreptitious Sub`rep*ti"tious (?), a. [L. subreptitius. See Surreptitious.] Surreptitious. [Obs.] -- Sub`rep*ti"tious*ly (#), adv. [Obs.]

subrigid.c: Subrigid Sub*rig"id (?), a. Somewhat rigid or stiff.

subriguous.c: Subriguous Sub*rig"u*ous (?), a. [L. subriguus; sub under + riguus watered, akin to rigare to water.] Watered or wet beneath; well-watered. [Obs.] Blount.

subrogate.c: Subrogate Sub"ro*gate (?), v. t. [L. subrogatus, p. p. of subrogare. See Surrogate.] To put in the place of another; to substitute. Barrow.

subrogation.c: Subrogation Sub`ro*ga"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. subrogation, LL. subrogatio.] The act of subrogating. Specifically: (Law) The substitution of one person in the place of another as a creditor, the new creditor succeeding to the rights of the former; the mode by which a third person who pays a creditor succeeds to his rights against the debtor. Bouvier. Burrill. Abbott.

subsacral.c: Subsacral Sub*sa"cral (?), a. (Anat.) Situated under, or on the ventral side of, the sacrum.

subsaline.c: Subsaline Sub`sa*line" (?), a. Moderately saline or salt.

subsalt.c: Subsalt Sub"salt` (?), n. (Chem.) A basic salt. See the Note under Salt.

subsannation.c: Subsannation Sub`san*na"tion (?), n. [L. subsannatio, fr. subsannare to deride by mimicking gestures.] Derision; mockery. [Obs.] Dr. H. More.

subscapulary.c: Subscapulary Subscapular { Sub*scap"u*lar (?), Sub*scap"u*la*ry (?), } a. (Anat.) Situated beneath the scapula; infrascapular; as, the subscapular muscle.

subscribable.c: Subscribable Sub*scrib"a*ble (?), a. Capable of being subscribed. [R.]

subscribe.c: Subscribe Sub*scribe" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Subscribed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Subscribing.] [L. subscribere, subscriptum; sub under + scribere to write: cf. F. souscrire. See Scribe.] 1. To write underneath, as one's name; to sign (one's name) to a document.
Subscribe Sub*scribe", v. i. 1. To sign one's name to a letter or other document. Shak.

subscriber.c: Subscriber Sub*scrib"er (?), n. 1. One who subscribes; one who contributes to an undertaking by subscribing.

subscript.c: Subscript Sub"script (?), a. [L. subscriptus, p. p. See Subscribe.] Written below or underneath; as, iota subscript. (See under Iota.) Specifically (Math.), said of marks, figures, or letters (suffixes), written below and usually to the right of other letters to distinguish them; as, a, n, 2, in the symbols Xa, An, Y2. See Suffix, n., 2, and Subindex.
Subscript Sub"script, n. Anything written below. Bentley.

subscription.c: Subscription Sub*scrip"tion (?), n. [L. subscriptio: cf. F. souscription.] 1. The act of subscribing.

subscriptive.c: Subscriptive Sub*scrip"tive (?), a. Of or pertaining to a subscription, or signature. “The subscriptive part.” Richardson. -- Sub*scrip"tive*ly, adv.

subsecute.c: Subsecute Sub"se*cute (?), v. t. [L. subsecutus, p. p. of subsequi. See Subsequent.] To follow closely, or so as to overtake; to pursue. [Obs.]

subsecutive.c: Subsecutive Sub*sec"u*tive (?), a. [Cf. F. subsécutif.] Following in a train or succession. [R.]

subsellium.c: Subsellium ‖Sub*sel"li*um (?), n.; pl. Subsellia (#). [L.] (Eccl. Arch.) One of the stalls of the lower range where there are two ranges. See Illust. of Stall.

subsemitone.c: Subsemitone Sub*sem"i*tone (?), n. (Mus.) The sensible or leading note, or sharp seventh, of any key; subtonic.

subsensible.c: Subsensible Sub*sen"si*ble (?), a. Deeper than the reach of the senses. “That subsensible world.” Tyndall.

subseptuple.c: Subseptuple Sub*sep"tu*ple (?), a. Having the ratio of one to seven. Bp. Wilkins.

subsequency.c: Subsequency Subsequence { Sub"se*quence (?), Sub"se*quen*cy (?), } n. The act or state of following; -- opposed to precedence.

subsequent.c: Subsequent Sub"se*quent (?), a. [L. subsequens, -entis, p. pr. of subsequi to follow, succeed: cf. F. subséquent. See Sue to follow.] 1. Following in time; coming or being after something else at any time, indefinitely; as, subsequent events; subsequent ages or years; a period long subsequent to the foundation of Rome.

subsequently.c: Subsequently Sub"se*quent*ly, adv. At a later time; afterwards.

subserous.c: Subserous Sub*se"rous (?), a. (Anat.) Situated under a serous membrane.

subserve.c: Subserve Sub*serve" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Subserved (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Subserving.] [L. subservire; sub under + servire to serve. See Serve.] To serve in subordination or instrumentally; to be subservient to; to help forward; to promote.
Subserve Sub*serve", v. i. To be subservient or subordinate; to serve in an inferior capacity.

subserviency.c: Subserviency Subservience { Sub*serv"i*ence (?), Sub*serv"i*en*cy (?), } n. The quality or state of being subservient; instrumental fitness or use; hence, willingness to serve another's purposes; in a derogatory sense, servility.

subservient.c: Subservient Sub*serv"i*ent (?), a. [L. subserviens, -entis, p. pr. See Subserve.] Fitted or disposed to subserve; useful in an inferior capacity; serving to promote some end; subordinate; hence, servile, truckling.

subserviently.c: Subserviently Sub*serv"i*ent*ly, adv. In a subservient manner.

subsesqui.c: Subsesqui- Sub*ses"qui- (?). [Pref. sub- + sesqui-.] (Chem.) A prefix (also used adjectively) denoting the combination of constituents (especially electro-negative and electro-positive bodies) in the proportion of two to three; as, a subsesqui acetate, i. e., a salt having two equivalents of acetic acid to three of the base.

subsextuple.c: Subsextuple Sub*sex"tu*ple (?), a. Having the ratio of one to six; as, a subsextuple proportion. Bp. Wilkins.

subside.c: Subside Sub*side" (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Subsided; p. pr. & vb. n. Subsiding.] [L. subsidere; sub under, below + sidere to sit down, to settle; akin to sedere to sit, E. sit. See Sit.] 1. To sink or fall to the bottom; to settle, as lees.

subsidency.c: Subsidency Subsidence { Sub*sid"ence (?), Sub*sid"en*cy (?), } n. [L. subsidens, -entis, p. pr. of subsidere. See Subside.] The act or process of subsiding.

subsidiarily.c: Subsidiarily Sub*sid"i*a*ri*ly (?), adv. In a subsidiary manner; so as to assist.

subsidiary.c: Subsidiary Sub*sid"i*a*ry (?), a. [L. subsidiarius: cf. F. subsidiaire. See Subsidy.] 1. Furnishing aid; assisting; auxiliary; helping; tributary; especially, aiding in an inferior position or capacity; as, a subsidiary stream.
Subsidiary Sub*sid"i*a*ry, n.; pl. Subsidiaries (?). One who, or that which, contributes aid or additional supplies; an assistant; an auxiliary. Hammond.

subsidize.c: Subsidize Sub"si*dize (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Subsidized (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Subsidizing (?).] [From Subsidy.] To furnish with a subsidy; to purchase the assistance of by the payment of a subsidy; to aid or promote, as a private enterprise, with public money; as, to subsidize a steamship line.

subsidy.c: Subsidy Sub"si*dy (?), n.; pl. Subsidies (#). [L. subsidium the troops stationed in reserve in the third line of battlem reserve, support, help, fr. subsidere to sit down, lie in wait: cf. F. subside. See Subside.] 1. Support; aid; cooperation; esp., extraordinary aid in money rendered to the sovereign or to a friendly power.

subsign.c: Subsign Sub*sign" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Subsigned (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Subsigning.] [L. subsignare; sub under + signare to mark: cf. F. soussigner. See Sign.] To sign beneath; to subscribe. [R.] Camden.

subsignation.c: Subsignation Sub`sig*na"tion (?), n. [L. subsignatio.] The act of writing the name under something, as for attestation. [R.] Shelton.

subsist.c: Subsist Sub*sist" (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Subsisted; p. pr. & vb. n. Subsisting.] [L. subsistere to stand still, stay, remain alive; sub under + sistere to stand, to cause to stand, from stare to stand: cf. F. subsister. See Stand.] 1. To be; to have existence; to inhere.
Subsist Sub*sist", v. t. To support with provisions; to feed; to maintain; as, to subsist one's family.

subsistence.c: Subsistence Sub*sist"ence (?), n. [Cf. F. subsistance, L. subsistentia.] 1. Real being; existence.

Subsistence Department Sub*sist"ence De*part"ment. (Mil.) A staff department of the United States army charged, under the supervision of the Chief of Staff, with the purchasing and issuing to the army of such supplies as make up the ration. It also supplies, for authorized sales, certain articles of food and other minor stores. It is commanded by any officer of the rank of brigadier general, called commissary general, and the department is popularly called the Commissary Department.

subsistent.c: Subsistent Sub*sist"ent (?), a. [L. subsistens, p. pr. See Subsist.] 1. Having real being; as, a subsistent spirit.

subsizar.c: Subsizar Sub*si"zar (?), n. An under sizar; a student of lower rank than a sizar. [Cambridge Univ. Eng.]

subsoil.c: Subsoil Sub"soil` (?), n. The bed, or stratum, of earth which lies immediately beneath the surface soil.
Subsoil Sub"soil`, v. t. To turn up the subsoil of.

subsolary.c: Subsolary Sub*so"la*ry (?), a. Being under the sun; hence, terrestrial; earthly; mundane. [R.]

subspecies.c: Subspecies Sub*spe"cies (?), n. A group somewhat lessdistinct than speciesusually are, but based on characters more important than those which characterize ordinary varieties; often, a geographical variety or race.

subsphenoidal.c: Subsphenoidal Sub`sphe*noid"al (?), a. (Anat.) Situated under, or on the ventral side of, the body of the sphenoid bone.

subspherical.c: Subspherical Sub*spher"ic*al (?), a. Nearly spherical; having a figure resembling that of a sphere.

subspinous.c: Subspinous Sub*spi"nous (?), a. (a) (Anat.) Subvertebral. (b) (Med.) Situated beneath a spinous process, as that of the scapula; as, subspinous dislocation of the humerus.

substance.c: Substance Sub"stance (?), n. [F., fr. L. substantia, fr. substare to be under or present, to stand firm; sub under + stare to stand. See Stand.] 1. That which underlies all outward manifestations; substratum; the permanent subject or cause of phenomena, whether material or spiritual; that in which properties inhere; that which is real, in distinction from that which is apparent; the abiding part of any existence, in distinction from any accident; that which constitutes anything what it is; real or existing essence.
Substance Sub"stance, v. t. To furnish or endow with substance; to supply property to; to make rich. [Obs.]

substanceless.c: Substanceless Sub"stance*less, a. Having no substance; unsubstantial. [R.] Coleridge.

substant.c: Substant Sub"stant (?), a. [L. substans, -antis, p. pr. of substare to be firm.] Substantial; firm. [R.] “[The glacier's] substant ice.” The Century.

substantial.c: Substantial Sub*stan"tial (?), a. [F. substantiel, L. substantialis.] 1. Belonging to substance; actually existing; real; as, substantial life. Milton.

substantiality.c: Substantiality Sub*stan`ti*al"i*ty (?), n. The quality or state of being substantial; corporiety; materiality.

substantialize.c: Substantialize Sub*stan"tial*ize (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Substantialized (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Substantializing (?).] To make substantial.

substantially.c: Substantially Sub*stan"tial*ly, adv. In a substantial manner; in substance; essentially.

substantialness.c: Substantialness Sub*stan"tial*ness, n. The quality or state of being substantial; as, the substantialness of a wall or column.

substantials.c: Substantials Sub*stan"tials (?), n. pl. Essential parts. Ayliffe.

substantiate.c: Substantiate Sub*stan"ti*ate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Substantiated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Substantiating.] 1. To make to exist; to make real. Ayliffe.

substantiation.c: Substantiation Sub*stan`ti*a"tion (?), n. The act of substantiating or proving; evidence; proof.

substantival.c: Substantival Sub`stan*ti"val (?), a. Of or pertaining to a substantive; of the nature of substantive. -- Sub`stan*ti"val*ly, adv.

substantive.c: Substantive Sub"stan*tive (?), a. [L. substantivus: cf. F. substantif.] 1. Betokening or expressing existence; as, the substantive verb, that is, the verb to be.

Substantive Sub"stan*tive, n. [Cf. F. substantif.] (Gram.) A noun or name; the part of speech which designates something that exists, or some object of thought, either material or immaterial; as, the words man, horse, city, goodness, excellence, are substantives.
Substantive Sub"stan*tive, v. t. To substantivize. [R.] Cudworth.

substantively.c: Substantively Sub"stan*tive*ly, adv. 1. In a substantive manner; in substance; essentially.

substantiveness.c: Substantiveness Sub"stan*tive*ness, n. The quality or state of being substantive.

substantivize.c: Substantivize Sub"stan*tiv*ize (?), v. t. To convert into a substantive; as, to substantivize an adjective. Fitzed. Hall.

substituent.c: Substituent Sub*stit"u*ent (?), n. [L. substituens, p. pr. See Substitute.] (Chem.) Any atom, group, or radical substituted for another, or entering a molecule in place of some other part which is removed.

substitute.c: Substitute Sub"stit"ute (?), n. [L. substitutus, p. p. of substituere to put under, put in the place of; sub under + statuere to put, place: cf. F. substitut. See Statute.] One who, or that which, is substituted or put in the place of another; one who acts for another; that which stands in lieu of something else; specifically (Mil.), a person who enlists for military service in the place of a conscript or drafted man.
Substitute Sub"stit"ute (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Substituted (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Substituting (?).] [See Substitute, n.] To put in the place of another person or thing; to exchange.

substituted.c: Substituted Sub"stit"uted (?), a. 1. Exchanged; put in the place of another.

substitution.c: Substitution Sub`sti*tu"tion (?), n. [L. substitutio: cf. F. substitution.] 1. The act of substituting or putting one person or thing in the place of another; as, the substitution of an agent, attorney, or representative to act for one in his absense; the substitution of bank notes for gold and silver as a circulating medium.

substitutional.c: Substitutional Sub`sti*tu"tion*al (?), a. Of or pertaining to substitution; standing in the place of another; substituted. -- Sub`sti*tu"tion*al*ly, adv.

substitutionary.c: Substitutionary Sub`sti*tu"tion*a*ry (?), a. Of or pertaining to substitution; substitutional.

substitutive.c: Substitutive Sub"sti*tu`tive (?), a. [Cf. F. substitutif, L. substitutivus conditional.] Tending to afford or furnish a substitute; making substitution; capable of being substituted. Bp. Wilkins.

substract.c: Substract Sub*stract" (?), v. t. [F. suostraire; L. subtus below (from sub under) + trahere to draw. See Substract.] To subtract; to withdraw. [Obs.] Barrow.

substraction.c: Substraction Sub*strac"tion (?), n. [OF. substraction, F. soustraction. See Subtract.] 1. Subtraction; deduction. [Obs.]

substrate.c: Substrate Sub"strate, a. Having very slight furrows. [R.]
Substrate Sub*strate" (?), v. t. [L. substratus, p. p. of substrahere. See Substratum.] To strew or lay under anything. [Obs.]

substratum.c: Substratum Sub*stra"tum (?), n.; pl. Substrata (#). [L. substratus, p. p. of substernere to strew under; sub under + sternere to strew. See Stratum.] 1. That which is laid or spread under; that which underlies something, as a layer of earth lying under another; specifically (Agric.), the subsoil.

substruct.c: Substruct Sub*struct" (?), v. t. [See Substruction.] To build beneath something; to lay as the foundation. [R.]

substruction.c: Substruction Sub*struc"tion (?), n. [L. substructio, fr. substruere, substructum, to build beneath; sub under + struere to build.] (Arch.) Underbuilding; the foundation, or any preliminary structure intended to raise the lower floor or basement of a building above the natural level of the ground.

substructure.c: Substructure Sub*struc"ture (?), n. [Pref. sub- + structure.] 1. (Arch.) Same as Substruction.

substylar.c: Substylar Sub*sty"lar (?), a. Pertaining to the substyle.

substyle.c: Substyle Sub"style` (?), n. (Dialing) A right line on which the style, or gnomon, of a dial is erected; being the common section of the face of the dial and a plane perpendicular to it passing through the style. [Written also substile.] Hutton.

subsulphate.c: Subsulphate Sub*sul"phate (?), n. (Chem.) A sulphate with an excess of the base.
